It cannot be only potential, because something with no actual existence cannot be described at all—not as potential, not as actual.99 So the subject must exist in actuality.

It could be actual in every respect, or actual in one respect and potential in another. The first is impossible. Something actual in every respect is separate from matter and has no connection to it. Nothing like that can move from potentiality to actuality. It already has everything it could possibly have. Anything that can move still seeks something it does not yet have, so it cannot be fully actual. Anything fully actual cannot seek a goal through motion. Motion also comes to a thing as a feature, and the subject of any such feature must have some potentiality. A purely separate being has none.

The subject of motion must therefore be a substance whose identity includes both actuality and potentiality. That is the body: its form makes it actual, while its matter remains potential.

Motion cannot be the form that makes a kind of body what it is, for several reasons. First, motion is an accident, and one of the weakest kinds of being. It is the state of being moved, a relation; it is not the power by which a thing moves. So it cannot make a substance into the kind of thing it is. A thing cannot be made complete by something less complete than itself. Second, the subject of motion is a body that already exists. A completely general, undefined body exists only in the mind; outside the mind, every body already belongs to a particular kind.100 Third, kinds of motion do not exist as fixed, complete kinds in their own right. A thing that exists in a settled, actual form does not give another actual thing its kind.101 Fourth, if motion were part of what makes a body a particular kind, that kind would disappear whenever the body rested or any part of its motion ended. The kind would then be only potential and would need something stable and actual to carry it. So motion comes to a body only after the body already has its kind.

This is the strongest account so far. Later, we will bring more light to the question.

XIX. An Eastern insight

Motion is a thing's being moved, its renewal and passing away. Its immediate cause cannot be something whose existence is entirely fixed, or the parts of motion would never pass away.102 The agent that directly brings about motion must itself be renewed and moving. Motion must belong to it by its very existence. Anything whose existence necessarily includes motion still has a nature distinct from motion, but motion cannot be separated from that nature. Its motion is not something made separately from its existence. It follows from what it is.

This makes motion an essential feature of the immediate mover's existence, not something added to it later.103 The immediate source of motion has a nature that remains the same, but an existence that is renewed.104 As we will see, the immediate source of motion in every kind of body is its nature: a substance that makes the body the kind of body it is.105 Nature is the body's first completion, in the sense that it is what makes a natural body an actual, existing body.

So every body is renewed in its existence, even though its nature remains the same. This also shows that the material world comes to be in time: bodily substances and all their qualities, both those of the heavenly spheres and those of bodies made from the elements.106

What we said in the previous chapter—that the subject of motion must be stable—is true if “subject” means the thing's nature, which motion belongs to as a feature; or if we mean motions that are not essential to the thing's existence, such as moving from place to place, changing in quality, or growing.107 The same is true of the claim that the subject of motion includes both what is actual and what is potential, though this needs explanation. If motion belongs to the body as a feature, then the subject is made up of what is actual and remains through the motion,108 and what is potential and moving.109 Each part of motion appears and disappears while the body's nature remains. If, instead, the relation between motion and its subject is a matter of how the mind analyzes them, as with essential features,110 then the receiver and the agent are one thing, and actuality and potentiality are two sides of one reality.

Here is the deeper point. Matter is potentiality and readiness; natural form comes to be anew, as we will explain. At every instant, matter is ready for a different form. Each new form has matter that is potential for it, and each form makes the matter actual. Since actuality comes before potentiality, this does not form a vicious circle. The forms are different in their nature, and matter changes its readiness with them. The matter of the elements is shared and remains through the changes; without something that remains, there would be no subject of motion.111

Because simple bodies have forms that look alike, people have thought there is one form that stays with them. But their forms are not one and the same in number. They are one in kind and meaning, while continually following one another without a break. These are not separate, disconnected things. The result is one continuous, flowing existence. From its imagined boundaries, the mind draws out general natures such as human, animal, and plant.112

XX. Nature is the immediate source of motion in every moving thing

Nature is the immediate source of motion in every moving thing, whether the motion is natural, forced, or voluntary. In natural motion, this is clear: nature causes it. In forced motion, the force applied from outside only prepares the way; it is a cause in an indirect sense. That is why the forced motion can continue after the force has stopped. Besides, every outside force must ultimately lead back to nature or to the will.113

In voluntary motion, the soul moves the body by using nature. Many people who study these questions say that the soul is the immediate cause of motions that come from the will. But the closer cause, once imagination, will, and desire are present, is the power that moves the muscles, tendons, and ligaments. That power is the very nature of those body parts and tools. The soul sends it into them so that it can manage the body through them.

We know by direct experience, even before we reason it out, that whatever inclines a body or turns it from one place or state to another must be an active power within it. This power is called nature. So the immediate source of bodily motion is a substantial power within the body. All accidental features depend on the form that makes a thing what it is, and that form is its nature. This is why philosophers define nature as the first source of a thing's own motion and rest, not of motion or rest that happens to it from outside. They have also shown that anything that can be pushed or drawn from outside must have a natural tendency of its own.114 So the direct source of every motion is nature.

As we have seen, the thing that directly causes motion has a flowing, renewed existence. If it did not, it could not produce natural motions: something changing cannot come from something entirely unchanged. Philosophers such as Avicenna agree that nature cannot cause motion unless it changes. But they say that some outside change must affect it. In natural motion, for example, the moving thing keeps getting nearer to or farther from its goal. In forced motion, other states keep changing. In voluntary motion, particular wishes and desires arise in the soul as the reasons for acting change.

I say that this does not solve the problem. All these changes must in the end lead back to nature. We have already seen that forced motion leads back to nature and that the soul can move the body only by using nature. So all these renewals depend on nature and are caused by it. Nature itself must therefore be renewed.

Someone might reply that philosophers have shown how change, such as motion, can come from something fixed, such as nature. For each motion, they set out two linked sequences. One is the sequence of the motion itself. The other is a sequence of changing states in nature, such as the body's successive degrees of nearness to its goal. They say that each part of one sequence causes a part of the other, and is also caused by it in another respect. This, they argue, is not a vicious circle, as in the discussion of how something that begins can be connected to what is eternal.115

I say that this account does not explain how a changing thing comes from something fixed, or how something that begins is connected to what is eternal. The question is about the cause that actually produces motion, not the cause that merely prepares for it. Every effect needs a cause that brings it about. The two sequences may explain what sets the stages of a motion in order, but our question is what produces the motion itself. Motion is an effect, so it must have a cause that produces it and is always joined to it. If each sequence caused the other, each would have to come before itself.

The only way out is to accept that nature is a flowing substance. Its changing reality arises between matter, whose character is to be potential and to pass away, and a pure agent, whose role is to give and pour forth existence. The agent continually brings forth something new in matter, and what was there passes away; then the agent replaces it without a break.

Anyone who looks closely at both sequences together will see that they both come after nature already exists. This brings us back to the same question: if the starting point is fixed, how did these two sequences arise? It is like the argument against an endless chain of causes. If every link except the last is only a middle link, and there is no first link, where did the chain come from? Here too, if no being has renewal and passing away as part of its very nature, where did all the changing things come from, whether there is one sequence or many? And the successive degrees of nearness and distance that were treated as a second sequence are not separate from motion itself. Their renewal is motion, not something added to it.

So the changing things depend on something whose very reality flows and changes. That can only be nature. Separate intellects are beyond change and coming to be. The soul, considered in its intellectual nature, is also beyond change; in its connection with the body, however, it is nature itself, as we will explain later. Accidental features depend for their existence on substantial forms. Motion itself is not a thing that changes; it is the renewal and change of a thing. It is the relation of renewal, not something that causes renewal.116

XXI. How the changing is connected to the unchanging

Here, “actuality” means what exists now, and “potentiality” means what can exist or become real.

Someone may ask:117 if every renewed thing is preceded by another renewed thing that causes it to be renewed, then the same question applies to the cause's renewal, and to the renewal of that cause's cause. This leads either to an endless chain, a circle, or change in the First Source—exalted far above that.

Our answer is this. If renewal is not part of a thing's own nature, then it needs something to renew it. But if renewal is part of its nature, it does not need a separate maker to make it renewed. It needs a maker to bring the thing itself into being through a simple act, not through a second act that comes between the maker and what is made. There is no doubt that something exists whose very nature requires renewal and flow. We call it nature; others call it motion and time.

Everything has some stability and some actuality. What flows from the maker is the particular kind of stability and actuality that belongs to it. If a thing's stability consists in being renewed, and its actuality consists in having a capacity, then the First Source gives it that kind of stability and actuality. Every thing also has some kind of unity, which goes with existence and is one with it.

If a thing's unity is the unity of many things that are potential or actual, then the One gives it a unity that gathers multiplicity in one of these two ways. Of all existing things, nature is the one whose stability is renewal. Matter is the one whose actuality is potentiality. Number is the one whose unity is actual multiplicity. A body and what is in it have a unity that is the potential for multiplicity.

So nature, in its stable aspect, is connected to the unchanging Source. In its renewed aspect, it is the link through which renewed things and new events come about. In the same way, matter, insofar as it has some actuality, comes from the active Source when form is joined to it. But insofar as it is potential and possible, matter is what allows bodily things to begin, pass away, and perish. These two substances—nature and matter—bring about change and passing away in bodily things through their own renewal and passing away. They connect what is eternal with what begins, and resolve a problem that has long puzzled careful thinkers.

XXII. How motion relates to the basic kinds of being

When we say that motion occurs “in” a category—a basic kind of being, such as substance, quality, or quantity—there are four possible meanings. First, the category might be the true subject of motion.118 Second, the subject might be a substance, with the category acting as the link between it and motion. Third, the category might be the general kind to which motion belongs. Fourth, the substance might gradually change from one kind or class in that category to another. The fourth is the right account; the others are not.119

The first account is wrong. When something grows blacker, this does not mean that the blackness itself becomes more intense. If the blackness stayed exactly as it was, with no new feature, it would not have grown more intense. If a new feature appeared while the old blackness remained as it was, then the change would be in its features, not in the blackness itself.120 But we are asking about a change in the blackness itself. If the old blackness does not remain when the thing grows blacker, it has not grown more intense; it has ended, and another blackness has taken its place. That would not be motion. So the subject of this motion is not the blackness itself, but the thing that has blackness. As it grows blacker, it gradually changes from one kind or class to another.

The same applies to motion in size. When a thing grows, either the same amount remains throughout the whole change, or it does not. If the same amount remains, then the added size must either overlap with it or be joined to it from outside. Overlap is impossible; and even if it could happen, the size would not have increased. Joining another amount from outside also does not work, because it would be like joining one line to another: neither line gets any longer. Nor does their sum become larger than it was before.121 If the first amount does not remain as the thing grows, then it is not the subject of the change. The subject is what carries it—prime matter, either alone or together with some general amount, as we hold. In that case, the body contains a succession of ever-larger amounts, with no final number of them in principle.

When Fakhr al-Din al-Razi read the claim that growing blacker takes blackness out of its kind, he thought this meant that blackness changes into something that is not black.122 In one of his books, he says that when blackness grows stronger, it leaves its kind. At every instant, the subject has one simple quality. But people call all the shades close to black “black” and all those close to white “white.” In strict terms, he says, there is only one pure black, an obscure limit, and likewise one pure white. The middle shades are mixtures. We call them black or white according to which limit they are closer to, since our senses cannot tell them apart. He says this is all correct, but that the same account must also apply to changes in size.

I say that this account is clearly mistaken to anyone familiar with these questions. I do not know which shade of black he counts as black, if all the others are not black.123 Each shade exists as an actual quality when it is at rest. If it is not black, what is it?

He also objects that if a moving thing has a different amount at every instant, and no one amount lasts through two times, then the instants must follow one another without any time between them. He says that the answer found in the notes—that these kinds exist only potentially—is not enough.124 If the kinds do not exist outside the mind, then the body's change in quality does not exist outside the mind either; the body would only be capable of changing, not actually changing. But if the kinds do exist, and each differs in kind from the others and exists for only one instant, then they follow one another with no time between them. That brings back the problem. We need a clearer answer, and we will return to it.

The blackness that exists while a thing is changing is one continuous reality between its limits. It lasts through the whole time of the change. At the same time, the mind can distinguish from it a different kind of blackness at each instant. These momentary kinds exist only as close potentialities. Existence comes before kind, as we have already learned. So the blackness as a whole exists in actuality, and the mind can distinguish within it many kinds that would exist at different instants. There is no problem in this. Indeed, this continuous blackness has a stronger existence than the momentary kinds, since it can serve as the reality of many kinds. It is like an animal, whose one existence includes all the features found separately in plants. A very deep black likewise includes, in one reality, what is found in weaker blacks.

The same is true of size. Razi's own answer is that, as blackness grows stronger, the subject changes all at once through a series of states, each of which lasts for a very short time—too short for the senses to notice. People therefore think that it has a new state at every instant. He gives the same account for changes in size. In the end, this means that there is no real motion in either category.125

I say this does not solve the problem. The same difficulty arises for motion in place and position, unless we accept sudden jumps, which our senses also show do not happen.126 So the first account is false. The second account is false for the same reason: if a thing cannot be the subject of an accidental feature—a feature that can change while the thing itself remains what it is—it cannot be the link through which that feature belongs to a subject. The only exception would be a different meaning of “link”: a general nature that serves as the link between the subject and motion, as we have described for motion in size.

Some people hold the third account: a category is the general kind of motion. They say there is a settled and a flowing kind of place, and the flowing kind is motion from place to place; there is a settled and a flowing kind of quality, and the flowing kind is change of quality; and there is a settled and a flowing kind of size, and the flowing kind is growth or decline. On this view, the flowing kind in each category is motion. This is not correct. Motion is the renewal of a thing, not a thing that is renewed—just as rest is a thing's settling, not a thing that is settled. Still, there is a point to consider: motion belongs to a flowing individual differently from the way an accident belongs to a subject that exists on its own. Motion is an analytical feature of the flowing individual. It belongs to it as a part belongs to a whole kind, and not as an added feature. Rest belongs to a settled individual in the same way. So it is right to say that quality has both settled individuals and flowing individuals, and that a flowing quality is motion, in the sense that the quality's existence is itself motion.127

Those who hold this view disagree about how the flowing and settled kinds differ.128 Some say that they differ in kind, because flow belongs to the nature of what is flowing. Others say they differ only by added features, as when one line is longer than another. Both arguments fail. The first fails because whiteness is part of what it is to be white, but that does not mean white things and black things must differ by a feature that defines their kind.129 The second fails because not every addition is merely an added feature: adding a defining feature or another unit can make a new kind. We need to know how defining features differ from added features that do not change kind.

Once the first three accounts are rejected, the fourth remains. Motion in a category means that its subject gradually changes from one kind to another, or from one class to another, rather than changing all at once.130

XXIII. Which categories can undergo motion, and which cannot?

Because motion has a weak kind of existence, it depends on six things: an agent, a receiver, what changes, what it changes from, what it changes toward, and time. Its relation to the receiver is clear. We have already discussed two ways it can relate to the agent. In one, the agent and receiver differ in nature, as in the categories of acting and being acted on. In the other, they do not differ in nature, as with features that belong necessarily to a thing's nature.

The starting point and end point of motion can be worked out from the definition of motion:131 motion is the continuous arrival at the limits of what is possible. Sometimes the beginning and end are opposites. Sometimes they are different states that cannot exist together. Sometimes the starting and ending states each last for a time, as in motion that stops and starts. At other times, as with the celestial spheres, they do not. One philosopher says that in a sphere's motion the beginning and end may be the same. He means that the beginning, considered as the point from which motion starts, is also its end, considered as the point toward which it moves.

That is not correct. When a sphere returns to the same position in its daily motion, its position at sunrise is not the same individual position as it was the evening before.132 In itself, the beginning is different from the end. We need to distinguish them only when comparing what came before with what comes after, as we do with every instant: each instant begins one thing and ends another. Calling the limits of a sphere's positional motion “points” is only a loose way of speaking.133 In fact, they are momentary positions whose existence is potential, though close to actual.

The relation of motion to what changes in it is even closer. Some have therefore said that motion is the very category in which it occurs. That is not always right.134 As we have said, motion is the renewal of that category.135 Motion itself is the category of being acted on when considered in relation to the receiver, and the category of acting when considered in relation to the agent.136137 For this reason, motion cannot occur in either of these two categories. Motion means leaving a state and taking on another, so it must be a departure from a settled state. If it occurred in a state that was itself unsettled, it would not leave that state; it would sink further into it.138

In general, to say that motion occurs in a category means that, at every instant, the moving thing has a different individual of that category. So the category in which motion occurs must have momentary individuals that exist potentially. The categories of acting and being acted on have no such momentary individuals.139 For example, if there were motion in the act of heating, then while the body was heating it would also be cooling. But it has not left the heating state; it is still heating. If it were leaving the act of heating, then the motion would be in some category other than being acted on. The same reasoning shows that there cannot be motion in the category of “when,” which concerns time.

Change can occur in relation, but relation does not exist on its own. It depends on the existence of the two things it relates. So there is no motion in relation in itself, as we have already explained. The category of having or possessing something changes only because the place of what is worn or held changes. That leaves, according to most philosophers, four categories in which motion can occur. We say there are five: substance, quality, quantity, place, and position. Rest is the opposite of motion—either as one opposite is to another, or as absence is to a capacity.140 This absence can still be described by reference to what is present. A body at rest, though able to move, has a feature that sets it apart from other things. If the feature were not there, it would not leave when the body began to move. So the body's capacity for motion has a cause and a receiver; rest is not a bare absence, like a person's lack of horns. A person's inability to walk, by contrast, is the absence of a capacity and occurs when the cause of walking is missing. In this case, the absence has a kind of existence and a cause, which is also the cause of the body's potential to move.

From this we can see that the cause of motion includes an element of absence. This absence is not just the absence of anything at all. It is the absence of something from a particular thing, in a particular state: the thing's being only potential.

XXIV. How motion occurs in each of the five categories

Motion in place is clear. So is motion in position, as when a sphere turns around its own center. A body that has no surrounding place—such as the outermost celestial body, which, according to the philosophers, has no empty or filled space around it—can only move in position when it rotates on its axis.141 A body that does occupy a place either moves as a whole away from the whole of its place, or its whole remains in the whole place while its parts move away from the corresponding parts of that place. In the latter case, the relation of its parts to the parts of the place has changed. In either case, its position in its place has changed through its rotation.

But the category in which motion occurs must allow degrees of increase and completion.142 This may not seem clear in place and position, but it is true of both.143 Each can increase or decrease. Motion in quality is a thing's growing stronger or weaker.

As we have said many times, motion is a thing's passage from potentiality to actuality. It is not the thing that brings about that passage. That is why philosophers say that when something grows blacker, it is not a blackness that becomes more intense; rather, the subject grows more fully black.144 The subject does not contain two blacknesses—one original and lasting, and another added on top of it. Two like things cannot occupy the same subject. Instead, at each stage it has a different degree of blackness. This continuous increase is the motion, not the blackness itself.

If the same blackness were there at every stage and simply became greater, then it would have to be either the very same blackness with an added degree, or no longer the same blackness. In the second case, it makes no sense to say that what has ceased to exist has grown stronger. The moving subject must have something that remains. But if the blackness itself remains unchanged, then it is not a flowing quality, as some people think. So it follows that at every instant the blackness has a different degree. When blackness grows stronger, it must therefore leave its first kind. It cannot be one unchanging quality with more added to it; each of its stages is a simple quality of its own.

I say that if we imagine the tip of a cone moving across a surface, there is one point that lasts throughout the motion. This gives us an example of motion considered as being between its limits. There are also other points that this single moving point coincides with, one after another, as it reaches the different positions along its path. In the same way, each motion has something like a flowing point that continues, and a series of imagined points marking where the moving thing is at each stage. So when blackness grows stronger, we can say there is something like a lasting base of blackness, with a weak unity, and many further degrees, each containing that basic blackness with an added degree. But these are distinct only in the mind, not as separate things outside it.145 This shows that blackness has one personal identity from the beginning of its growth to its end, and becomes more complete at every moment. The claim that it passes from one kind to another, with a different kind at every stage, does not conflict with this. These kinds exist and differ only potentially, in the mind, not as separate realities outside it.

Some have said that this shows the soul is not merely a bodily temperament. Temperament is a flowing, renewed reality. Between any two of its limits, it contains infinitely many kinds in potential, though these kinds are not actually distinct from one another—just as points and parts of a distance are not actually separate.146 Yet everyone feels in themselves one personal reality that does not change, even though it remains one through a continuous span of time until death.

I say that this speaker seems to have sensed something of the soul's renewal when he said that it remains one by continuity until the end of life. A continuous existence through time cannot avoid change within the thing that continues; we will explain this later. Besides, we do not need this argument to show that the soul is different from bodily temperament. Conclusive proofs already establish that.

1. Note and clarification

As we have suggested, blackness, from the start of its increase to its end, has one continuous identity. Yet at every imagined instant it has a different kind of quality from the one before and after. According to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, the degrees of growth in blackness and heat are different kinds. If we accept their view, three conclusions follow.

First, as blackness grows stronger, infinitely many kinds exist in one continuous reality. Since they accept that one continuous thing has one existence, this shows that existence is real outside the mind and distinct from what a thing is. Existence is what makes things real; the mind draws a general meaning of “what a thing is” from each existence, and that meaning belongs to and is united with the existence in a certain way. If what a thing is were real in itself, and existence were only an idea drawn from it, as later philosophers have argued, then infinitely many kinds would exist separately in actuality, between two limits. This would lead to absurd results, like an actual series of indivisible parts.147

Second, since one personal blackness exists through its growth or weakening, it follows that one and the same individual can belong to many kinds. As its existence becomes more complete or less complete, the meanings that define its kind also change. This is a kind of transformation. It is possible because existence is the reality, and what a thing is follows from it like a shadow follows light. The same can therefore happen in substance.

Third, this one growing existence remains continuous, but it is also renewed and can be divided in thought into an earlier and a later stage. Some of its stages have passed away, some have just come to be, and others are still to come. Each connected part comes into being at a certain time and is absent at another. This does not mean that the whole contains indivisible parts, as some people claim; that is impossible. The continuous, lasting existence is itself the continuous, flowing existence, and it is also each of its connected parts and momentary stages. It has a unity that runs through a series of moments, because it gathers them as potentialities close to actuality. So we can rightly call it one, many, lasting from the start of a change to its end, and renewed at every moment. How remarkable this kind of existence is, and how little people notice it!148 Our own existence has the same character, though people overlook this too. It takes a subtle mind and clear insight to see that what remains and what passes away are one and the same thing. Let us now return to the proof that motion occurs in substance.

You know that one existence can have different states and stages; it can become more complete or less complete. Those who accept growth and decline in quality and increase and decrease in quantity accept that one motion is a single individual, occurring over one continuous path, in one individual subject. They argue that the subject's being in the middle between a definite starting point and end point is not an undefined state or kind. It is a particular state, fixed by its particular agent and receiver and by the other things around it. The motion that is traced out is also one continuous whole, with no actual parts, though it has parts and limits potentially.

We say that if such an account is allowed for kinds of quantity and quality, then it should also be allowed for substantial form. A substantial form could grow more complete in its own nature, with one personal existence that remains continuous while its degree of unity and substantial being changes. At each imagined instant, the mind could draw from it the meaning of another kind, though those kinds would exist only potentially.

Avicenna and others give an argument against this kind of growth in substance.149 They say: if there were motion and growth or decline in substance, then either the kind would remain in the middle of the change or it would not. If the kind remained, the substantial form would not change in itself, but only in an added feature; then the change would be a change of quality, not a change in substance. But if the substance did not remain the same kind as it grew, each stage would create a new substance. The same would happen at every imagined instant, so between any two substances there would be infinitely many kinds existing in actuality. This is impossible in substance. It is possible in blackness or heat only because the body already exists; in a bodily substance, there would be no actual subject on which substantial motion could occur. That is their argument.

I say their argument assumes what it must prove, and confuses what a thing is with its existence. It also mistakes what exists potentially for what exists in actuality. When they ask whether the kind remains in the middle of a change, if they mean whether the same individual existence remains, we answer yes, as explained above. One continuous, gradual existence through time is one thing. Growth is greater completion within that existence; decline is the opposite.

If instead they mean whether the specific kind first drawn from that existence remains with all the qualities it had at the start, then we answer no. But that does not mean a new substance—or a new existence—has come into being. It means that another essential feature has appeared, one that was close to actuality in the thing's potential nature. The features that belong to a substance change as its existence becomes more or less complete.150 This does not produce infinitely many kinds that exist separately in actuality. There is one personal, continuous existence, with infinitely many potential limits at the different instants we imagine within its duration. So infinitely many kinds exist in meaning and potential, not as actual, separate existences.

There is no real difference between growth in quality, which is called change of quality; growth in quantity, which is called growth; and growth in substance, which is called coming to be. Each is a gradual completion and motion in the way a thing exists, whether the moving reality is quantity, quality, or substance. To say that the first two are possible but the last impossible is an unsupported assumption. The existence of a thing is primary; what it is follows from its existence, as we have explained many times.

The subject of any motion must remain through its own existence and identity.151 But for a bodily subject to remain the same, it is enough that matter persists while it takes on some form, quality, and quantity.152 Each of these may change in its particular details.153 Consider the claim, accepted by Avicenna and other philosophers, that one matter can take on one form after another while remaining the same matter. Its continuing identity comes from the general fact that it has some form, and from a single separate intellect that gives it form. The philosophers say it is not impossible for matter to receive a new form at every moment in place of the former one, while its identity continues through some form or other. Each individual form comes from that matter.

If that is possible for bodily nature itself—the kind of body that is matter, not a general kind predicated of different bodies—then it should also be possible for particular forms whose matter is this natural body.154155156 This also resolves a problem about motion in quantity that later philosophers struggled to solve. The Illuminationist philosopher and his followers even denied that it exists, because they said that adding one amount to another destroys the first amount.157

In the same way, they said that separating one part of an amount from a continuous whole destroys that whole. So the subject of this motion does not remain. Avicenna also found this difficult and admitted that he could not prove there is a stable subject for growth in plants, or even in animals.158 In one letter to a student who asked about this, he wrote:

“A stable thing in animals may be easier to explain. I have explored the question deeply in my Eastern Philosophy, first by raising doubts and then by seeking a solution. In plants, the explanation is harder. If nothing remains stable, then the plant's identity is not by kind but by number. But how can it be one by number if its duration, unlike a stable thing, is divisible without end in potential?159 No part of the duration is more important than another. How could an infinite number of individuals keep appearing during a limited time?

“Perhaps the element is what stays the same. But how can it be stable if quantity does not renew itself on one element, but one element replaces another through nourishment? Perhaps one form can take on several matters. But how could one form be the form of several different matters? Or perhaps one form remains in one matter, which is more likely, until the individual ceases to exist.160 But how can that be, when the parts of a growing plant increase equally? Each similar part becomes larger than before. The power is spread through all of them, and no one part has a stronger claim than another to be the original form. Perhaps the part that existed first is the original and remains,161 but its relation to what came before is like the relation of the later part to what comes after. Perhaps the plant that we think is one is not really one individual by number: every part added to it is a new individual, joined to the first by continuity.162 Or perhaps the first part is the original, and the later parts flow from it as likenesses;163 when the original ceases, they cease too, but not the other way around.164 This might be true of animals, or of most animals, but not of plants, since plants do not divide into parts that can each live on their own.165

“Perhaps animals and plants have an unmixed source of their own. But this does not fit the view that seems right to me.166 Or perhaps parts that look alike to the senses differ in their true nature and substance.167 The first matter might divide when new things come to be, without losing its continuity, and the original source would remain within it. Or perhaps a plant is not one individual at all, except during the period when its growth stops, as it must at some point. These are knots and snares. If the mind examines them and follows their consequences, I hope it will find a way, by God's help, toward the truth. As for the view held by most thinkers, we should try, as I have done, to help one another understand the truth and not lose hope in God's mercy.”

From this we can see that Avicenna was unsure about the question. The same student, or another, later wrote to him: “If the master would complete his explanation of what stays the same in animals other than humans, and in plants, that would be a great kindness.” Avicenna replied only, “If I can.” So this was a question he could not settle.

Our answer is that the subject of this motion is the particular body, not the particular amount. A body's identity includes some amount across the range from one limit of motion to the other, as physicians say of a person's bodily temperament. Motion occurs in the particular amounts and their degrees. What remains from beginning to end is not the same as what changes. Separation and joining destroy only an imagined continuous amount taken without its natural matter,168 or a bare body stripped of its other forms. In its existence as body alone, it has a definite amount. But a natural body of a particular kind, made up of bodily nature and other forms, keeps its kind through a definite form that gives it its final, defining feature, together with some bodily nature that corresponds to its nearest general kind. A general kind is considered undefined, while the defining feature makes it definite. So the changing parts of the general kind and matter do not destroy the subject as long as its form remains.169 The claim that adding one amount to another destroys the first is true only when both amounts exist separately in actuality. It does not apply when they are potential parts of one gradual change.

XXV. A clearer account of motion in quantity

Anything made up of several meanings is complete through what acts as its final defining feature. Its identity remains as long as that feature remains definite. The other parts of its definition—its general kinds and other defining features, which follow from its existence and make up its essence—do not have to remain in one particular form. They may change without destroying its identity.170

For example, extension and the ability to occupy dimensions define a body as body in the sense in which it is matter. In itself, this is a distinct kind of thing with a potential similar to prime matter: it is the potential for extension and its opposite. It is completed by being actual. A change in it changes the body simply as body. In the same way, the power of growth defines a growing body, and completes its nature. Its completion does not come from being a body alone; its bodily nature is the source of its power and carries its potential. So changes among individual bodies do not change the identity of the growing substance. Bodily nature belongs to it in a general, unrestricted way, not as one fixed, particular body.

The same is true of animals, whose nature is made up of growth and sensation. It is also true of things whose existence is made up of something like matter and something like form, such as a human being, considered as soul and body. When a plant grows or shrinks, the particular body it has as a body changes, but its particular identity as a growing substance remains. Considered as a wholly general natural body, it loses its particular body during growth and decline. Considered as a particular growing body, it does not lose its identity or its parts; its parts are nothing but bodily nature in whatever individual form it takes on, through one continuous existence.

An animal remains the same by the continued presence of its sensitive substance, its sensing soul. In old age, many plant-like powers disappear, yet the individual remains the same. Once this rule is clear, we can see that motion in quantity exists. In growth and decline, the subject is the body as a particular kind of body; in expansion and contraction, it is prime matter.171

We can also see that in the changing world of bodies, the substantial natures of things may change and pass away, while something like an original pillar remains. In complex natural things, this is the existence of the final defining feature. Its existence includes all the meanings that are called essential to this kind, even though those meanings also belong to other kinds as separate existences with different natures.172 The source of the final defining feature in a complete kind, such as a human being, has a level of existence that gathers together what appears separately in the kinds below it. The complete kind includes what is found in those kinds and adds something more.173

Since we have concluded that all bodily natures have essential motion, as the proofs will make clearer, we also conclude that every celestial or elemental nature has a stable intellectual substance, like an original pattern, and a substance whose existence changes. The stable intellectual substance relates to the bodily nature as completion relates to incompletion, and as an original relates to its derivative.174 God is nearer to us than anything near. These intellectual substances are like lights and rays from the first necessary Light. They are the forms in God's knowledge, not independent beings existing for themselves. Their existence depends on the Real, as the images in our minds depend on us.175 Philosophers say that a thing sensed, as sensed, exists in itself in the same way that it exists for the sensing substance; and that a thing understood, as understood, exists in itself in the same way that it exists for the understanding substance. This is a well-established point among the greatest philosophers, even if it troubles those whose understanding has not yet matured. Its explanation belongs elsewhere. Let us return to our subject.

Motion can occur in substantial forms just as it can in quantity and quality. The settled and flowing features of a body both help it remain the same in one respect, but not in another. In every motion, what remains is a shared reality between the two limits; what changes are the particular limits. The same is true of substantial form.176

When blackness grows stronger, it has one continuous, personal existence from beginning to end. It remains one through its bearer, and through the general meaning of blackness. Together, these make up the black body that undergoes this motion; anything that grows blacker must be a black body. Between the start and end are infinitely many potential limits, each different in meaning and kind according to the philosophers. The same is true of substantial form as it gradually becomes more complete: in one respect it is one lasting existence; in another, it is a continuous process. It has the same kind of potential limits.

The proof that the individual continues is the same in both cases. Each is one continuous existence through time. One continuous thing has one existence; and existence is the personal identity of a thing. If the motion were not one continuous whole, it would be right to say that the blackness does not remain as it grows stronger, and likewise that substantial form does not remain as it becomes more complete. But that is not so. The reason, as we have said, is that each thing's particular existence is primary and is definite in itself. It can have different stages and degrees while remaining one identity. At each stage it has general essential features, and different meanings can be drawn from it while remaining united with it.

To draw this out: motion is like a person whose soul is nature, just as time is like a person whose soul is the timeless order.177 In relation to the soul, and even to the intellect, nature is like a ray from the sun: it takes on its particular identity from them.

1. Discussion and conclusion

You might object to our claim that nature alone is the immediate cause of every motion and bodily act. If nature had to move the body's parts against their own natural tendency in order to obey the soul, the soul's commands should not tire the body. And if the soul's tendency and nature's tendency pull against one another, as in trembling or illness, we would expect a struggle between them.

Understand this clearly. The nature that is one of the soul's powers, and through which it carries out some actions, is not the same individual nature as the one found in the body's elements and organs.178 The soul's control and use of the first is natural to it, because that power comes from the soul itself. Its control of the second is indirect and forced. Fatigue, trembling, and similar conditions arise when the second nature sometimes resists the soul. So the body has two kinds of nature under the soul's command: one that obeys willingly, and one that obeys by force.179180

The soul also has two kinds of natural powers and helpers. One kind carries out natural actions, such as the basic powers behind motion in quality and quantity: attraction, expulsion, holding, digestion, turning food into the body's substance, growth, and reproduction. These serve the soul willingly and readily. The other kind carries out voluntary actions through the powers behind motion in place and position, such as writing, walking, sitting, and standing.181 These serve the soul unwillingly, under pressure. Both groups are armies in the world of motion, under the soul's command as animal soul.

As intellectual soul, it has other helpers from the world of awareness.182 All of them serve it willingly: the basic powers of imagination, estimation, and sensation, and the sources of animal and rational desire and choice. This nature that obeys the soul, together with its powers and branches, remains with the soul. The other nature passes away. Here lies a secret of bodily resurrection, which we will explain later, God willing.183

XXVI. Another proof that things change in their very substance

Nature within a body does not, by itself, produce the body's natural features.184 If it did, it would act on its own body without that body's mediation. But a bodily power cannot act apart from matter. The reason is that a thing must exist before it can bring anything into being. Its way of acting follows its way of existing. If it exists through matter, its action must depend on matter too. Matter exists in a position, so it can act on or be affected by something only when its position relates it to that thing. Without such a relation, it cannot act there.

If a power could act without matter's participation or without a spatial relation to what it affects, it would not depend on matter in order to act. And anything that does not depend on matter in its action would not depend on matter in its existence; it would be immaterial. This also means that nature cannot act on the very matter in which it exists: matter has no position in relation to itself or to what is within it. Otherwise, anything with a position would need another position, and so on without end. A bodily nature cannot act on its own matter; that would require the individual matter to exist before itself. All the features that necessarily belong to nature—natural motion, heat in fire, moisture in water, and the like—must therefore follow from nature without a separate act that produces them. There must be a source higher than nature and its necessary effects.185

Motion itself is one of those necessary effects. Nature and motion therefore come into being together.186 Nature must be renewed in its very being, as motion is; indeed, motion is nature's own renewal. Natural qualities and amounts arise and last with nature, as do its other states. Existence flows through nature into these effects. This is what philosophers mean when they say that form and matter are co-causes: form does not produce matter by itself, nor does it act as a tool or an intermediary that exists before matter. They exist together.187 The same is true of nature and its natural features, including motion. Nature must therefore be renewed and changed in every body. The changing positions of the heavens are renewed with celestial nature, just as natural changes and changes in amount in simple and compound earthly things are renewed with their natures.

Here is another proof from the Eastern school. Every bodily substance exists in a way that necessarily includes features that cannot be separated from it. Their relation to the individual is like the relation of a defining feature to the kind. People usually call these features “individuators.” More accurately, they are signs of individuality: they identify a thing without causing it to be an individual. For example, “growing” describes a plant, “sensing” an animal, and “reasoning” a human being. These words point to the vegetative, animal, and rational souls that make up the different levels of life.188 The same is true of the defining features of things made of parts. Each underlying reality is simple, though we describe it by a general feature that follows from it. In truth, these are particular, simple ways of existing, not separate definitions.

These necessary features arise from an individual as light comes from a lamp, or heat from fire. With this in mind, consider how every bodily individual undergoes changes in all or some of its individuating features: time, amount, position, place, and the like. Their change follows the change in the existence that entails them; in a sense, it is that very change.189 The existence of every bodily nature is itself extended, measurable, positioned, located, and temporal. So when its amounts, colors, or positions change, the individual bodily substance changes too. This is motion in substance, since the existence of substance is itself substantial, just as the existence of an accident is accidental.

1. An illustrative note

Every bodily substance has a flowing, renewed nature and also a lasting aspect, related to that nature as the soul is related to the body. The human spirit lasts because it is immaterial, while the body's nature is always breaking down, dissolving, and flowing. The body is renewed while the individual continues through a steady succession of similar forms. People are unaware of this; they are bewildered by the fact that creation is renewed.

The same is true of natural forms. In their material, spatial, and temporal existence, they are continually renewed and never fully at rest. In their intellectual existence—as separate Platonic forms—they remain forever in God's knowledge. I do not mean that they last through their own power, but that they last through God's own lasting existence, rather than because God repeatedly keeps them in existence.190 There is a difference between these two ideas, which will be explained later. The first is a passing, worldly existence; the second is fixed in God's knowledge and does not pass away. Nothing can leave God's knowledge, and God's knowledge cannot change. ‘In this is a message for people who worship.’191

XXVII. Why a thing's very form can come to be through motion

The argument made by Avicenna and others, as we have seen, is this: a form cannot grow stronger or weaker. If it could, its kind would either remain through the change or not. If the kind remained, then the form itself would not be changing; only its associated features would. If the kind did not remain, the form would be disappearing, not growing stronger. Another form would then have to take its place. These successive forms would either last for more than one instant or not. If one lasted, motion would have stopped. If none did, forms would follow one another instant by instant. That would make motion a sequence of separate instants, which is impossible.192

This argument can be split in two. First, it implies that instants follow one another without any time between them. But change in quality and other kinds of motion show that this cannot be right. Second, motion requires a subject and matter that exist and persist. Matter by itself is not an actual thing, so it cannot be the subject that remains through a change of substantial form. In a change of quality, by contrast, the subject exists without the quality. Once the argument is set out this way, the first point—the supposed sequence of instants—does not matter. The central issue is the second point.193

The argument says that motion in form must consist of successive forms, none lasting longer than an instant, and that when a form disappears, the thing itself disappears. So no thing would remain through the motion. But every moving thing remains throughout its motion. There is a problem here. If “the thing itself” means the whole made up of form and matter, it is true that the whole disappears when its form does. But that whole is not what moves. The moving subject is the matter together with some form—any form—just as in a change of amount, the subject is the matter together with some amount. If instead the argument means that the matter itself disappears, it is mistaken. Otherwise, matter would have to come into being each time a new form appeared, whether all at once or gradually. Every new thing needs matter, so this would lead to an endless chain of new matters, which is impossible. If nothing remained, the new form would not need matter at all; if something did remain, the loss of one form would not make it cease to exist.194

It is surprising that Avicenna raised this very question about how matter and form depend on each other: if a specific form disappears, does matter disappear with it? His answer was that matter keeps its individual unity through the general unity of the form, not through one particular form. So even if motion occurs in form, a change in form does not have to destroy matter. The truth is that matter remains, and form also remains through continuous renewal—a continuity that does not rule out individuality.195 This is what philosophers mean when they say that each degree of strength or weakness is a different kind: each degree is actually distinct from the others. That does not prevent a single individual blackness from growing stronger, with endlessly many possible kinds within it. The same is true of forms as they change continuously.196

Avicenna also offered another argument, though he pointed out its weakness: substance has no opposite, so it cannot move, since motion is a passage from one opposite to another. His reply is that if opposites must take turns in the very same subject, forms have no opposites. But if it is enough for them to take turns in the same underlying matter, then water and fire are positive forms that share matter and are as far apart as opposites can be.197

XXVIII. Further evidence that natural substances in heavenly and earthly bodies are renewed

Perhaps you will say that this is a new teaching, one no philosopher has held. The things that do not remain fixed are usually said to be only time and motion. Philosophers disagree about which of these is unstable in itself and which is unstable as a result. Most say that time itself is unstable and motion follows it; Suhrawardi held the reverse. But no one has said that nature, as a substance, is unstable in its very being.198

First, what matters is proof. A reasonable person does not leave a well-known view unless the evidence requires it. Second, the philosophers' words can be understood as distinguishing a thing's essence from its existence. Motion and time have an essence that is renewal and passing away; nature has an essence that is fixed, while its existence is renewal and passing away.

Third, motion means a thing's gradual passage from potentiality to actuality, not the thing that has already passed from one to the other.199 It is a relation. Relations and other features that depend on something else change or remain as the thing they relate to changes or remains. This is true of the relation itself, whether we call it renewal or passing away. There are three things here: the renewal of something; what it changes through; and the thing that changes. In motion, these are the renewal, the category in which the change takes place, and the subject.

The same distinction applies to a thing's passage from potentiality, or its coming into being.200 These differ from the thing that passes from potentiality or comes into being, and from what it passes through or what brings it about.201 It is like whiteness: there is the quality of being white, the whiteness itself, and the thing that is white. Here, the gradual passage from potentiality to actuality is what motion means. It exists in thought, not as a separate thing in the world. What brings about this passage is nature; what undergoes it is matter; what brings it about is another substance, such as an angel or a heavenly body; and what measures the passage is time. Time is the amount of renewal and passing away. It is not something separate from motion in the way that a mathematical body is separate from a natural body, as we will explain later.

Fourth, it is false and unfair to say that no wise person has held this view. The first and most truthful source of wisdom is God. He says, “You see the mountains and think them fixed, but they pass like clouds,”202 and “Are they confused about a new creation?”203 He also says, “On the day the earth is changed into another earth,” and “He said to it and to the earth, ‘Come willingly or unwillingly,’ and they said, ‘We come willingly.’” He says, “All come to Him in submission,” “We can replace you with your like and bring you into a form you do not know,” “If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation,”204 and “To Him all things return.” These and other verses point to what we have described.

One sign that bodily natures are continually renewed is God's saying, “He rules over His servants and sends guardians over you. When death comes to one of you, Our messengers take his soul; they do not fail.” The point is this: if a thing's existence is intertwined with its passing away, the very causes that sustain it are also the causes of its destruction. That is why scripture attributes both preservation and the taking of souls to the messengers, without neglect in one case and excess in the other.205

Earlier philosophers also stated or hinted at this view. The teacher of the Greek philosophers writes in the book known as The Theology that no body can remain fixed and spread out, whether simple or compound, unless a soul-power is present in it. A body's nature is to flow and pass away. If the whole world were a body without soul or life, all things would pass away and perish.206

The same author continues: if the soul were itself a body, or one of the finest bodies, it too would flow and pass away, and all things would return to matter. If everything returned to matter, and matter had no form to make it actual, the world would cease to exist. But if the world were only body, that would be impossible. This is another clear statement that all bodies are renewed. It also points to what we said earlier: matter tends toward nonexistence. Each time a form flows from the source into matter, the previous form passes away, and a new one takes its place. One of the greatest divine philosophers, Zaytun the Elder, said that beings both last and pass away: they last because their forms are continually renewed, and they pass away because each earlier form ends when another comes to be. Shahrastani reports these words in The Book of Religions and Sects. We will quote many more leading philosophers on the renewal and passing away of bodies as we continue. I have also written a treatise on the temporal coming-to-be of the whole world and everything in it; readers who want to explore the argument can turn to that work. Ibn Arabi's words support the same idea.207

One of the most astonishing things, Ibn Arabi says in The Bezels of Wisdom, is that a person is always rising, without knowing it, because the veil between stages is so fine and the forms so alike.208209 In The Meccan Revelations, he says that all existence is always moving, in this life and the next, because nothing comes to be without something that brings it about. God is continually turning toward creation, and His words never run out.210211 “What is with God remains” points to what we have said: God's intellectual words remain because God remains, while their bodily images pass away.

XXIX. Why circular motion is the oldest, most lasting, complete, and noble motion

To see which motion came first, begin with growth and shrinking, which are changes in amount. Both depend on changes of place: something must move into a growing body, or move out of a shrinking one. Changes of place and position do not depend on changes in amount. Expansion and contraction also involve changes in quality, such as heating or cooling. But these changes of quality do not last forever; they need a new cause. For example, fire heats water when the fire moves closer or the water moves toward it. So changes of place came before changes in amount and quality.

Changes of place may be straight, circular, or a return along the path already traveled. A straight motion cannot continue forever, because distances in space are limited. Nor can a return motion or a change in direction continue as one unbroken movement: the body comes to rest between movements in opposite directions. Rest occurs only in time, as the potentiality of motion, and a thing's potentiality must come before its actuality. Time therefore needs a motion that keeps it going. A motion whose parts pass away cannot preserve time; it must be preserved by a motion that can continue through renewal. Only circular motion can do this. It does not depend on other kinds of motion that affect bodies, while they depend on it. It is therefore the oldest motion.

Circular motion is also the most lasting. Other motions are interrupted by rest, which is their absence. Because this absence still carries the potential for motion, it needs something that exists and changes in time. It therefore needs one span of time after another. As most philosophers say, circular motion is what preserves time.

It is also the most complete. It cannot increase in amount, as other motions can, or grow faster or slower, as we will see in the discussion of the heavenly bodies. Its cause and goal are not things we can sense, but an unchanging intellect beyond this world. The goals of natural motion through place change in how near the moving thing is to its proper place: the motion grows stronger as the thing comes nearer. Forced motion weakens as the moving thing gets farther from what forces it. A thing is stronger when it is closer to its source and weaker when it is farther away. Circular motion does not vary in this way.

Finally, it is nobler than the other motions because it is complete, and what is complete is nobler than what is lacking. The body that moves in a circle must therefore be the oldest, most complete, and noblest body in nature. The excellence, completeness, and lasting power of its motion require the same qualities in what causes it. By holding it in motion, that body's power renews the directions of natural, straight-line motion and the dimensions of space. We will explain this later in the discussion of directions and the heavenly bodies.

XXX. Time is real and measures motion as a continuous quantity

Motion can be divided in thought, and the parts can be counted. To establish that time is real, the natural philosophers point to what we observe: different motions sometimes cover the same stretch of distance but differ in when they begin or end; sometimes they begin and end together but cover different distances; and sometimes they agree in one respect and differ in the other. This shows us that there is a measurable flow in the world in which different motions can occur, whether alike or different. It is not the same as the measured sizes or boundaries of bodies: those remain fixed, while this does not. It measures something that does not stay fixed, namely motion. A full account of this proof belongs to natural philosophy.212213

The philosophers of first principles give a different proof. Every event comes after something that precedes it, and the earlier and later cannot exist together. This is not like one coming before two, since they can exist together. Nor is it like a father coming before a son, since the father can still exist afterward. Nor is it simply one absence after another, since a thing can be absent after it has existed. It is a kind of “before” that cannot, by its nature, exist at the same time as what comes after it.

Between any such before and after, we can imagine further stages that come earlier or later, with no fixed dividing point. This passage of before and after must belong to something that is inherently changing and passing away, yet continuous, in step with motion through divisible distances. Because it can be divided and made larger or smaller, it is a quantity. Because it is continuous, it is a continuous quantity that does not remain fixed, or else something whose continuous quantity does not remain fixed. Either way, it is a substance or an accident.214215216

If it is a substance, then because it is continually renewed, it cannot be separate from matter and potentiality. It is either the extent of a material substance whose identity is continually renewed, or the extent of that renewal and its passing away. In short, it is either the measure of motion or of something that has motion in its very nature, measured by its continuity and divided in thought into what comes before and after.217

This kind of existence has both continuity and stability, and renewal and passing away. To continue, it needs an agent that sustains it; to come to be and pass away, it needs something that can receive it. It is therefore bodily or belongs to a body. It also has one continuous identity and many renewed stages. As one thing, it must have one agent and one recipient. A single attribute cannot belong to one subject through many agents. Its agent must be free of matter and its ties; otherwise, the agent would need another motion and another time to undergo its own material changes.218

Its recipient must be the oldest and most complete of natural substances and bodies, since only time itself can precede time in this special sense. It cannot be formed from another body, or another body formed from it, because that would break time's continuity.219220 It must be fully formed, not made from the elements, and by nature it cannot undergo change of place, change of amount such as growth or shrinking, expansion or contraction, or change of quality. These changes would break it and would mean it no longer came before the other bodies.221 We will explain this more simply as we continue.

XXXI. Gradual Existence as the Immediate Goal of Time and Motion

You should know that we will show later that the proper goal of the celestial motion is the soul's conceptions, which give rise to longing and will. Through these, the celestial soul draws closer to its highest source.222

In his Notes, Avicenna writes: “The goal of celestial motion is not motion itself, simply as this particular motion. It is to preserve the nature of motion.” But the individual motion cannot be preserved, so the kind is preserved through individuals, just as the human kind survives only through individual people. One person cannot preserve it alone: every individual comes to be and must therefore pass away. Celestial motion is renewed, yet it is one motion through its continuity and permanence. In that respect, and when viewed as a whole, it is like something fixed.

Elsewhere he writes: “The goal of a particular nature is a particular individual, such as the individual that comes to be after it. That individual can also be the goal of another particular nature. The endless succession of individuals is the goal of the lasting power within the heavenly substances.”223224

He also writes: “The cause of the sphere's motion is the soul's conception, renewed from one conception to the next. Each conception, together with a particular position, gives rise to another conception. The first prepares the soul for the second. Repeated conceptions may be alike in kind but many in number, or they may differ from one another.”225

He adds: “The second conception resembles the first in kind, not as the same individual. It can therefore give rise to a motion like the first in kind, but not the same motion as an individual. If the two conceptions were identical in every way, there would be only one conception and one numerically single motion.”226 And he says: “Every position of the sphere calls for another position; the cause is the renewal of one perception after another.” These are his exact words. In effect, they affirm motion in substantial forms in two ways.

First, the celestial soul's conceptions are renewed in a gradual, continuous way. That is what motion in a substantial form means. Avicenna and others have established that the form of a substance is itself a substance. The sphere's conceptions belong both to the principles that move it directly and to things that follow from those principles indirectly. They also hold that the sphere's goal is not anything below it. Its purposes and imaginings, then, are substantial forms nobler than the earthly substances.227

Second, a body's position is either part of its way of existing or inseparable from it, as they themselves have said.228 Every position of the sphere is natural to it; none is forced, since nothing can force the celestial bodies. You have already learned that the immediate source of every motion is nature. In truth, the sphere's nature and its animal soul are one thing, one reality. A change of position therefore means a change in the individual way the sphere exists: one individual existence follows another, continuously and gradually.

Avicenna also says in his Notes: “The celestial nature, precisely as celestial nature, requires its natural place and position, but not one particular place.” Otherwise, moving away from that place would be forced.229

He also says: “All these positions and places are natural to it.” I say: this means every position and place of the sphere is natural to it. Yet it moves from one to another while each is natural. This makes sense only if the sphere's nature is itself renewed, with a shared unity and a connected multiplicity, along with the positions, places, and other features that follow from it. Avicenna and his followers may not accept this view, but it is the truth that cannot be avoided.230

What best fits their own account is that the celestial nature first requires position and place in general, without requiring any particular one. The particular positions and places serve only to preserve the kind indirectly, not as the nature's own goal. But this does not hold up under closer examination. First, they have established that nature's goal must be a particular individual. A general meaning has no existence outside the mind until it is made particular. Existence belongs first to the individual, then to the kind, and then to the general class. That is why, in Aristotle's Categories, primary substances are called first substances, their kinds second substances, and their general classes third substances.231232

Second, as we have learned in the study of existence, what truly exists in any thing is its particular reality of existence, made individual through itself. General natures, by contrast, have no existence outside or inside the mind apart from their dependence on an existing thing. Position and place are among the features that make an existence particular and among the things that follow from it. A change in them is either the very change in the thing's way of existing or follows from it. It is not true, as people commonly think, that this body, as one fixed individual, is the unrestricted cause of time. If it were, it would not itself be in time. But every body and bodily thing is in time and is made particular by time; the cause of something cannot itself be made particular by that thing.233

Time, through its continuous unity, relates equally to all its earlier and later parts. It brings about time and the things in time through one act, and the source of their beginning is also the source of their continuing existence. A gradual thing that has no fixed state survives only by continually coming to be. As our approach shows, every body, bodily nature, and bodily feature—shape, position, amount, quality, place, and the other material features—is always flowing and passing away, either in itself or through something else.234235

The unrestricted source of time must therefore have two aspects: a unifying, intellectual aspect and a renewing, changing aspect. Through its unity, it brings about time as one connected reality. Through its renewal, it is affected at one point and acts at another, according to the particular identities of its parts. This source is the outermost sphere itself, which has two sides: its separate, intellectual nature is the side of unity, and its bodily nature is the side of multiplicity and renewal. The outermost body brings time into being, sustains it, and keeps it going.236

By the same reasoning, its body also brings into being directions and places. A particular body needs time and motion for its capacity to change and for its gradual coming-to-be. In the same way, it needs something around it to establish its place and position. How, then, could place and position come before it by nature? These features either help make an individual what it is or necessarily follow from its existence. No act can be inserted between a thing and what necessarily follows from it.237238

All bodily existences are incomplete: they need time and place, position, amount, and quality. The first source of these things must therefore be separate from them in its being and existence. Time cannot be caused by an earlier time, place by an earlier place, or position by another position, and the same is true of amount and the rest. These things are renewed effects, but their first cause must be a stable, immaterial reality outside the chain of time and place: God in His oneness, or His divine knowledge, His perfect words that never fade, or the realm of His command, where when He says “Be,” it is.239

XXXII. Nothing Precedes Time and Motion Except God, Exalted in Glory

You have learned that time and the things connected with it are gradual existences, continually coming to be. Anything that precedes time—whether it is an existence, a nonexistence, or something else—if its “before” cannot coexist with what comes after, must itself be time or something in time.240 So before every time there would be another time, and before every motion another motion.

We have also established that a thing's cause must not depend in its own existence on the thing it causes.241 Therefore, nothing precedes time except God, His power and command. Different thinkers have called this command God's detailed knowledge, His attributes, the angels, or the divine forms known to the Platonists. People follow different paths according to what they love.

If anything else preceded time and motion through a succession of renewed states, then, when it existed, time and motion would not yet exist. Before they existed, they would have been possible.
