The philosophers say that coming-to-be means a thing's existence is preceded by nonexistence. They treat this as a feature that follows the thing's existence. But the thing's existence comes after the cause has acted, and the cause acts only after the thing has some reason to need a cause. So coming-to-be cannot be the reason for this need, or a condition or part of that reason. Otherwise, it would have to come before itself by several steps, which is impossible.

I say that calling coming-to-be a feature that follows existence is loose wording. As we have seen, coming-to-be is not a feature added to the existence of something that has come to be. We have also seen that each thing's existence at a particular level includes its being at that level. But this does not weaken the point. A thing that has come to be certainly needs a cause. The need must come either from its possibility or, in some way, from its coming-to-be.524 If we imagined both removed, the thing would be necessary and eternal, and so would not need a cause. Since we have ruled out coming-to-be as the source of the need, only possibility remains. The truth, however, is that the need for a cause comes from neither of these. It comes from the fact that a thing's existence depends on, and is held up by, something else.

The claim that an essence's possibility comes before its existence is correct when we consider the essence in itself. But existence comes before essence in the order of reality, as an actual thing comes before what is only potential, and form before matter. Until there is existence, no essence is realized at all. As we have said, existence is also what makes a thing this particular thing; nothing exists without becoming a particular. Possibility comes after essence because it is a feature of essence. How, then, can possibility be the cause of existence when, by supposition, possibility comes after existence itself?

The familiar argument—“it was possible, so it needed a cause, and then it came to exist”—is sound when we consider the essence as the mind sets it apart from existence. We do not deny that an essence's possibility explains why it needs a cause in that way. Its possibility comes before its existence, meaning before it is described as existing.525 This description takes place in thought, even though the existence we are describing is real.

Coming-to-be does, however, give rise to a need for a preparatory cause, and such a cause is only an incidental cause.526 Every thing that comes to be is preceded by a possibility of existence. This possibility is itself something real, not merely an idea in the mind.527 It has degrees of strength and weakness, and can be near to its result or far from it. A near possibility is readiness; a more distant one is capacity.

This possibility must either be a substance or an accident. It cannot be a substance that exists entirely on its own,528 since then it would not belong to anything. Nor would there be any reason for one thing, rather than any other, to have the same independent possibility.529 So the possibility of a thing that comes to be must have a bearer. It may be a form in matter or an accident in a subject. In either case, it comes before the thing in time and ends when that thing exists.530

The bearer of this possibility must be connected to the thing that comes to be. Otherwise, there would be no reason why it was the possibility of this thing rather than another. The bearer of its capacity and possibility must be the very bearer of its existence, the bearer of one of its parts, or the bearer of something that exists along with it.531 So although this possibility is itself real, it is the nonexistence of the thing that is to come to be, and its capacity to become that thing. It cannot exist at the same time as the thing's actual existence. This is why some ancient thinkers counted nonexistence among the causes of a thing that comes to be.532 They therefore counted five causes: nonexistence, the agent, the end, the matter, and the form.

The truth is that nonexistence is not a direct cause, but an incidental one.

If it were a direct cause, it would not disappear when the thing came into existence. The matter that carries the thing's possibility, by contrast, is one of its direct causes. Also, the priority of nonexistence to existence is priority in time. This is the same as the priority of earlier parts of time over later ones. So nonexistence comes first only incidentally, not in itself. Perhaps the ancients counted nonexistence as a direct cause because what comes to be in time is, in reality, made up of parts of motion and time. These have a weak kind of existence: as each part or instance passes away, another part or instance comes into being.533 From this point of view, nonexistence can be called a direct cause of what comes to be.

V. Ways One Thing Can Come Before Another

Priority and posteriority are among the features of anything that exists. There are several kinds of priority: priority in rank, in nature, in excellence, in time, and in essence or causation. There are also two more kinds, which we will explain.

Priority in rank means that whatever is closer to an actual or assumed starting point comes first. For example, Baghdad may be said to come before Kufa. There are two kinds of this rank. One follows the natural order of things, though it is not priority by nature in the technical sense: a body comes before an animal, and an animal before a human being. The other follows a chosen order or position in space. For example, the row nearest the prayer leader comes before the next row, if we take the prayer niche as our starting point.

Priority in rank can be reversed: what came first can become last, and what came last can become first, if we choose a new starting point. If we make the human being the starting point, whatever is closer to a human being comes first. On this basis, a human being would come before a body, even before a substance. In the earlier example, a worshipper comes before the prayer leader when we count from the door toward the prayer niche.

Natural rank appears in every chain that is ordered by the nature of its members rather than by a chosen arrangement. This includes causes and effects, qualities and the things that have them, and kinds arranged from broader to narrower. If you move upward from the lowest effect, you eventually reach the highest cause.534 If you move downward, the highest comes first. The same applies to the broadest kinds, the most specific kinds, and other ordered series. Philosophers base their proof against an infinite chain on such series when their members exist together.535

Priority by nature is like the priority of one over two, or of a line over a triangle. Remove what comes later, and what came before it can still remain; remove what came before, and what came after it cannot remain. The measure of this priority is whether something can exist, not whether it must exist.

Priority by causation means that the existence of what comes first causes the existence of what comes later. The cause comes before its effect both in existence and in necessity, because the cause makes the effect necessary. Priority by excellence or honor is what we mean when we say that Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, comes before the other prophets. Priority in time is familiar. The earlier thing does not exist at the same time as the later one. This differs from priority by nature, where the earlier thing can exist together with the later one.

Anyone who says that the agent makes the very essence of a thing, rather than its existence, and that the agent's own essence, rather than its existence, is what acts, must add another kind: priority by essence.536 The same is true of anyone who says that a possible thing's essence comes before its existence simply as an essence, without considering any kind of existence.

Of the two further kinds of priority I mentioned, the first is priority in reality. Existence comes before the essence that exists through it, because existence is, in our view, what truly makes something exist. The essence exists through existence in a secondary sense. The same is true of two things that share a feature such as motion, position, or quantity, when one has the feature directly and the other only through its relation to the first. The first comes before the second in this further sense.

This is different from priority by excellence, since what comes later in excellence must still possess some share of the quality in which it is surpassed. It also differs from priority by nature and by causation, since in those kinds the later thing shares something with the earlier one. This further kind of priority is plainly different from priority in time or rank.

You might ask: in each kind of priority, what is the feature that makes the first thing prior and the second later? What makes one thing prior in the case just described? I answer: simply that it is established or exists, whether in a direct or a figurative sense.

The second further kind is priority through the Real, and posteriority through Him. This is a subtle kind of priority, understood only by those with deep knowledge. They say that God has different levels of divinity, and also inner aspects that do not break His absolute oneness.537 In short, the existence of every necessary cause comes before the existence of its essential effect in this way. Philosophers define an active cause as something that acts on something distinct from itself. So the cause's own being comes before the effect's being through causation.538

But the priority of existence over existence is another kind. Here, there is no action and response, no acting and being acted on. The two are like one thing with different aspects and states, moving from one state to another. What marks this kind of priority is the divine aspect. Once you understand the meaning of each kind of priority, you will also understand its opposite—posteriority—and the idea of two things being together, as these terms are understood.

VI. How These Kinds of Priority Share a Meaning

People disagree about whether the word priority applies to all these kinds by name alone or by a shared meaning, and whether that meaning stays the same or changes by degree. Most later philosophers take it to have one fixed meaning in every case, without degrees. Some say that the shared meaning is this: whatever is prior, simply by being prior, has something the later thing lacks, while everything the later thing has is already present in the prior thing. This is not right. A thing that is earlier in time is gone by the time the later thing exists. Yet the time that belongs to the later thing is not present in the earlier one,539 nor was it present there before.540 The time belonging to the earlier thing is likewise never present in the later thing. Each part of time has its own existence, unlike every other part. Nor is it true without qualification that the later thing has nothing the earlier thing lacks. Later created things can have many features that the first created thing does not have, such as possibility and being a substance. The definition should at least be limited to whatever makes one thing prior. Even then, it is refuted by what we have said about parts of time and other cases.

Others say that all kinds of priority share this feature: the prior thing has something that makes it more entitled to priority than the later thing. This is not right either. There is nothing in an earlier thing that makes it more entitled to be earlier than a later thing. If we compare them with some unspecified time, neither is more entitled than the other. If we compare them with their own particular times, those times are different, so they cannot both have the same one in which to be more entitled. Nor can we say that one has this advantage because of its priority, since we are trying to explain what priority means. Suppose we compare two things that are earlier and later in time. The first is earlier in every respect, and the second later in every respect. There is no third thing in this comparison. If instead we compare both with a third thing, one may be earlier than the other, but both are still earlier than the third; one is not earlier while the other is later. Besides, both definitions take for granted the general idea of priority that they are meant to explain.541542

Some people say the word is used in completely unrelated senses. But Avicenna's discussion in The Healing suggests that one meaning applies to all the kinds by degree, while in some cases the word may also have been transferred to a new use or used figuratively.543 He says that people first used “before” and “after” for place and time. Then they extended “before” to anything nearer to a chosen starting point. This could be a natural order, or a chosen arrangement based on craft, luck, or chance. They then extended it to excellence and to anything that comes first even without being better. The shared idea is that the first has something the other lacks, while the other has only what the first has. A master or leader is called “before” a servant or follower in this way: the right to choose belongs to the leader, not the follower, and the follower chooses only after the leader, acting on the leader's choice.

They then applied the word to relations involving existence. One, for example, can exist without many things, while many things cannot exist without one. This does not mean that one gives existence to many. Rather, many things need one so they can exist as a whole made up of parts. Finally, they used it for cases where two things have separate sources of existence, but the existence of the second comes from the first. The first then gives the second a necessity it does not have in itself; in itself, the second is only possible. In this way, the first is prior through necessity, as the movement of a hand is prior to the movement of a key.

The Illuminationist author says in Al-Muṭāraḥāt that priority applies to some kinds in one shared meaning, and to others by a shared word or figuratively. The genuine kinds, he says, are priority in itself and priority by nature. Both mean that the essence of one thing comes before the essence of another. A cause, whether complete or incomplete, must come before its effect in essence and existence, so priority has one meaning in these two cases.

Priority in time is the most familiar kind in ordinary speech. But when we call one person earlier than another, what we first mean is that one person's time comes before the other's. He says he has shown in this book that the priority of one time over another is by nature alone: time cannot come before time through time, since time has no other time. The relation between two times is therefore natural; when applied to two people, it is figurative.

Positional rank may seem to be about place, but time also plays a part. Hamadan does not come before Baghdad by its own nature or simply by its place. It comes first for someone traveling from Khorasan to the Hejaz, because that traveler reaches it earlier in time.544 Natural rank works in the same way: one end of a series comes first only because someone chooses a starting point. If they start at the lower end, the higher end becomes later.545 The starting point is not a place; it is the time when the traveler begins. So time is involved in rank, and priority in time returns to priority by nature, as we have seen.

Priority by excellence is either figurative or a case of unrelated word meanings. It is figurative when an honored person is given the first place at a gathering or allowed to begin an event. The comparison then comes down to place or time, and place itself relates to time. If that is not what is meant,546 then “priority” is simply a different word used for excellence. Anyone who says the word applies to all the kinds only through unrelated meanings is mistaken.547

The Illuminationist author concludes that the only genuine priority is priority by causation, whether it is called natural or essential. I see several problems with his account. First, it is not right to say that priority and posteriority between parts of time are only natural priority.548 As we have learned, priority in time means that the earlier and later things do not exist together. Natural priority does not require them to be separate in this way. These are different kinds, though one thing can be prior in two ways for two different reasons. A preparatory cause, for example, comes before its effect in time because it does not exist together with the effect, and by nature because the effect depends on it. Someone could also question whether an earlier time is naturally prior to a later one, even if the times follow one another by nature; the two ideas are different.549

Second, his claim that time cannot come before time because there is no time for time is not convincing.550 Time renews and changes through its own nature; it does not need some separate event to make it change.551 Other things need time in order to change, just as an essence exists through existence while existence exists without needing another existence. There are many similar examples: size in a measurable thing, number in a collection, and whiteness in what is white.

Third, it is not right to say that priority by nature and priority by causation have one meaning, even if they share something, as some say all kinds do. Each kind has its own feature that makes one thing prior and another later. In priority by nature, the relevant feature is existence itself. One can exist without many, but many cannot exist unless one exists first. Existence is what makes one prior to many, or a part prior to a whole. Many times the one exists without the many; the many never exist without the one. I do not mean that one and many are equal because of their descriptions as part and whole. They are alike in receiving existence through their relation to one another. That is why Avicenna defined priority as what does not reverse in existence.

In priority by causation, the relevant feature is existence in its necessity and actuality, not merely existence itself. A cause and its effect exist together, but they are not equally necessary: the cause must exist, and the effect is necessary only once the cause exists. The effect's necessity comes from the cause's necessity. In natural priority, by contrast, the difference lies in existence itself. This is another kind of priority. Yet both, together with posteriority, may be grouped under the broader name “essential priority,” because both involve a difference in existence, whether in existence itself or in how firmly it is established. Those who say that a maker causes the essence of a thing, rather than its existence, add another kind: priority by essence. Here the maker's essence is established before the essence of what it makes. They can group all three kinds under essential priority, if they use that term broadly enough to cover differences in existence and the relation between a feature and what bears it.552

The feature that makes one thing prior to another must be what differs between them. Since priority and posteriority are relational ideas, their kinds differ according to the things to which they are related.

Fourth, it is not right to treat priority by excellence as figurative or as an unrelated use of the word. Here, too, there is a feature that can vary by degree: excellence or lack of excellence. Whiteness, knowledge, leadership, vice, goodness, and badness can all be greater or lesser. A brighter white is prior to a weaker white as white; someone more vicious comes before someone less vicious in vice. The feature that makes one prior is not existence, necessity, time, place, or rank. This kind should clearly be counted as its own kind of priority.

VII. Whether Priority Changes by Degree Across Its Kinds

It is clear that the meaning of priority varies by degree when we compare its different kinds in general. It is harder to prove that this holds between every pair of kinds, and the issue is not very important. Philosophers have said that priority by causation comes before priority by nature, which comes before the other kinds; priority in time comes next, followed by priority in place.

Bahmanyār says in Al-Taḥṣīl that all kinds except priority by nature and by causation are not genuine priority. Priority in time, he says, exists in thought and assumption, because time has no actual parts, only parts we imagine by dividing it. But this does not mean that time priority is not a kind of priority, as the author of Al-Muṭāraḥāt thought. It means that time is one reality outside the mind, not actually divided into parts. Where there are no actual parts, there is no real priority between them in the outside world. Yet this does not make time priority a different kind in name only. The same is true of priority by nature between parts of time: it too exists only in thought, Bahmanyār says.

The truth is that the difference between parts of time belongs to their changing existence in the world, regardless of what anyone thinks or imagines.553 The mind can judge that one part comes before another because, outside the mind, time's parts exist in an order. They are not actual parts with separate existence, but they are very close to being parts, as in other cases where the mind describes things based on the world outside us. The evenness of four and the sky's being above the earth are examples. This does not mean that the parts of time lack a shared nature. What makes them alike is also what makes them differ, as with existence itself.

This also answers the objection that priority and posteriority are relative pairs and so must exist together. How, then, can one part of time come before another? We reply that both the earlier and later parts exist together within the one continuous flow of time. Its unity is also its division, and its priority is also its presence. This is because time has a weak kind of existence and an incomplete unity.554

VIII. Kinds of Being Together

The kinds of being together correspond to the kinds of priority and posteriority in meaning, not in existence. Being together is not the other member of a relative pair with priority and posteriority, so it does not have to exist wherever they do. It is instead like the absence of a feature that something could have.555 Two things can lack priority in time without existing together at the same time; nor does the absence of natural priority mean that they are together by nature. Things entirely separate from matter have neither temporal priority nor temporal togetherness. The relation of such a thing to a person like Zayd is neither priority nor posteriority nor togetherness in time. Things that exist together in time must both be temporal, just as things that share a position or place must both be spatial. Whatever does not exist in time has no temporal priority, posteriority, or togetherness.

Likewise, two things are together in essence only if they are both effects of one cause. If neither depends essentially on the same cause nor one on the other, they are not together in essence and have no priority or posteriority in that sense. Things that are together by nature may be relative pairs. Since each depends on the other, they must also depend on one cause, as explained elsewhere.556 So things that are together by nature are either produced by one cause,557 or are kinds under the same wider kind, or the like. They may depend on each other for their existence, as brothers do.558 Or they may not, as with kinds under one wider kind: they are together by nature because neither comes before the other in its nature. They may also be together in rank if both are naturally later than the wider kind,559 or they may not be.

Two things can exist together in time in every respect. They cannot share a place in every respect. Bodies can match in one spatial relation: two people, for example, may be equally far from someone approaching from in front or behind. But they must differ in their relation to someone approaching from the right or left. Two bodies cannot share a place in every respect without one coming before the other in time. And some simple universal bodies cannot be together in place at all.

A cause must be together with its effect because they are relative to one another. This togetherness does not cancel the priority of the cause's essence over the effect's essence. Even if they are present together as cause and effect, this does not mean that their very existence is simultaneous in the same way. The relation necessarily follows from their being cause and effect.560 The cause is prior to the effect in this respect.

A cause cannot exist without its effect also existing. I do not mean merely that the two are relative pairs. Their existence must actually be together. If the cause is enough by itself to be a cause, then as long as it exists, it is a cause and the effect exists. If it needs something in addition to itself, then while it is only in that state, it is a cause only potentially; it does not yet have to produce an effect. The true cause is then the thing together with what must be added to it. That extra condition may be a choice or desire, or something separate that the cause awaits. Once that condition is present and nothing else is lacking, the effect must exist. The two then exist together in time, in the timeless order, or in some other way. But they are not together in the way their existence is constituted: the effect's existence depends on the cause's existence, while the cause's does not depend on the effect. It follows that removing the cause removes the effect, but removing the effect does not require that the cause be removed. The cause must be removed before its effect can be removed. Removing or restoring the cause brings about the removal or restoration of the effect. By contrast, removing or restoring the effect is a sign that the cause has been removed or restored. The effect exists with its cause and through its cause; the cause exists with the effect.

IX. What Essential Coming-to-Be Really Means

If this coming-to-be describes existence, it means that existence itself depends on something else in its very identity, not through some added feature. Its very being is such that, if we set aside the existence that supports and brings it about, it would be nothing at all. It is therefore poor in itself: its very identity depends on something included in what it is, while that other thing does not depend on it, since it is rich and independent. This is one kind of “after”: existence after existence, even if both occur at the same time or in the timeless order.

If coming-to-be describes an essence, it does not mean that the essence depends on something else when we ignore its existence. Meanings and essences considered without existence have no relations of dependence, priority, or posteriority. Nor does an essence, considered simply as itself, demand that it be connected to anything else. Rather, its coming after nonexistence means this: if we consider the essence just as it is in itself, it is not existent. This is a simple denial; it does not mean that a positive state of nonexistence belongs to the essence at that level. When we consider an essence in this way, both existence and nonexistence are denied of it. So are all other ideas, except the idea of the essence itself. Every simple denial is true except the denial of the essence itself; every positive claim is false except the claim that it is itself. The essence, considered as itself, is only itself. This does not mean that both sides of a contradiction are false. The opposite of “this thing exists at that level” is “this existence is denied at that level.” The qualification belongs to the existence being denied, not to the denial. The two meanings are different. Nor does reality lack one side or the other: what is real is existence, as we have shown. Existence is what truly exists, is real, is made, and comes to be. Essence exists only in a secondary sense, as something derived from existence. It is empty of everything, and even of the opposite of everything.

What belongs to a thing in itself comes before what it receives from another. Every possible thing is therefore “not” in itself, then “is” through its cause. The simple “not” belongs to it in its own nature; the actual “is” belongs to it because existence is given by its cause. So its condition in itself comes before its condition as dependent on something else. This earlier state, which remains as long as the essence remains, is its essential coming-to-be. We will show that this priority and posteriority are not a separate kind, as some learned thinkers thought, but belong to priority by nature.561562

Al-Dawānī explains Avicenna's statement that every effect is an “is after a not” in response to an objection. The objection is that an effect is no more, in itself, entitled to be nonexistent than to be existent, since it needs a cause for either state. Al-Dawānī says that because an effect's existence comes after its cause's existence, in the rank of the cause's existence the effect has only nonexistence; otherwise it would not come after the cause. But this explanation faces the same problem we discussed earlier. The fact that an effect's existence comes after its cause means only that the effect is not existent in the cause's rank. It does not mean that the effect is nonexistent there.

I say that this explanation is wrong, but not for the reason just given. Since the effect's existence comes from the cause, which gives it its actuality, form, and source of being, how can we say that in the cause's rank the effect has only nonexistence? The truth is that the cause's existence is the fullness, strength, completion, necessity, and actuality of the effect's existence. What belongs to the effect as lack, limitation, and possibility is not in the cause. This is how we should understand Avicenna's words: the effect is not an “is” in itself, but it is an “is” from its cause. Every possible thing is made up of two sides: existence and actuality come from the cause; nonexistence and possibility come from the thing itself. The second side is absent from the cause.

Someone may ask: if the effect does not exist at the rank of the cause, then it must be nonexistent there, or else there would be a third option. Also, nonexistence means the absence of existence. So if the effect's existence is absent at that rank, it must be nonexistent there. I reply that the opposite of “it exists at that rank” is the simple denial of that existence. It is not the positive claim that “its nonexistence exists at that rank.” The first denies a qualified existence; the second makes a qualified claim about nonexistence. Denying the first does not establish the second. It is possible that neither existence nor nonexistence is attributed to the effect at that rank, as with things that have no cause-and-effect relation. Neither their existence nor their nonexistence comes before or after the other's existence.

I say that if existence is not affirmed of an essence at a certain rank,563 then a simple denial of existence is true there, as we have said. This does not mean that the essence has the positive feature “its existence is denied,” because that would require the essence to exist as a subject. Just as all simple denials are true of things that do not exist, and all positive claims about them are false, so too with an essence considered apart from existence and nonexistence. Simple denials are true, and positive claims are false. This does not make both sides of a contradiction false or make them disappear.

As for things that have no relation of cause and effect,564 if one could exist only through the existence of the other, it would have the same kind of priority over it: priority by nature. The same holds for the relation between an essence and its existence. An essence is connected to existence because it can be described as existing later. If it is not first described as existing and only later as existing, then it has a kind of priority over its existence.

The remaining question is whether the absence of one thing in the rank of another is enough to make the other prior, when the other has no presence in that rank. An essence has no presence before existence, so how can we say that it comes before existence? Our answer is that the mind's act of setting an essence apart from its existence—and from all other kinds of existence—is itself a kind of existence for it in reality. In this way, the essence comes before the existence it has when considered without that act of setting it apart. The same consideration both separates the essence from existence and joins it to existence. We do not say that this separation is a state the essence has in that earlier rank. We say that the separation itself is a kind of presence for the essence. To be an essence from which all existence is denied in that rank is itself a kind of being and existence. Likewise, considering it as itself alone, neither existent nor nonexistent, gives it a kind of standing. This is because existence is the source of everything. Without existence, there is no essence at all. When a cause gives something existence, the mind can consider the meaning and essence of that existence separately, since existence is incidental to the essence. Anything that has a feature incidentally can be considered before that feature.

The mind can therefore analyse one existing thing into essence and existence, even though outside the mind there is only one thing. Once analysed into two, each is distinct from the other but can also be joined to it. This gives the essence a kind of priority when we consider it in this way. In reality, however, existence comes before essence in another sense: priority in reality, as we explained earlier.

The result of this discussion, the scholar says, is that in the earlier rank a possible thing has only the possibility of existence and nonexistence. In that rank, it is nonexistent only in the sense that it is possible to exist or not exist. If that is enough to establish essential coming-to-be, the argument is complete; if not, it is not.

I say it is surprising that he admits that the thing has the possibility of existence and nonexistence in that rank. Possibility is a negative idea: it means that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary. So he has admitted that this lack of necessity belongs to the essence in itself. This must involve some kind of presence. We now have everything needed for priority: the prior thing has some presence in that rank, while the later thing is absent from it. The essence has a presence there, as do its defining features. How could it not? The essence, considered in itself, cannot be separated from its own nature and essential features. It therefore has a kind of presence through itself, even if, in reality, that presence depends on existence, as we have explained.

1. A Difficulty and Its Solution

The objection is that if the nonexistence of an essence comes before its existence, it must come before it by nature. Philosophers recognise only two kinds of essential priority: priority by causation and priority by nature. It cannot be priority by causation here. This would mean that no simple complete cause could exist,565 contrary to their view.566 They suggest this answer: a cause is whatever an effect needs in order to exist.567 The need itself, and what comes before that need—such as possibility and the related considerations—are outside the cause, because they are not being considered in this definition. For this reason, they explicitly say that essential possibility is not part of the cause.568

I say that this answer is very weak.569 The parts of an essence, such as its broader kind and the feature that distinguishes it, or matter and form, may be taken for granted when we discuss an effect's need for a cause.570 Yet these parts still count among the causes of the essence's existence. The same must be true of earlier stages before an essence exists. So it makes sense to say: it was possible, so it needed a cause, and then it came to exist. The “so” between each step points to a causal link. Philosophers also say that possibility causes a possible thing to need a cause, just as the capacity to receive causes something to be ready to receive existence and actuality. The cause must therefore be made up of parts.

The sound answer is this:571 bringing existence itself from a cause is one thing; making an essence exist is another. As we have said, existence is what truly exists, while essence exists through it. Bringing existence from its maker does not require an essence, possibility, or any extra condition. It depends only on the being of the agent. So some things can have a simple cause: the agent's existence itself, without any condition of matter, form, essence, capacity, or possibility. But for an essence to be made existent, the cause must be composite. Since the existence being made is a state of the essence, it must come after the essence itself, its possibility, and its capacity to receive that state. There is no simple cause in this case. At the very least, the complete cause must include three things: the agent's being, the essence of what receives existence, and its capacity to receive it.

This capacity for existence can also be near or far. If we consider an essence's possibility in itself, without relating it to its cause, it is a distant capacity. If we consider it in relation to its cause, it is near to becoming actual. Here, becoming actual means existing, as when prime matter receives a form and becomes one thing with it.

PreviousStage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of MotionNextStage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands

Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands

Among the features of things simply as they exist, which do not require a special natural or learned ability, are knowing, being knowledge, and being known. So knowledge and its aspects belong in first philosophy, which studies the general features of existence itself. This discussion has three parts. The first concerns what knowledge is and the features that belong to it by nature; it contains several chapters.

I. Defining Knowledge

Knowledge may be one of those realities whose existence is the same as what they are. Realities of this kind cannot be defined, because definitions are made from broader kinds and distinguishing features, which are general ideas, while each existence is individual in itself. Nor can knowledge be given a complete description. Nothing is clearer than knowledge: it is an inward experience that every living, knowing being first finds in itself, without confusion or doubt. Something so clear cannot be explained by anything clearer. Since everything appears to the mind through knowledge, how could knowledge itself appear through something other than knowledge?572

Some things that are clear in themselves still need reminders and explanations. These help a person notice what they have overlooked, gather up the meaning, and make it clearer. Existence is like this: it is the clearest of things, yet people may still need help noticing it.

Some scholars argue that knowledge needs no definition because anyone who knows something can also know, without proof or reasoning, that they know it.573 Knowing that you know means knowing that your own self has knowledge. And knowing that one thing has a feature requires knowing both—the thing and its feature. If knowledge of knowledge had to be learned, we could not know that we know something without reasoning. But we can. So knowledge of knowledge must be immediate, not learned through proof.

This argument does not show that everyone knows the full nature of knowledge. It shows only that everyone knows it in some way, without distinguishing it from other things. To know that one thing has a feature, you need only have some idea of the thing, the feature, and their relation.574 Logic explains that a judgment requires an idea of what is being discussed, an idea of what is said about it, and an idea of the link between them. Everyone knows they have hearing, sight, hands, feet, and a head. Most people do not know what these things are in their full nature or through a precise description.

II. Why Knowing Things That Are Absent from Us Requires Their Images to Be Present in Us

In our earlier discussion of existence, we showed that things have images in the mind, especially things that do not exist—and even things that cannot exist.575576 We make true, positive judgments about them. For example, we judge that a partner to God is impossible, that two contradictions cannot be true together, and that a mountain of gold or a sea of quicksilver would be a material substance, even though no such thing exists outside the mind. For a judgment that one thing has a feature to be true, the thing being judged must exist in some way in the setting where the judgment is made. These things, then, have existence in some mode. They cannot be described in the outside world as impossible or nonexistent there. A thing does not exist until its existence is necessary; once it exists, it is no longer nonexistent. So what is true of nonexistence and impossibility can be true only in knowledge, not in the outside world.

Here is an objection: if judging something impossible means that it cannot exist, then the mental images of possible things would also be impossible to exist outside the mind. These images are the very essences of the things, and they cannot exist outside the mind in that form. This would leave no difference between what is possible and what is impossible: neither could exist outside the mind in its own way.

The answer is that considering an essence in itself is different from considering it as existing. An essence as it exists in the mind cannot also exist outside the mind, whether it belongs to a possible thing or not.577 Likewise, an essence considered with the condition of existing outside the mind cannot exist in the mind. Mental existence and outside existence cannot turn into one another. But this does not mean that an essence, considered in itself, cannot be described as existing in either way. When the mind judges an essence possible or impossible, the essence must be present in the mind. But the judgment concerns the essence in itself, not the essence as it exists in the mind. Another sign that there is a realm of knowing, where things appear to us, is that many things are truly described as shared, general, kinds, or broader kinds, even though none of these features exists in the outside world. So things must have another realm and another way of existing, where they can be general and have similar features.578

Strong evidence for this realm comes from what happens when the senses receive heat or cold. The images that appear in the senses are not themselves the kinds of heat or cold that we feel in the body.579 They belong to another of the four kinds of quality. If the strong image of heat in the sense of touch were itself something we could touch, the person touching it would feel what is in the sense organ.580 The same is true of taste. The strong sweetness a person senses through the tongue is not an outside sweet thing located in the tongue. If it were, anyone who ate that tongue would taste the same sweetness. These images that are present to the senses are mental qualities, features of the soul rather than the body. Mental heat is not the same kind of thing as heat outside the mind; otherwise it would burn. It is a quality of the soul.

The same is true of mental cold and color, and of letters and sounds we hear inwardly, as in silent speech. If these were audible qualities, they would have to exist in struck or vibrating air. Then every person with normal hearing would hear our inner speech. These examples show us that sensible things have another kind of existence, one that is not itself sensed. They point to a realm beyond bodies and their features.

Those who deny that this knowing presence differs from outside existence raise objections. They say that if outside things existed in our minds, then black and white would exist together whenever we imagined them. They also say that if essences such as a human being, the heavens, or the earth were imprinted in the mind, they would be individual images in one particular mind and so would have to exist outside the mind.581 If these images had the same essence and features as outside things, they would have to show the same effects: heat would burn, a human being would move, grow, and write, and blackness would make the eyes contract. But they do not. If the images did not have the same essences as outside things, then one thing could not have two kinds of existence, which is what we are trying to establish. They also argue that if knowing things meant that those things existed within us, the soul would be both moving and still, hot and cold.

We answered these objections at the start of this book. Knowing things has a mode of existence distinct from their material existence. When an essence exists in this knowing mode, it loses many features and effects that belong to it in matter, including opposition, mutual exclusion, and crowding.

Some people answer that a thing's features may differ according to what receives it. Heat may take on certain features when it exists in physical matter, and lack those features when it exists in a soul that has no position or size, while remaining the same essence in both cases. But this does not answer the objection if the problem concerns heat itself—its warmth and its power to burn. The answer does not explain why those features disappear.582 We must use the account we have already laid out for mental existence.

III. The Proposed Accounts of Knowledge and What They Share

Many people say that the philosophers' accounts of intellect and what it understands are deeply confused. They point out that Avicenna speaks of understanding in several different ways. At times, he treats it as something negative: when he explains that God's being intellect and understood does not add anything to His being or His attributes, he says that it means He is free of matter, which is a lack of something.583 At other times, he describes understanding as images present in the intellect, matching the essences of the things understood. He says that for a thing to understand itself is for its image to be present to itself.584 In The Pointers, he says the same: to perceive something is for its reality to be present to the one who perceives it. At still other times, he treats understanding as a relation. He says that the simple intellect of the Necessary Being is intellect not because many images exist within Him, but because those images flow from Him,585 so that the simple intellect is like the source that creates distinct images.

When the simple, unified intellect is present in us, it can likewise be the source from which our particular kinds of knowledge arise. Avicenna also describes knowledge as a quality that relates to an outside object.586 He says that knowledge is a feature of the soul, a quality in itself and a relation only in an indirect sense. He also says that when the known thing changes, knowledge changes, because it is a quality related to that thing.

The Illuminationist author, Suhrawardi, says that knowledge is appearance, and that appearance is the very reality of light. Light may shine by itself,587 or it may shine on something else. If it shines by itself, it is aware of itself. If it shines on something else, that other thing may or may not shine by itself. If it does not, it may be dark in itself, or it may shine on something else, or it may not shine at all but be darkness for something else. In the first case, that other thing perceives the light. In the other three cases, it does not perceive the light and is not aware of itself. This is the core of Suhrawardi's view: a thing knows itself by being light to itself, and knows something else through a relation of light between two things that are both light.588

These accounts seem to contradict one another. But they can be understood as different ways of describing one view: knowledge is an existence free of matter, an existence from which material coverings have been removed.

If this free existence belongs to itself, it understands itself. If it belongs to something else, as in the case of physical qualities, it understands that other thing—or imagines or senses it. This is the general meaning of knowledge. We will now challenge what the different accounts seem to say, build the view we take to be true, and then, as far as possible, show how the other accounts can be understood in line with it.

First, the claim that understanding is something negative is plainly false. When we look inward while understanding something, we find that something has come to be present to us; we do not find that something has simply gone away. Also, if knowledge were a kind of absence, it would have to be the absence of something in particular. The most obvious thing for it to be the absence of is its opposite, ignorance. Ignorance can be simple or confused. Simple ignorance is simply not knowing something. If knowledge were the absence of this ignorance, it would mean not not-knowing, which is the positive presence of knowledge. So knowledge would be positive, not negative. If it were the absence of confused ignorance, there would be a middle state between knowing and not knowing, because the absence of confused ignorance does not necessarily give us knowledge. So knowledge cannot be the absence of confused ignorance either.

Confused ignorance combines knowledge and ignorance. If knowledge were its absence, that absence would either cancel the knowledge within it, which would mean knowledge cancels itself, or cancel the ignorance within it, which brings us back to the first case: knowledge as the absence of ignorance. Someone might reply that knowledge does not mean the absence of ignorance; it means freedom from matter and its features. This is wrong for three reasons. First, freedom from matter is not true of one person but not another. We would not say that the sun is free of matter in relation to Zayd but not in relation to Amr, as we say that Zayd understands something and Amr does not.589 If knowing something meant that it was free of matter, then instead of saying “Zayd knows that the world began,” we could say “Zayd is free of matter in the claim that the world began.” That is not what we mean.

Second, knowing that something has no position or direction is not the same as knowing something. If knowing meant exactly the same as being free of matter, then whenever we knew that something was immaterial, we would also know it as an object of knowledge. But we do not. Someone may know that a thing is immaterial and still doubt whether it understands anything, or understands itself. A proof is needed to establish that every immaterial thing is an intellect, understands itself, or understands something else. One meaning cannot be both unknown and known at the same time. Third, as we said, when we know something we find a positive state within ourselves, distinct from other states of the soul such as wanting, choosing, fear, desire, or anger. So perceiving something is not simply an absence.

The second account says that knowledge is an image imprinted in the knower. This also fails, for three reasons. First, if understanding were the presence of an image within the knower, we could not understand ourselves. But we know from our own experience that we do. So the argument fails. For us to understand ourselves, either that understanding would have to be our very self, or another image of our self would have to exist within us. Neither answer works. If understanding ourselves were simply our self, then anyone who knew their self would also know that they understand their self. And anyone who understood something that understands itself would know that it understands itself—and would understand its understanding of itself. But that is not what happens.590

The second answer also fails. The image of our self would have to be like our self. That would mean two identical things together, or one thing existing in another when there is no reason to treat one as the container and the other as what it contains. It would also mean that one thing was both a substance and an accident. Our self is a substance that does not depend on something else to exist. But something that exists in a substance after that substance is already present is an accident. Finally, every mental image is general, even if we add a thousand details to it: it can still apply to more than one thing. But we know our self as one particular being that cannot be shared. Anything added to the self can be pointed to as “that”; we point to the self itself as “I.” So knowledge of the self cannot be an extra image of the self.

The second reason the image account fails is that lifeless bodies are also joined to forms, but do not perceive them. So the form's mere presence in a thing cannot be what makes that thing aware of it. If someone replies that knowledge is the presence of an image in something capable of understanding, this defines knowledge by knowledge itself. Our senses receive images too, yet images are not all received in the same way. We sense an object by means of an image from it, and we sense several things together, even when those things have opposites.

The answer that knowledge is the presence of an image free of matter in an immaterial thing also fails. Understanding is a positive state, while freedom from matter is a negative idea. A negative idea cannot be part of the very nature of something positive, such as understanding. So either understanding is simply the presence of the thing, which we have already rejected, or it is another positive state that occurs when the image is free of matter. We will return to this difficult point and show how the account is true in one sense and false in another.591 In any case, it amounts to admitting that perception is not just the presence of an image.

The third account says that knowledge is a relation between the knower and the known, with no further state in the knower.

This is also wrong. As we explained when discussing relations, a relation cannot exist on its own; it exists only when the two things it connects exist. Yet we often understand things that have no existence outside the mind. We also understand ourselves, though a relation between us and ourselves exists only as something we think about. If knowledge were only a relation, we would not know anything unless we first thought of the relation and compared the two sides. But we are always aware of ourselves, whether or not we think about this relation. People who say knowledge is a relation take this view to avoid some problems with treating knowledge as an image, but they overlook that a relation requires both things to exist. Their account would make nonexistent things impossible to know. It would also make all knowledge true, because they take ignorance to mean that a mental image does not match a real thing outside us.

The fourth account, chosen by the author of Al-Mulakhkhaṣ, says that knowledge is a quality in the soul that is also related to an outside thing.592 This view is deeply flawed. First, it would mean that God's knowledge of Himself and of other things is a quality added to His own being. God is one and self-sufficient, so His perfect attributes cannot be the weakest kind of created feature. If knowledge were a quality added to God, God would have existed before that quality and would not yet have known anything. Nor could this quality itself be necessary in itself, since that would mean there was more than one Necessary Being. Then God's knowledge of things would come from something possible and dependent on Him. But the source of all perfection cannot receive perfection from something else.

Also, proof shows that our knowledge of ourselves is not separate from ourselves. If knowledge were a quality, our self would be a quality too, even though it is a substance. In imagination we see high mountains, wide deserts, the sky, and the earth. These are substances, so our knowledge of them cannot consist only of qualities. Anyone who says that every mental image is a quality has no proof for this. If they say that the images are not enough and another quality must be present as well, they must prove it. Suhrawardi's view, by contrast, contains some truth and some error. He is right that when a separate substance knows itself, its knowledge consists in being light to itself; light is existence. This brings us back to our view that knowledge is existence.

What is wrong in his account is that he treats knowing something other than oneself as a relation to it.593 This cannot be right, since knowledge divides into concepts and judgments, general and particular knowledge, while a relation is not divided in those ways. It would also mean that every animal, which has particular forms of awareness, has intellect, since Suhrawardi says that anything aware of something must be light to itself. And according to his view, bodies and sizes can know through this direct presence. He also says that every one of us knows their body directly in this way. We hold that physical bodies, as they exist in matter and extend in different directions, are not aware of anything.594

Our chosen view—that knowledge is existence free of matter and position—also seems to face many objections, but they can all be answered with careful thought. One objection says that a mental image must either match the outside thing, in which case some outside thing must exist for it to match, or fail to match, in which case it is ignorance. How, then, could perception be only a relation between the perceiver and the thing perceived? This was raised by an early commentator on The Pointers. Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi replied that some images match what is outside the mind, and these are knowledge; others do not, and these are ignorance. A relation itself cannot match or fail to match something outside the mind, because it cannot exist there.595

I say that the objector's words suggest that an image that does not match the outside world is ignorance in the sense of having no knowledge at all—not ignorance as a false belief, which is itself a kind of knowledge.596 The word “knowledge” and the word “ignorance” each have two meanings here.597 Otherwise, the objection has no force. In fact, it supports the view that knowledge is the image itself. When a false image exists in the mind, it is certainly one kind of knowledge, even though it does not match anything outside the mind. There is no relation connecting it to an outside thing. So knowledge can exist without such a relation.598

A second objection says that an image is needed only when the thing does not exist outside the mind; when it does exist, knowledge might simply be a relation to it. The reply is that perception and knowledge name the same general reality, whether it appears as understanding, imagining, or sensing. If this reality is an image in some cases, with a relation added to it, then it cannot be a relation in other cases.

Another objection says that if perceiving black were simply having black present in something, then a black body would perceive black.599 The answer is that not every kind of presence is perception. The image must be present in a way free from matter and position.600

A third objection says that if perceiving means having an image that is free of matter, then whenever we know that a thing exists independently, we should know that it understands. And once we know that God is neither a body nor material, we should not need a separate proof to know whether He knows Himself or whether His knowledge is identical with His own being.

I say that knowledge is not the general idea of an image free from matter. If that were all it meant, then merely thinking about this idea would make us sure that a thing knows. Rather, knowledge is an actual existence free from matter. We cannot grasp an existence in its full reality through a mental picture; we know it through its own actual presence.601 If such an existence were present to our intellect, we would know without doubt that it understands itself and what is present to it. No proof would be needed.

A fourth objection concerns knowing ourselves. If understanding ourselves is simply our self, then our knowledge that we know ourselves must also be the self.602 And if that knowledge is the same as our knowledge of ourselves, it too must be the self.603 This would continue without end and create an endless chain of mental combinations.604 But if knowing that we know ourselves is not the same as knowing ourselves, then it seems that knowing ourselves cannot be the self either.605

Al-Tusi, in his commentary on The Aims of the Pointers, reports this objection from al-Masʿūdī. He answers that knowledge of ourselves is our self in one sense, but not in another: the mind can consider one thing in many ways.606

I say that answer does not remove the problem.607 A better answer is this: our direct awareness of ourselves is the very existence of our self. But our idea that we are aware of ourselves is not that existence. It is another mental image, different from our particular self.608609 Our knowledge of that knowledge is yet another image, and so on, until we stop considering it. This does not mean that two identical images exist at the same level. As we have said many times, existence—whether in the outside world or in the mind—has no copy or image that matches it in its own identity. When we know our particular existence through an added idea, that idea is an accident that exists in us, but it is different from our existence and is not its copy. The same applies to knowledge of any kind.610 Each kind of knowledge is a way of existing. We know an existence only through its own presence, not through another image of it. So we can know an existence as a particular only in a general way.

Another objection says that when we see something, the thing we see is Zayd himself, who exists outside us. To say we see only his copy or likeness, they say, would make us doubt the most obvious things. The commentator answers that what we see is Zayd; the act of seeing is the presence of his likeness in the sense organ. Confusing the thing seen with the act of seeing caused the objection.

I say the truth is this:611 the true object of sight is an imaginal individual that exists in the outside world, but not in the eye itself. I will explain this further in its place, if God wills. That is a brief outline of the views philosophers have held about knowledge and the problems with each. Now I will set out more fully the view I have been pointing to.

IV. What Knowledge Really Is

Knowledge is not something negative, like being free of matter. Nor is it a relation. It is existence—but not every kind of existence. It is actual existence, not potential existence; and not all actual existence, but existence free of nonexistence. The more free of nonexistence an existence is, the stronger its being knowledge.

Here is why. First matter is unclear in itself and does not exist in a complete, actual way. It becomes a definite thing only when it takes on a body and the features that come with a body, such as motion.612 A body, simply as a body, does not have existence that is free of nonexistence. If we imagine one part of it existing, the other parts and the whole are absent. If that part exists, the whole is not there; and the other parts are absent too. Existence is either the same as unity or bound up with it. What has no unity has no existence. Likewise, predication and being one and the same depend on unity. What cannot be one with anything has no existence at all.613 No part of a continuous body, even one we mark off in thought, can be said of the whole; and the whole cannot be said of any one of its parts. Yet the body's identity comes from its parts being joined, and it becomes more complete as that connection continues. But how could a thing's completion bring about its disappearance?

In short, a body is a reality that separates itself as it exists, and carries the possibility of its own nonexistence.614 Its existence and the existence of one part—say, a forearm—are the nonexistence of another part or of another body. So a body always carries the possibility of its own passing away. This is existence at its weakest: a thing exists in a way that brings about its own absence. This is like the relation between many things and unity. A group is one, but its unity consists in there being many members.

First matter is weak in a different way: it is pure potential to become many things. A body, by contrast, exists in a way that contains the potential for its own absence. Such a thing is never fully present to itself. And if it is not fully present to itself, nothing else can fully grasp it either. Knowing and perceiving require this full presence. So no one knows a body or its changing features through the body's material image itself. We know it only through another kind of image, not the material, spatial image outside us. That material image cannot exist in something else without being in its material setting or being involved with what is in that setting. The same goes for the material form of a body: it has no existence on its own. Each thing exists only at its own edges and limits, and its edge is outside what it is. But understanding reaches a thing itself and the parts that belong within it.

What we have said shows that existence by itself is not enough for something to perceive or be perceived. It must be an existence without bodily position and direction, which are features of a category of material things. Actual existence, free of these absences, is perception. This may be what earlier writers meant by the further state that occurs alongside the presence of an image: a stronger and more independent existence, not divided into parts and not located in any one region of the material world. Every image that gives us knowledge has this kind of existence. A mental image is not something we can point to in space. What the senses directly perceive is not, in truth, the same as the material qualities called heat or cold, the first things we touch. These qualities are sensed only indirectly. What is directly sensed is an image whose existence is the same as its being sensed. As we have explained, the existence of what is understood and its being understood are one. The directly sensed image is not in a spatial position, although the sense organ and the outside object must be related in space for the image to arise. This spatial relation is not needed for imagination, inner thought, or reason. Nor is the image present in the mind in the same way as an image exists in physical matter. We will explain the differences between these two kinds of presence next.

V. How a Mental Image Is Present to the Soul but Exists Differently in Matter

There are eight differences. First, material qualities crowd each other out.615 Something with one shape or color cannot have a different shape or color at the same time. The same is true of conflicting tastes, smells, and sounds. But mental images do not crowd each other out. The power that brings our senses together can take them all in at once.616 Each of the five senses can also perceive different kinds within its field: sight sees opposite colors, taste senses opposite flavors, and so on. So an image in perception has a different kind of existence.

Second, a large thing cannot exist in a small material thing. A mountain cannot fit in a mustard seed, and an ocean cannot fit in a pond. This is different in perception: the soul receives large and small things alike. It can hold the image of all the heavens and the earth and everything between them at once, without becoming cramped. As our master and leader Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is reported to have said, “The heart of the believer is greater than the Throne.” Abū Yazīd al-Basṭāmī is also reported to have said, “If the Throne and all it contains were in one corner of Abū Yazīd’s heart, he would not even notice.”

The reason is that the soul has no size or position.617 If it did, it would have fixed limits and could not take in anything larger or smaller than those limits. Some part of the thing would then escape it, or some part of the soul would fail to grasp what it received. One thing would be both known and unknown, or both knowing and not knowing, at the same time. This is impossible, both by reason and by experience. We know that the soul is one. When it perceives something large, it perceives all of it with its whole self, not with a part, since it has no parts.

Third, a weak quality in matter disappears when a stronger one arrives. But mental images remain together. A strong image does not erase a weaker one, especially in imagination and thought. The intellect can remember a faint effect after a stronger one, and can picture something small after something large, or something weaker after something more intense.

Fourth, material qualities can be pointed to by the senses and occupy a place in the world. Mental images cannot be pointed to or located in space. Fifth, one material image can be perceived by many people: many people can read the same writing or hear the same sound. A mental image cannot be shared in this way. No one else can look into what is in my imagination,618 or taste what I taste. That is why people say that the fire in the soul does not burn,619 a lover’s burning heart does not heat anything, and the ice in their chest does not cool anything.

When the intellect says that fire burns and water cools, it does not mean that the images in the mind burn or cool. It means that things outside the mind do so. Likewise, when we say that a substance exists on its own and does not depend on something else, we are speaking of the thing represented in the mind, not the mental image itself. The image in the mind can depend on the mind that holds it.

Sixth, when a material image disappears from its subject, it cannot be restored—or replaced by the same kind of image—without new learning or a new cause.620 A mental image, by contrast, can often be brought back once we have formed it, without having to learn it all over again. Seventh, when a material thing is incomplete, it needs a separate cause to complete it. A tree needs water and soil to grow. An animal needs other causes to reach full growth. The same is true of natural and made things: they need causes outside themselves to complete what is missing. But images in the soul, such as the images in a soul that has received divine support,621 can begin incomplete and reach the perfection suited to them through their own resources, without a separate being completing them.

Eighth, the opposite of a material thing cannot be truly said of it. Outside the mind, fire is fire, not nonfire; blackness is blackness, not nonblackness. But mental fire is not fire in the ordinary, concrete sense; a mental body is not a body in that sense. The same is true of colors, sounds, tastes, and smells.622 We can say of them both that they are what they mean and that they are not what they mean, depending on how we use the words: in one sense, the mental image is fire; in another, it is not. This is the key to understanding the point,623 and how one image can be described in opposite ways without contradiction.624

The reason is that this kind of image, stripped of material limits, has a higher and more complete existence. When we affirm that it has material features, we mean that the source and root of those features are present in it. Material images are like molded figures of the more complete images. We deny those material features because the more complete images are too high and noble to exist in this lower material form. This flesh-and-blood animal, made of opposing elements and constantly changing forms, is an image and shadow of the simpler animal in the soul. Above it stands the intellectual animal: one simple reality that gathers within itself all the material and mental members of its kind. Thus there is an intellectual horse, the general model of horses. The same is true of other animals and other kinds of things, as we explained when discussing essences.

The point here is to show how mental images that match material things can also be described in ways that seem opposite to their material forms, without contradiction. This depends on understanding how something can grow stronger or weaker in existence. When existence becomes stronger, a thing can rise out of its earlier kind into a higher kind, even though it becomes more fully what it was. As the common saying goes, once something passes its limit, it turns into its opposite. The same happens when one material being develops: an embryo first takes on a natural form, then a soul, and then intellect. What it could not be said to have earlier can now be said of it, while features that were true of it before may no longer apply.625

VI. On the Claim That Knowledge Is an Accident

In our view, images formed through the senses or imagination do not exist as accidents in the sense organs. The organs are like mirrors and places where these images appear, not the things that contain them. The images themselves are immaterial substances, while their qualities are features of those substances. All of them exist in the soul, as possible things exist through God.

As for intellectual knowledge, the common view is that we know things because their images are imprinted in our souls. Knowledge is then an image of an existing thing, stripped of its matter. It may be the image of a substance or of a quality. But this raises a serious problem, described by Avicenna in The Healing: knowledge must match what is known. If the thing known is a substance that exists on its own, then knowledge of it must match that substance and belong to the same kind. Whatever belongs to the same kind as a substance must fall under the same broad category. But substance is a category said of the things beneath it. So the mind’s image of a substance must itself be a substance. Yet knowledge is usually called a quality of the soul, an accident that exists in the soul. The same thing would then be both a substance and an accident, though nothing that is a substance is an accident. This is the well-known problem. We have already indicated how to answer it, and will return to it later. Avicenna’s answer is that the nature of a substance is to exist outside the mind without depending on a subject. The same description applies to the essence of a substance as the mind understands it: it is an essence that, if it existed outside the mind, would not depend on a subject.626 In the mind, however, it does not exist in that way. Motion is similar: its nature is to be the completion of something that exists potentially, but motion in the mind is not itself a completion of something in that way.

I say that this answer does not satisfy me. If the arguments for mental existence are sound, they show that things exist in the mind with all their features, relations, and meanings, but in a different way from their fading, material existence. We imagine a human being not only as a kind of substance but also as something that exists on its own, understands itself, and does not depend on a subject. Avicenna’s answer cannot explain this. If we applied it to every feature, broader kind, and distinguishing feature of an essence, nothing of the essence would remain in the mind. If the image of an animal in the mind were not a substance, body, living thing, perceiver, mover, or anything else that belongs to an animal, what would make it an animal? Would it be an animal because it is an actual bodily substance that lives, senses, and moves? No. Or would it be an animal because, if it existed outside the mind, it would be an animal?

What could that last claim mean? If it means that this very mental image, as one individual, could exist outside the mind, that is false. The individual in the mind has become general and can apply to many things; it cannot leave the mind and become that very bodily individual with a particular position and direction. That would confuse different kinds of existence and erase their differences. An individual in the mind can be general and apply to many; an individual outside the mind cannot. If instead the claim is that the essence, as it exists mentally, would be a substance if it existed outside the mind, then the image is an accident of the soul. If it existed outside, it would still be a quality of the soul, not a substance or any other outside category. If the claim is that this essence exists in the mind in such a way that, under an impossible assumption, it could become another essence outside the mind, that claim adds nothing. The same could be said of any essence in any kind of existence. We could say: if a substance were an accident, it would exist in a subject; if a body were an intellect, it would have every perfection; if a possible thing were necessary, it would create the world.

This view also leaves no real difference between mental forms and mere likenesses or shadows. A mental image would be like a picture painted on a wall: it would count as a person, horse, elephant, trees, or rivers only because, if it existed outside the mind, it would be those things. But it could never exist outside that surface. The truth is that the intellectual images of substances outside the mind are the real meanings and realities of those things.627 A substance, or a body, has a meaning and a sensible image. Its sensible image is the substance as sensed; its intellectual image is the meaning of substance, understood by the intellect as existing on its own. The intellect understands this without needing another image to be present in the intellect. The same applies to the idea of an animal: it includes the understood meanings of body, life, and sensation. These meanings do not have to be separate existences.628

Nor is the intellectual meaning something that exists in a subject that could do without it. This is a higher, more complete kind of existence. All these meanings can be said of one body as what it is, even though that body exists in a position and direction and none of the intellectual images has a position or direction. It is even more fitting to say that these meanings are one with an intellectual reality. One understood meaning being one with another in intellectual existence is more fitting than an understood meaning being one with something sensed and one with it in sensory existence. Avicenna himself, at the start of the fourth section of The Pointers, says that the understood animal exists in the sensed animal.629 The animal understood as a general kind clearly has an existence that cannot be pointed to or located in space. Yet it is connected to, and one in meaning with, the animal we sense. This does not mean that the intellectual image is an accident in each individual animal.
