The second kind is when the soul’s learned, detailed intellectual forms are present in the imaginative faculty, where it can observe them one by one.705

The third kind is a simple intellect: the intelligibles are present in it in act, not in potentiality, yet it is free of multiplicity and detail. Avicenna points to this simple intellect in the psychology section of The Healing. He says that there are three ways to understand. In the first, the intellect holds an idea in a clear, ordered, detailed form. In the second, the soul has learned an idea but has turned away from it and is attending to something else. We cannot hold many things in view all at once. The third is like what happens when someone is asked a question about something they have learned, or nearly learned, and the answer comes to mind at once. The person is sure of the answer before working out its details. As the person gives the answer, the details and their order unfold in the mind. This immediate certainty is the starting point of the later explanation.

Someone might say that this, too, is knowledge only in potentiality, though close to becoming actual. Avicenna says that is wrong, because the person already has certainty in act and does not need to acquire it through a distant or nearby potential. That certainty must mean either that the person is sure the answer is there whenever they want to recall it, or that the answer is already certain in act. In the first case, the person is actually certain that the answer is present in them; in the second, the answer is certain in act as well.706707708 It is impossible to be sure that something presently unknown is stored in you. You cannot know the state of something without knowing it in some respect. Since your attention is directed to what is actually known, and you are certain that it is stored in you, then in this simple way it is already known to you; you are now about to make it known in another way.

There is something remarkable here. When this person begins teaching someone else, they unfold what they grasped all at once through the second kind of learning, arranging it step by step and alongside the words they speak. One of these is discursive knowledge; the other is simple knowledge. Simple knowledge does not consist of one image after another in the soul. Rather, it is one source from which images flow into the faculty that receives them. It is the active knowledge that gives rise to what we call discursive knowledge and is its source. This is the soul’s universal intellect, akin to the Active Intellect. The detailed forms belong to the soul insofar as it is a soul. If it had no detailed forms, it would have no knowledge belonging to the soul. How the rational soul can have a principle beyond itself, with a kind of knowledge different from the soul’s own, is a question you must examine within yourself.

Pure intellect contains no multiplicity and no sequence of images. It is the source of every form that flows from it into the soul. We should understand separate beings in the same way: their knowledge of things is like this simple intellect. Their intellect does not receive forms, or exist as a picture of the forms in the world considered as soul.709 Every intellectual act of perception is a relation to forms free of matter and its accidents. The soul has this relation because it is a receptive substance shaped by those forms; intellect has it because it is an active, originating substance.

In short, this is what Avicenna says. I reply that this simple intellect can be established only if we accept that the knower becomes one with what it understands, in the way we have proved.710 It is surprising that Avicenna accepted claims like the ones he makes here while strongly rejecting that union. If simple intellect exists in the human soul and in beings wholly separate from bodies and matter, and it contains intelligible meanings, how can it give souls forms that are not already present in it? How can it bring souls from potentiality to actuality through something it does not contain? And how can it store the forms of intelligibles that the soul has forgotten, while remaining simple?

In the same chapter, Avicenna asks what happens to ideas that we learn and later forget. Do they remain fully present in the soul? If so, we would still understand them. Are they stored in the soul, the body, or one of the body’s powers? But bodily powers cannot hold forms grasped by the intellect. Or does each intellectual form exist on its own, with the intellect sometimes attending to it and sometimes turning away? That would be like a person’s reflection appearing in a mirror when the conditions are right. He rejects the first two options and says the last is correct. He also says he will show in the First Philosophy that such forms do not exist separately. This leaves simple intellect as the storehouse for intelligibles. But his account then faces the same question: how could the details of many forms be gathered in simple intellect without accepting that knower and known become one?711

This is one of the central questions of divine philosophy. It opens the way to a special understanding of divine unity, known through direct experience by those close to God.

The question can be settled only by applying principles established earlier in this book: existence is fundamental, and essences are drawn from it; existence can grow stronger or weaker; and the stronger existence becomes, the more it gathers and contains universal meanings and intellectual essences. When existence reaches the level of a simple intellect, wholly free from bodies and dimensions, it becomes all intelligibles and all things in a way more complete and nobler than they are in their ordinary forms.712 Anyone who has not experienced this way of understanding cannot explain simple intellect, the source of detailed knowledge. That is why even many learned philosophers have found it hard to accept. Suhrawardī, for example, rejected it openly in The Discussions, The Pointers, and The Philosophy of Illumination, as did Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī and others like them.

Suhrawardī says in The Discussions that the philosophers in Aristotle’s school explained God’s knowledge of Himself by saying that, since He knows Himself, He must also know what follows from His essence. His knowledge of those consequences is contained in His knowledge of Himself. When we understand humanity, for example, we also understand what follows from it. They then distinguish three cases: detailed knowledge already present; knowledge held in potentiality, ready to be recalled; and the case where someone is asked many questions at once and first grasps, in a single general act, that they can answer them all, then spells out each answer in detail. This general knowledge is one act of knowing many things, but it is not merely potential, because the person feels that it differs from the state before being asked. Suhrawardī says later thinkers found this explanation too loose and incomplete.713

He also writes that saying “knowledge of what follows from a thing is contained in knowledge of the thing itself” is imprecise. A critic could ask whether God knows Himself and what follows from Him together. If not, that is another problem and seems impossible. If He knows both, then since what follows from Him is not identical to Him, His knowledge of Himself differs from His knowledge of what follows. The two acts of knowledge would be separate. And because what follows depends on its source, knowledge of it must depend on knowledge of the source. As for the example of having many answers at once, the critic may deny that many questions are asked together: perhaps each is asked one by one, with an answer after each. Or perhaps before explaining the answer, the person has only a potential ability to give it, and the two kinds of potentiality differ only in degree.

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī makes a similar argument in The Eastern Investigations. He says knowledge is either potential or actual and detailed. The third kind, simple knowledge, is impossible. If one simple intellectual image truly matched many different things, it would have to share their different essences, which is impossible.714 If, instead, simple understanding consisted of different images for different things, then detailed knowledge would already be present, since that is all detailed knowledge means. The account, he says, is therefore confused. Perhaps the philosophers mean only that the forms of many things arrive at once in simple knowledge, while detailed understanding receives them one by one over time. If so, he agrees, but this is no middle stage between pure potentiality and fully actual knowledge. It only means that several acts of knowledge may happen together or one after another.

He adds that their view fails even if knowledge is only a relation: a relation to one thing is different from a relation to another, so many relations would amount to many separate acts of knowledge. A person who is certain they can answer a question knows only that they have the ability to give an answer that will meet it. They do not yet know the answer’s real nature.715 That nature remains unknown, though the fact that the answer will address the question is known. This is like knowing that the soul moves the body without knowing the soul’s true essence. So, he concludes, the philosophers’ account is false, and the proof given earlier shows that one act of knowledge cannot be knowledge of many things.

I say that this question is too lofty and difficult for a thinker like this to reach its depth through reasoning and a store of familiar arguments. If it could be solved by discursive thought and following inherited opinions, Avicenna and those near his level would not have overlooked it. Yet Avicenna’s own writings show a contradiction: he affirms simple intellect while rejecting the union of knower and known.

XVI. Whether the Soul Can Understand Many Things at Once

On the account we have established—that when the soul moves from potentiality to actuality it becomes a simple intellect that is all things—the matter is settled for us. Here is why. Knowledge and understanding are kinds of existence; existence is one with essence, and knowledge is one with what is known. Some kinds of existence are low and weak; others are noble and strong. The weak kind is like a thin outer shell, containing few meanings and fixed on one thing, such as a single quantity, however thick or extended it may be. A noble kind is like the inner core, able to contain many meanings, even if its dimensions are small or it has no dimensions at all, as with the rational soul.

Knowledge also has many kinds. Some are weak, like sensation: one act of sense cannot perceive many different things. Others are noble, like intellection: one act of intellect can grasp countless intelligible things, as happens in simple intellect.716 In general, the higher knowledge is in existence, the more it contains what is known and the more it gathers essences into one. Knowledge belonging to the soul is between imagination and simple intellect. It can relate to two things at once, as when the mind judges that one thing belongs to another. To make that judgment, we must have both ideas present together: the subject and the predicate. Someone judging about two things must have both before the mind at that moment. Otherwise, only one idea would be present, and there could be no judgment. The judgment would then always have to contain several ideas. Likewise, if we know a thing by a complete definition, we know its whole essence. If we could not know all its parts together, we could never know any thing’s essence at any time.

We can also know several truths together because one premise alone cannot produce a conclusion. If we could not know both premises at once, we could never know the conclusion. We also know both sides of a relation together, and a necessary thing together with what depends on it. These arguments show that several acts of knowledge can be present at once.717

This is confirmed by the soul’s experience. When the soul knows many things and reaches the level of intellect, free from the human body’s covering, it does not lose its knowledge. Rather, that knowledge becomes clearer and more open. Having moved beyond the differences of time and place, it has all its known things present at once, as with the separate intellects, whose objects of knowledge are all present together in act.

You may object that when we turn our minds to understanding one thing, we cannot at that same moment turn them to understand something else. I have already pointed out that knowledge, like existence, differs in strength and weakness. Intellectual knowledge is different from imagination and sense perception. When we understand the statement “A human being is a substance, extended, growing, sensing, and rational,” the intellect grasps all these meanings together. An image corresponding to them appears in imagination. If we reverse the words—“rational, sensing, growing, extended, substance”—the meaning grasped by the intellect does not change, but the images in imagination turn around and change their order.

Given this, the difficulty people find in grasping several things at once may come from the imaginative power, which has trouble presenting many different images together. These images are pictures or representations of the intellectual things the soul grasps with its intellect. The intellect itself can grasp them together. The feeling that we cannot understand many things at once may come from imagination’s difficulty in picturing them all at the same moment.718719 Imagination can still hold together images that do not represent intelligible things. That is why it is said: the intellect makes many things one, while sense perception makes one thing many.

XVII. How the Simple Soul Can Understand Many Things

We have already established that a simple thing cannot, by itself and without anything between, give rise to more than one thing.720 But how can one simple power give rise to many acts of understanding? An effect becomes many through one of four things: the cause itself is many; the thing receiving the effect differs; the tools differ; or the effects are arranged in a sequence. The rational soul is simple. Even if it were made of parts, their number could not match its countless acts of understanding. The many acts cannot come from many receivers either, since the receiver is the soul itself.

Nor can the acts depend on one another in a sequence. Understanding black does not depend on understanding white, or white on black. The same is true of many ideas and judgments that do not make one another possible or produce one another. The remaining answer is that the tools differ. The senses, with their different organs, are like scouts bringing reports from different places. They prepare the soul to take in immaterial intellectual forms. Particular sensations multiply because the body moves in different ways to gain what is useful and avoid harm. The soul benefits from these sensations, which prepare it to form its first ideas and judgments. It then combines these, producing endlessly many further ideas and judgments. So the many first ideas arise through the different senses and tools; the ideas we learn arise as the first ones are combined in a natural order, each earlier one helping produce what comes after.

XVIII. Different Ways to Classify Knowledge

As we have said many times, knowledge is immaterial existence itself. Existence is not, in itself, a general kind or species that can be divided into different types by distinguishing features, into individuals by their particular traits, or into groups by added conditions. Every act of knowledge is a simple, individual reality; it does not fall under some more basic universal kind. So when we divide knowledge, we are really dividing what is known, because knowledge and its object are one, as existence and essence are one. This is what is meant by saying that knowledge of a substance is a substance, and knowledge of a feature is a feature. Knowledge of each thing is of the same kind as the thing known.

Some knowledge exists necessarily by itself: God’s knowledge of Himself, which is identical with His being and has no separate essence. All other knowledge is possible by itself. This includes knowledge that is a substance, such as an intellect’s awareness of itself, and knowledge that is a feature. Most philosophers call all acquired knowledge a feature because it exists in the mind. In our account, a feature-like act of knowledge is the existence of the known thing whose form is present to the soul.

We have already said that understanding is not a picture of an object settling inside the soul. The form stands before the intellect, and the soul becomes one with it. The same is true of imagination: forms of any size and number can be present to the soul, not as things lodged inside it, but as things before it, with which the soul’s imaginative power becomes one. Other philosophers say that because these forms match the essences of the things perceived, some are substances and some are features. They call them mental substances and mental features. But as things that exist in the outside world, they are all features, since they exist in a subject—the soul or the intellect. Anything that exists in a subject is a feature. We have shown why this rule is weak and why it is mistaken to say that one thing can be both substance and feature. We have also explained how to answer the problem by following the sound account of knowledge.

There is another way to divide knowledge. Some knowledge is active, some is received, and some is neither. God’s knowledge of all things other than Himself is active, as is a cause’s knowledge of its effects. Knowledge is received when someone other than God learns something that is not their own effect, and this requires a change in the knower—for example, a form appearing in the soul or in one of its bodily powers. Knowledge is neither active nor received when an intellect knows itself, or things whose forms are always present to it, without any new image appearing.721 One act of knowledge can be active in one respect and received in another. This happens with new knowledge that then produces effects, as when a mistaken belief affects material things outside the mind.

Knowledge applies to its different cases in degrees, just as existence does. These degrees differ in priority, age, strength, and weakness. Knowledge of God’s own being is knowledge in the fullest sense. It is the oldest kind of knowledge because it causes all other knowledge, and it is the clearest and most evident in itself. It seems hidden to us because it is so clear and our sight is too weak to grasp it; the very reason it is hidden from us is the reason it is most clear in itself. The same applies to knowledge of a cause compared with knowledge of its effect, and to knowledge of a substance compared with knowledge of a feature that depends on that substance. But “knowledge” as an action, a change in the knower, or a relation—such as teaching, learning, or being a knower—is a shared word used in different senses, or a figurative use.

XIX. A Sign That the Soul Has a Sacred Power

Know that all knowledge comes from the holy world, but souls differ in their readiness to receive it. When the soul is fully ready, it makes no difference whether the knowledge is a first truth or a further conclusion. A person’s grasp of first truths is like the way they grasp a theoretical conclusion once they see the middle steps that prove it: in both cases, the knowledge seems to come without a cause. But nothing exists without a cause. The cause may be open and visible, or hidden from view. The one who places knowledge in ready souls is, in truth, a cause hidden from the senses: the Teacher of great strength in the highest realm. Its action in souls is very subtle. Yet it may come from within to the outward mind, as with the prophets, or appear from the hidden world in the visible world, as with the saints. The visible causes—study, repetition, and listening to a human teacher—only prepare the soul; they do not compel knowledge to appear. That is why these methods may succeed or fail.

Every move from first truths to theoretical conclusions must either come through a human teacher or not. If it does, the chain must eventually reach something learned without a teacher, through the person’s own insight. Otherwise teaching and learning would continue without end.722723 Anyone who studies a subject deeply and keeps at it will discover something that their teachers and earlier scholars did not, whether much or little. The door to the unseen world is open to everyone unless a barrier within them blocks it. As a person works and turns inward, the mind becomes finer, the natural spark grows ready, and the soul becomes like flint ready to strike a flame from the unseen realm or catch one of the lights of the world of pure intellect.

We have already shown that sensing particular things prepares the soul to receive universal ideas. We have also seen that when ideas fit together, the mind can judge that one belongs to another. Often, when the mind holds one idea in view, it forms the matching idea of another because it has sensed particular examples of it. The mind can then become certain that one applies to the other, without getting this knowledge from a teacher, a book, a report, or repeated testimony. So people can learn from themselves. This kind of direct insight is called intuition. People differ in how ready they are for it. Some are so slow to grasp things that they might spend a lifetime on one question and still fail to solve it. Others are the opposite: a slight turn of attention is enough for them to see the answer.

Since people’s minds differ in clarity, strength, and readiness for insight, there may be a soul at the highest level: one that shines brightly with the light of the unseen world and quickly receives knowledge from the source of all good and mercy. Because it is so ready, such a person grasps many truths in a very short time, without searching for them or wanting to do so. The sharp mind moves straight to conclusions without working through the middle steps, then moves from those conclusions to others, until it reaches the furthest human questions and highest human stages. This is called a sacred power. It differs from other souls in both how much it can hold and how it understands. In quantity, it can hold more middle steps in view. In quality, it moves faster from one idea to another, from first truths to derived truths, and from starting points to final conclusions.

It also grasps pure intellectual realities as they are in themselves, not only through general meanings and definitions. Reaching the realities of those intelligible things is the heart of understanding. General knowledge is still a means to reach them, once its meanings are firm and settled in the soul. That is why it has been said, “Knowledge is the seed of direct vision.”724 Most people first set out the question they want to answer and then search for the middle steps that prove it. The sacred soul finds the middle step first, then reaches the conclusion. That is how proofs from a cause work in reality.

XX. Knowing a Cause Gives Knowledge of Its Effect, but Not the Other Way Around

The first claim725 is this: a cause either causes an effect by itself or does not. If it needs some added condition to have an effect, then it is not the real cause by itself. The real cause is the whole made up of it and that condition. The same question applies to that whole, until we reach something that produces its effect by its own nature. Anyone who knows this cause must know that its nature makes it the cause of that effect. If they know the cause as it is, they must know it in the very way that makes the effect follow from it. Once they know that it causes the effect, they must know the effect too, because knowing one side of a relation in the way that brings the relation about gives knowledge of the other side.726 This is the argument found in the books of the philosophers.

I say that there are two kinds of cause. One causes its effect by its essence, as four is the cause of evenness and a triangle is the cause of having three angles. Once we know the essence of this kind of cause, we must know what follows from it, because the effect follows from the cause’s essence. The other kind does not cause its effect through its essence, but through its existence, either in the mind or in the outside world. For this kind, knowing the cause by itself does not give us knowledge of its effect. Nor does knowing that it exists in the general sense of “existing.” What produces the effect is not the essence itself or existence in general, but this particular, individual existence. Until we know that specific existence, we do not know its effect. And, as we have seen, we can know a real existence in itself only by becoming one with it or by knowing something that contains and gives rise to it.727 Then knowledge of its effect is the effect’s own existence, just as knowledge of the cause’s existence is the cause’s own existence.

So if we know a cause in the way described, we must know its effect, and the effects of that effect, all the way through its chain of effects. This answers an argument by Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī. He says that if “knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect” means that knowing the cause’s essence gives knowledge of its effect, that is true only when the effect follows from the essence of its cause.728 If it means knowing the cause as cause and the effect as effect, that is true but not useful, since related things are known together, with neither coming before the other.729 And if it means knowing the cause in every respect, that is also unhelpful, since knowing a whole includes knowing its parts.730

If someone knows every aspect of the cause,731 one of those aspects is that it produces this effect. Yet the whole does not produce its part; if anything, the part helps make the whole.732 But the philosophers mean none of these things. They mean that knowing a cause in the real way that makes it a cause establishes that its effect must exist.733 The cause, with its true causal reality, stands to the necessary existence of its effect as an essence stands to what follows from that essence. Every effect follows from its cause’s essence, whether that essence is existence itself, something other than existence, or something that includes existence.

Someone might object that the cause’s own being differs from its being a cause. The cause’s causal role is understood only in relation to its effect, while its own being is not understood in relation to anything. The First Principle, however, exists in itself and causes everything else. It would be contradictory if its being as a cause had to be understood through its effect.

It would also follow that the cause existed alongside its effect even though it comes before it. Since cause and causal role differ, and since the cause’s own being is not understood through the effect, knowing the cause itself need not give knowledge of the effect.

We answer that the cause’s role cannot be an added, positive feature on top of its essence and existence. Otherwise, that added causal role would itself need another cause, and the chain would continue without end. The cause’s role is its own specific being. But how can one thing be both a substance and a relation, when a relation is a feature? As we explained in the discussion of relations, a substance’s existence differs from its essence as the mind understands it. A substance may cause something by its own reality. When we understand its essence in that way, we do not also understand that it is a cause or stands in a relation. Its being a cause is a different intelligible aspect from the essence of the substance. Existence considered in itself is the substance’s own existence. Considered as causing or relating to something, it is the existence of that relation.734735 This is what a relation really is, not what people suppose when they say relations do not exist in the outside world. Otherwise, statements such as “this is a cause and that is its effect” or “this is a father and that is a child” would be false.736

Someone may then say that the cause has a particular essence, different from the effect, and neither is part of the other. Since they are different, why can we not know one without knowing the other?

Not at all. The difference between cause and effect is not like the difference between Zayd and ʿAmr, or one body and another, where we can think of either while ignoring the other. The particular existence of an effect follows from the cause’s existence. The effect’s existence relates to the cause’s existence as something that follows from an essence relates to that essence.737 The cause’s existence is the effect’s complete existence and perfection. Their difference is like the difference between what is stronger and what is weaker. Complete understanding must match the existence of the thing in the outside world—indeed, it must become one with it.738 So if a thing is the direct cause of an effect by its own nature, knowing it as a cause must directly give knowledge of the effect.

The second claim is that knowing an effect does not give knowledge of its particular cause. Whatever produces a thing must be its cause. If we know the cause because we know some other thing, that knowledge must itself cause our knowledge of the cause. But the effect’s existence is one with our knowledge of it, as we explained.739 So the effect would have to cause, in some way, our knowledge of its own cause.

But if an effect, in its particular existence, follows from a particular cause, then for the effect to cause the existence of that very cause would mean that something comes before itself, which is impossible. Still, an effect is possible in itself: in its essence it is equally able either to exist or not to exist. It therefore needs something to tip the balance, some cause or other, though not necessarily a particular cause. Knowing that an effect exists in this respect gives us knowledge that some cause exists. That is why possibility makes a thing need a cause in general.

Since an effect needs a cause because it is possible, knowing its essence gives knowledge of some cause in general. But the cause produces its effect through its own particular essence. If it produced an unspecified effect, it would need another condition to make the effect particular; then the true cause would be the cause together with that condition. So a particular cause, through its particular reality, produces a particular effect. Knowing the particular cause gives knowledge of that particular effect, but knowing the effect does not give knowledge of its particular cause.

If an effect does not specify its particular cause, one might ask, how does it come from this cause rather than another? The particular effect requires a cause in general. But the particular cause specifies the particular effect.740 The effect does not choose its cause; the cause produces that effect. Since the cause, by its own nature, brings this effect into existence, no other cause can also produce it; two complete causes cannot act on the same effect at once. There are many similar examples. The broad kind “animal” applies equally to “rational” and to other distinguishing features. Animal nature by itself does not explain why one animal is human. It needs some distinguishing feature; in this case, rationality makes it human.

Likewise, a kind needs some particular existence in order to exist as an individual, but its existence as Zayd comes from Zayd’s own particular being. It is not true, as some people say, that certain kinds—such as beings created without matter—bring about their own particular identity. An essence cannot cause individuation, because a thing becomes an individual through its existence, and existence is not caused by essence. Rather, particular existence makes the essence an individual, just as a particular distinguishing feature makes a broad kind into a specific kind. Knowing an individual feature gives knowledge of the kind in that particular case. Knowing a particular distinguishing feature gives knowledge of its specific kind. But knowing that a kind or species exists only tells us that some individual exists, not which one; and knowing that a broad kind exists only tells us that some distinguishing feature exists.

Someone might object that if we directly know the particular existence of an effect, without an added mental picture, then this must also give us direct knowledge of the particular being of its cause. In that case, knowing the cause and knowing the effect would each give knowledge of the other.

That is not so. We have seen that a cause exists more strongly than its effect. The effect’s weak and limited existence cannot contain the cause’s existence or rise to its level. In the same way, knowledge of the effect does not give us full knowledge of the cause. This is why Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī said: “The First Cause is connected to what flows from it to us, while we are connected to it only through that cause. We may therefore observe it only as far as a thing receiving what flows from it can observe its source. We must not compare its understanding of us with our understanding of it, since its understanding reaches farther, is fuller, and contains us more completely.” Anyone who thinks that the First Cause does not know particular things is far from the truth.

XXI. Knowledge of an Effect Requires Knowledge of Its Cause

This question,741 like the one before it, can be settled only by understanding the nature of existence.742 Complete certainty about something requires the intellectual form to match its actual existence in the outside world.743 Anything that has a cause is possible in itself; otherwise, it could not depend on a cause. As we have already said, things do not cause or depend on one another through their essences. If they did, every effect would follow from an essence, the First Principle would have an essence, and knowing any essence would reveal God’s full reality and all the causes of that essence. The parts that make existence complete would then also make an essence complete, since existence would be only an abstract relation. All of this is impossible. Every effect has an essence and an existence. If we consider only its essence, we need to know its parts—its broad kind and the feature that distinguishes it within that kind—in order to understand it.744745

If instead we consider that essence as existing, then, because it is possible, it needs a cause in general. Knowledge of it in that respect must come after knowledge that some cause makes it exist. But if we consider its particular existence, that existence is formed by its particular cause.746 We cannot fully know its particular existence without knowing the reality of that particular cause. In its possible essence, the thing is neither existing nor necessary. In relation to its cause, it must exist and cannot change.747 In the same way, knowing its essence does not require us to know that its cause exists or must exist. But certain knowledge of its particular existence comes only from knowing its cause. Knowledge through the cause is then necessary and cannot change.

Just as one effect cannot have two complete causes acting on it, we cannot have full knowledge of it through some other route, apart from knowledge of its cause.748 Otherwise, there would be two complete causes for one thing in one respect: one cause that brings the thing into existence and another that gives us knowledge of its existence. That is impossible, because our knowledge of the thing is one with the thing itself. If the thing’s existence matches our knowledge of it, the cause’s existence must also match our knowledge of the cause, because one effect has one cause. So we have shown that we can know caused things as they truly are only by knowing their causes.

Someone may object that when we know a building exists, we know that it has a builder, even though the building does not cause the builder; the reverse is true. I answer that knowing the building does not, by itself, reveal who built it. It shows that the building needs a builder. That need belongs to the building itself and follows from its essence. So this is still reasoning from a cause to an effect. Knowing that one thing needs another requires knowing both sides of the relation, so the builder is known as one side of that relation.749 All proofs that begin from effects work in this way. Like proofs that begin from causes, they give knowledge through the relation between cause and effect. An effect is an effect in its own existence, but in its dependence and need for a cause, it shows that some cause must exist. A proof from an effect gives certainty because it shows that some cause must exist; it gives only a likely answer about which particular cause, based on a sign or feature of that cause. This is how the matter has been explained elsewhere.

In general, a belief about something that we have not learned through its causes may be very strong and clear, but it can still change.750 Knowledge that comes from knowing the thing’s causes does not change, even if the effect itself changes. True knowledge of a thing is, in reality, one with its existence. These are among the most subtle questions in divine philosophy, understood only by those who have reached the highest level of knowledge.751 We will explain this further when we discuss God’s knowledge.

As for something that does not depend on a cause or on parts that make it up, knowledge of it is either self-evident, impossible to attain, or possible only through evidence and effects; in that last case, we do not know its full essence. God has no proof or definition.752753 Nothing causes Him to exist, whether as an agent or as an end; nothing makes Him up, whether matter and form or a broad kind and a distinguishing feature.

Yet nothing is without Him. He is the proof of everything and closer to everything than anything else, as the Qur'an says: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein,” and “He is with you wherever you are.”754 He is the proof of His own being, as the Qur'an says: “God bears witness that there is no god but Him”; “Is your Lord not enough as a witness over all things?”; and “What is the greatest witness? Say: God.”

There is a serious problem here, especially for our view that cause and effect belong to existence itself, while essence is only derived from it. Our knowledge of ourselves is identical with our own existence, and our existence is one of the things that has a cause. We have established that knowledge of something caused comes only through knowledge of its cause. If our knowledge of ourselves is so certain, then our knowledge of the cause of our existence should be just as certain. Nothing is more certain than our knowledge of ourselves, because knowing ourselves is identical with being ourselves. Nothing can be more present to a thing than the thing is to itself. So we should know the cause of our existence with equal certainty. But the cause of our existence leads back to the Necessary Being, and we have said that only the Necessary Being can know God’s full reality. As the Qur'an says, “They do not encompass Him in knowledge,” and “All faces are humbled before the Living, the Self-Sustaining.”

One of those who seek God has found an answer to this problem, though words cannot fully express it because the path is so subtle and hard to see.755 We can still point toward it. Since knowing ourselves is identical with our own existence, the knowledge of the cause of our self-knowledge must be identical with the cause’s own existence, not with our existence. The cause’s existence is identical with the cause itself. It is present to itself, not to us. An effect’s existence depends on its cause, but it is not identical with that cause. Knowledge follows the same pattern as existence.

So although we know ourselves through knowledge of our source, our knowledge of that source is its existence, together with its act of bringing us into being. Since the source causes us, our knowledge of it comes before our knowledge of ourselves, just as its existence comes before ours. Knowledge follows existence in strength and weakness, and in being a cause or an effect. A thing exists in itself as an effect, but it exists more fully in its source and cause. Its being with its maker is stronger than its being with itself: with itself, it exists only as something possible; with its maker, it exists as something that must be. All things exist in the First Principle in a way higher than any other way of existing. A prophetic prayer says: “O Being, O Source of being, O One who exists before every existence, after every existence, and gives existence to every existence.”

XXII. Knowledge Through Causes Gives Only Universal Knowledge

Know that we can know a thing either through a form that matches its essence or through its very existence. We know ourselves and the forms present to our souls in this second way. Later philosophers say that God knows things through mental forms added to His being. Any knowledge through an image or form is universal. Even if we add a thousand details to it, the idea can still apply to many things. So, if we know things through their first causes and explanations in this way, we will know all their effects, even particular individuals, only in a universal way.

The philosophers who defend this view, such as Avicenna and his followers Bahmanyār and others, explain it as follows.756 In The Healing and The Salvation, Avicenna says that the Necessary Being cannot understand things by learning them from those things. Otherwise, either the things He understands would make up His own being, or understanding them would be an added feature of His being. In the first case, His being would depend on things. In the second, He would not be necessary in every respect.757 He would depend on something outside Himself and would have a state that came from another thing, which would mean that another thing could affect Him.758 The principles we have already established rule out these possibilities.

Since God is the source of all existence, He understands from Himself what He causes to exist. He is the source of complete beings directly, and of things that come to be and pass away through their kinds first, and then, through those kinds, through their individuals.759 He cannot know changing things as changing, by a knowledge tied to one time and one individual. He cannot know at one time that something exists and at another that it no longer exists. If each state required a separate image, neither image would remain alongside the other, and God’s being would change. On the other hand, if He knew perishable things only through their abstract essences and what follows from them, He would not know them as perishable. And if He knew them as joined to matter, its features, time, individuality, and composition, He would know them through sense or imagination, not intellect.

So God knows every thing in a universal way, yet no particular thing, not even a speck in the heavens or the earth, escapes His knowledge. It takes a subtle mind to understand how this can be. Here is how it works. When God knows Himself and knows that He is the source of every existent thing, He knows the first beings that come from Him and what follows from them. Every thing must be made necessary in some respect by its cause. These causes lead to one another until they bring about particular events. God therefore knows the causes and how they match their effects. He knows what must follow from them, the time between events, and their cycles. He could not know the causes without knowing these results. This lets Him know particular things through their qualities, as one kind of thing, or through their relation to a particular time or state. If we consider that state together with all its features, it too is unique. It depends on the causes that make each kind appear in its own particular individual. In this way, a particular thing can have a description that belongs to it alone.

Avicenna continues: if you know all the movements of the heavens, you know every particular eclipse, conjunction, and separation that occurs. You know them in a universal way. You can say of a certain eclipse that it will happen after a certain period of motion, at a particular time, from a particular direction, and in a particular season; that the moon will move from it toward a given opposite position; and that a certain interval will separate it from a similar eclipse before or after it.760 You know every feature of each eclipse, yet you know it universally, because the same description could apply to many eclipses. Still, through some proof you know that this eclipse will happen only once.

This does not make the knowledge any less universal, if we remember what was said earlier. That was Avicenna’s account. His view is that God knows every existing thing, including each particular, but knows each one through a set of universal qualities and relations that identify it alone.761 He does not mean that God knows only the kinds of things and misses their individual features. Some later philosophers, including Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi and his peers, disagreed with Avicenna about forms being established in God’s being. But they did not complete the account of knowledge either. They did not reach the explanation they wanted. We have answered their objections to Avicenna and shown where their arguments fall short. God willing, we will explain the true way God knows things later.

XXIII. Knowledge of Particular Things Must Change If They Change

In The Healing, Avicenna tries to explain how particular things can be known without changing the knower. He says: if you knew an eclipse in the way it happens, or remained forever as you are, you would know not merely the general idea of an eclipse but every eclipse that occurs. Its happening and its absence would be the same to you, and would not change anything in you. In either case, your knowledge would be the same: that an eclipse with certain features occurs after another eclipse, or after the sun reaches a certain position, after a certain length of time, and so on. Your statement would be true before that eclipse, while it occurs, and after it. But if you include time in your knowledge and know at one moment that an eclipse is not happening, then at another that it is happening, your knowledge cannot remain the same. A new act of knowledge would arise in you. You could not be as you were before once the eclipse occurred. And you are a being in time and moments, while the First Being is not; it is even less fitting to describe Him as making a new judgment about something from within one time and then another.

To explain: knowledge received from things, rather than from their first causes, must change when those things change. If you know Zayd is in the house while he is there, and then he leaves, either your first knowledge remains or it does not. If it remains, it is no longer knowledge; it has become error. The belief has changed in quality, from knowledge to ignorance. If it does not remain, then the change is even clearer.762 Some people say that knowing something will exist is the same as knowing it exists once it does. This is wrong for two reasons.

First, if it were true, then if we knew today that a future night would come, we would already know it was night when that time arrived—even if we were in a place where we could not tell night from day.763 In the same way, if we knew the sun would rise later, we would know it had risen when it did, even if we could not see it or hear about it. But that conclusion is false, so the claim that leads to it is false. Second, knowledge must match what is known. “This will exist” differs from “this exists now.” The first means that something absent now will exist later. Since these two states differ and cannot hold at once, the images in the mind must differ too. Knowledge taken from changing things must change with them. Knowledge that comes from a higher source and another beginning does not follow its object in this way.

Al-Tusi writes in his commentary on the treatise on knowledge that many things may differ either in their natures or in number while sharing one nature. Things that share a nature may either fail to exist together or exist together. The first kind must exist with or in time; the second must exist in or with space.764 Time is the first cause of change, because it continually passes and changes what exists in it or alongside it. Space is the first cause of plurality among things that exist together.765 This means that their parts have an order and stand in different positions: one part is in a certain direction or at a certain distance from another.766 Anything with this kind of arrangement is material.767

When universal natures exist as many individuals, their first causes of individuality and distinction are time, as with movements; space, as with bodies; or both, as with changing individuals. A nature that is not in time or space is not tied to either. We do not ask when or where humanity exists by itself, or when five is half of ten. But once we mean this human being, or these particular fives and tens, their individuality may tie them to a time or place. Even different kinds of things, such as the heavenly bodies and the universal kinds of earthly elements, can still be tied to time and space.

With this in mind, we can return to the question. If something is perceived as belonging to a time or place, it is perceived only through a bodily tool, such as an outer or inner sense. Such a tool perceives changes that are present in its own time and judges them to exist. It misses what belongs to another time and judges it absent, saying it was or will be but is not now. It perceives separate things that can be pointed out and judges where they are and how far away they are. But a perceiver that is not limited in this way would perceive fully. It would know which event occurs in every time, how long it lasts, and how much time lies between it and any earlier or later event. It would not judge anything absent; it would know that each thing exists in its own time and not at other times. It would know where every individual exists and how it relates to every other thing in every direction, including the distances between them. It would know all of this as it truly is, without judging things to be here or there, present or absent, now existing or not existing. Such a knower is not in time or space, so all times and places are equally present to it.

Only a being that exists in a certain time and place is limited to saying “now,” “here,” “present,” “absent,” “in front of me,” or “behind me.” A being that knows everything knows all things most fully. It does not judge some things absent, but knows every thing in the “clear book” of existence: what has passed, what is present, what will come, and whatever else can be said of things. That is how a timeless knower knows particulars in a universal way. The image is like a rolled-up scroll. A reader looks at one letter after another and loses sight of what came before or what comes later. The person holding the whole scroll sees all its letters at once, with the same relation to each one. This kind of knowledge cannot belong to a being in time or space. It needs no bodily tool or separate image. Nothing, universal or particular, can escape it. Not even a leaf falls without its knowing.

Particular knowledge in the narrower sense—knowing something through a bodily tool, at a certain time and place—belongs only to a bodily perceiver. So saying that God does not know particulars in this bodily way does not diminish Him. It only confirms that He has no bodily senses. Such knowledge would change His being and His essential attributes. It changes only what is known and the relations between Him and those things.

I see several problems with this account. First, as we have explained, bodily matter is a source of absence and ignorance.768 Prime matter, as it is in itself, has no image that matches it in reality. The same is true of absences, possibilities, and other weak or unfinished kinds of existence. If we try to understand prime matter as it is, we cannot—not because our intellect is weak, but because prime matter itself has no form in existence, only a capacity to receive forms. The capacity for a form is not the form. This applies to material bodies and to things that have position and shape as well.

Second, philosophers have argued that something cannot be understood as a sensible thing except through a bodily tool.769 Their argument is conclusive. Third, the way a thing exists in reality does not change depending on who perceives it.770 A material thing is always material in itself.771 A thing that changes in itself always changes. The reality of space and spatial things is that each part is separate from the others and does not exist together with them. This does not change for different perceivers. Even if the eye were as large as the greatest sphere, the difference between near and far would remain.772

The same applies to time and timed things: each part of time makes the others absent, so no two parts can exist together. We have shown that all substantial forms in matter, whether heavenly or earthly, have changing existence and come into being anew at each moment. How can an existence that changes in its very nature be fixed, eternal, and unchanging for some other knower?

Fourth, knowledge of things must come either from the things themselves, be identical with those things, or come from their causes in a cause-and-effect order. If knowledge comes from the things themselves, it must change when they change. If it is identical with the things, the change is even clearer. If it comes from causes, this can mean two things. One: the causes are known through separate intellectual forms, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, including Avicenna, usually say. Those universal forms are arranged by universal causes and lead to universal results. They may include particulars in a universal way, but they do not tell us about each individual as an individual. Even a thousand added details cannot make an image-based idea apply to only one thing. The other possibility is that knowledge is the existence of the things themselves. This is the fullest kind of knowledge.773 Through it, all things—universals and particulars, their natures and their individuals, with all their features and states—are known as they are. But this account depends on understanding the simple intellect of the Necessary Being and the separate luminous intellects, which contain lower things in a higher way. These are keys to the unseen world. Through this kind of knowledge, every existent thing, even a lifeless object, is alive.

Fifth, for this philosopher, knowledge is not a relation alone. He defines it as the form of a thing being present in the soul.774 A form present in matter is not any of the four kinds of perception he recognizes—sensation, imagination, estimation, or intellection—because each requires some degree of separation from matter.775 A form embedded in matter is not free of matter, much less free of the features and relations that come with it. If such a material form were directly perceived as it exists in matter, there would have to be a fifth kind of perception, although perception has already been limited to those four.

This confirms what I have argued: merely being related to something that exists does not, by itself, amount to intellectual knowledge. Avicenna makes the same point in The Healing when explaining God's knowledge. He warns us not to think that God's intellectual relation to things is a relation to them in whatever state they happen to exist. If it were, every cause that produces a form in matter would itself be an intellect, simply because that form could be made an object of thought by separating it from matter.776

For an intellectual relation, the object must be present as something that can be understood. If God's knowledge depended on things as they exist outside Him, He would know only what exists at a given moment.777 He could not know a thing before it came to exist. Nor could He know Himself as the ordered source of that thing until He actually brought it about.778 Yet God's own nature is such that every existence can proceed from Him. Knowing Himself as that source therefore includes knowing what can proceed from Him, whether or not it yet exists outside Him. The divine world of knowledge embraces both actual and possible beings.

That is the end of Avicenna's argument. The point is that the existence of an object and a knower, taken separately, is not enough for intellectual knowledge of the object. The object must be present in a form that can be understood. It must have a way of existing as something known, not merely a material existence outside the knower. Forms that are separate from matter can have this kind of existence. Material things, considered only in their material existence, cannot enter an intellectual relation in that same way.

XXIV. Explaining the Different Meanings of “Intellect”

Know that, as we will explain in the Book of the Soul, the human soul has two powers: one for knowing and one for action. These two powers cannot be separated from each other, unlike the powers in other animals.779 As for the power of action, human acts can be good or bad. We may know that something is good or bad without learning it through reasoning, or we may need to reason it out.780 Reasoning it out requires fitting premises. Three things are involved: a power that distinguishes good from bad; the premises used to work out what is good or bad; and the actions themselves, which are called good or bad.

The word “intellect” is used for all three, but in different senses.781 First, it can mean the power that distinguishes good from bad. Most people mean this when they say that someone is intelligent. They might say that Muʿāwiya was intelligent, though some would refuse to call him so and say an intelligent person must be religious. In this use, “intelligent” means wise and good at working out what good to do and what evil to avoid.

Second, speakers may say “reason requires this,” “reason rejects that,” or “reason accepts or refuses this.” Here, they mean what most people accept at first glance: ideas or opinions accepted by all or most people, and judgments people commonly praise.

Third, ethics books use “intellect” to mean sticking to tested and familiar actions over a long time, until those actions form a habit or character. This sense relates to the conclusions reached by practical reason as the starting ideas of thought relate to the theoretical intellect.

As for the knowing power—the “intellect” discussed in the Book of the Soul—the philosophers use the word either for the power itself or for what it understands. What it understands may be an idea or a judgment that the soul has from birth, or something it learns. Sometimes “intellect” means only the knowledge gained through learning.782

The power itself can receive knowledge of the realities of things. It is either empty of every form or not. If empty, but able to receive forms, it is like prime matter: it has only the power and readiness to receive forms and has not yet become any one of them. In that state it is called the potential or material intellect. If it is not empty, then it either contains only first principles, or it also contains conclusions reached through thought.783

If it contains only first principles, which are tools for gaining further knowledge, it is called the intellect in habit. It has the ability and habit of reaching conclusions and can move toward the intellect in act.784 It is not yet the intellect in act, because no actual intellectual existence has yet been formed. First principles and general ideas alone do not make a thing fully actual; an indefinite, common idea must become a specific thing. In the world of thought, first principles relate to detailed intellectual forms as the general idea of a body relates to particular kinds of physical thing. A physical thing does not exist outside the mind through the idea of body alone; it must become a particular thing with its own nature. In the same way, the intellect does not become actual through the general idea of existence, thinghood, or simple principles such as “one is half of two” and “the whole is greater than one of its parts.”

If the soul at this level has many first principles, strong readiness, and quickly receives intellectual light, it may be like a wick that is so full of heat it almost lights itself. This is called the sacred power, as in the verse, “Its oil would almost shine even if no fire touched it.” Otherwise, it remains the intellect in habit. If it has also gained theoretical conclusions, these are either not present to it now but can be brought to mind as soon as it turns its attention to them, or they are present and clearly in view. In the first case it is called the intellect in act; in the second, the acquired intellect. At this level, if it sees these forms in the source from which they flow, it is called the Active Intellect.785

People argue about whether “intellect” means the soul at one of these levels, the level itself, or the forms present in the soul. This argument is not very useful, since intellect, knower, and known are one in each of these levels. Farabi says that earlier philosophers used “theoretical intellect” in four ways: potential, actual, acquired, and active. They did not count the intellect in habit because it is not much different from potential intellect in its degree of actuality. Both are still potential, though one is closer to being actual.786

The potential intellect is either the soul itself, a part of it, or one of its powers, ready to draw out the essences or forms of all existing things, without their matter.787788 It can make all these forms into its own form or forms.789 The forms drawn out of matter are called intelligibles when they become forms in this knowing power. They receive their name from the power that knows them.790

This power is like matter that receives forms. Imagine wax that receives an engraved figure or shape across its whole surface and depth, until the whole piece of wax becomes that shape. This helps us understand how forms become present to the power that resembles matter and a subject for those forms. It differs from physical matter because physical matter receives figures only on its surface, not throughout its depth.791 Yet this knowing power does not remain separate from the forms, with its own essence set apart from them. It becomes those forms themselves. Imagine a shape pressed into wax so that it extends through its length, width, and depth. The wax then becomes that shape. This is how we should understand forms becoming present to the power that Aristotle calls the potential intellect. While the forms of things are not in it, it is intellect only in potentiality. When they appear in it in this way, it becomes intellect in act.792793

Before they are drawn out of matter, the forms are intelligible only in potentiality. Once they are drawn out, they become forms of this knowing power. They become intellect in act because they are now intelligible in act. Being an actual intelligible and being actual intellect are one and the same.794 To say that the power knows in act means nothing other than that the intelligibles have become its forms and it has become those forms.

Before they become intelligible in act, the forms themselves may have other features: they may be somewhere, have a position, be a quantity, have bodily qualities, act, or be acted upon. These features can belong to them one at a time or in different subjects.795 Once they become intelligible in act, many of those features fall away and their existence changes. The intellect may understand the meaning of “where” without itself being somewhere, or the features that make one place more specific than another.796

Once the forms become intelligible in act, they are counted among the things that exist, and all existing things can be understood and become forms of this power. So actual intelligibles are also actual intellect. They can be understood too. The thing understood is the same as the intellect that understands it, but in a different respect. One form can make the power actual in relation to itself, while the power remains only potential in relation to another form not yet present. Once that second form appears, the intellect becomes actual through both forms. If it becomes actual through all intelligibles and is itself one of the things understood, then when it understands itself it understands nothing outside itself.797798799

If some things are forms that have never been in matter, the intellect does not need to draw them out of matter. It finds them already separate and understands them.800801 Their existence as understood forms is the same as their existence in themselves before anyone understands them.802 The same applies to what has become intellect in act in us: its actual intellect consists in the intelligible forms present in it.803804

These separate forms can be understood fully only after most or all other forms have been understood and the acquired intellect has arisen.805 At that point, all those forms become forms of the acquired intellect. The acquired intellect is like the matter or subject that receives them; the intellect in act is like the form of the acquired intellect. The intellect in act is in turn like the subject and matter of the acquired intellect. It is the form of the potential intellect. In this way, forms begin to descend toward bodily forms in matter. Before that, they rise, step by step, away from matter in different degrees, ordered by their level of completeness. The most complete form gives form to what is less complete, until we reach the acquired intellect. From there, forms continue downward to the potential intellect, the other soul powers, and nature.806

This is the end of Farabi’s account. It clearly supports the view that the knower becomes one with what it understands. It also says that a person can become a simple intellect that gathers all intelligibles within it. Given such direct statements by Farabi, by the author of The Theology of Aristotle, attributed to Aristotle, and by Porphyry, whom Avicenna says wrote a book on intellect and intelligibles and defended their union with the Active Intellect, how can later thinkers reject this honored teaching without first understanding it? Anyone who has not reached it should follow the advice Avicenna gives at the end of The Pointers.

XXV. Alexander’s Account of the Intellect, Following Aristotle

In his treatise, Alexander says that Aristotle described three kinds of intellect.807 First is the potential intellect. By “potential,” I mean a subject that can become something through receiving a form. Prime matter is potential because it can become any kind of thing. In the same way, the intellect that has not yet understood anything is potential. It has not yet become one of the things it can understand, but it can become all of them.808809 The power in the soul that is like this is called the potential intellect. It is not yet any existing thing in act, but it can become able to understand all existing things by receiving their forms.810

The universal perceiver must not already be one of the things it can perceive. Otherwise, when it tried to understand things outside itself, its own form would get in the way and block them.811 The senses show this. The eye has no particular color of its own, so it can see colors; the air used for smell has no smell of its own, so it can receive scents.812813 Touch does not sense heat, cold, softness, or roughness by being exactly like the thing it senses. If it were itself a natural body, it could not be free of all the qualities it perceives.814 This does not mean it is free of every bodily quality, only that it is free of the particular things it perceives. It could not perceive them if it already had them.815

The intellect, too, must not be one of the things it distinguishes. It can understand all things because it can become all things it understands.816 So it is not any existing thing in act; it is all things in potentiality. This is what “potential intellect” means. The senses are bodily powers and are acted upon.817 Each sense perceives only a limited range of things. The intellect, however, does not understand through a body or as a power belonging to a body, and it is not acted upon in the same way. It is not any existing thing in act or a particular thing that can be pointed to. It is a receptive power for forms and intelligibles. This is the potential intellect found in every human being with a complete soul.

The second kind is the intellect that has begun to understand and has the ability to understand more. It can take the forms of intelligibles into itself. It is like a person who has learned a craft and can now use it on their own. The first intellect is not like a trained craftsperson; it is like someone who has only the ability to learn the craft.

The third kind is the Active Intellect, which is different from the first two. It makes the potential intellect an intellect in act by giving it the habit of understanding. Aristotle compares it to light: just as light makes colors visible in act, the Active Intellect makes the potential intellect actual by giving it the power to understand. By its nature, the Active Intellect is intelligible in act because it produces acts of understanding. It is also an intellect, since the forms that are in matter become intelligible in act when the intellect separates them from matter. Once each form is understood, it becomes both actual intelligible and actual intellect. Before that, it was neither by nature.818

The Active Intellect may govern what happens in this world on its own, returning things to their higher, immaterial principles. Or it may do so through the motions of the heavenly bodies. Or nature may act through both the intellect and those motions.819820 It may seem that the Active Intellect should not govern lowly things, as some people who deny the unseen world have thought. But there is no reason to think these actions beneath it. Everything it does is wise and well ordered. In general, there is an intellect and care guiding what happens here, just as the other intellects complete the souls of the heavenly bodies. Whether our souls can understand through this intellect, and whether it is present in us from the start or acquired, is another question.821 But the soul does not receive it as a place receives an object. The soul changes into the intelligibles, as matter changes into forms. The sense power also becomes one with the sensible forms.822

This is the end of Alexander’s treatise. I have quoted it to strengthen the case that the soul can become one with the Active Intellect and with the intelligibles. Since this point is very subtle and difficult, it needs more explanation. Perhaps those ready to seek it will find a way to reach it.

XXVI. Answering a Difficulty About the Potential Intellect Becoming Actual

You may see two problems with saying that the potential intellect becomes intellect in act. First, as we said earlier, this seems to mean that one reality changes into another. The human soul is a natural form belonging to a body. Together with the body, it makes one natural kind: the human being.823 How, then, can it become an intellectual substance and an intelligible form, separate from matter and bodies? We have already pointed to the answer: a thing’s existence is not the same as its essence.824 Existence can grow stronger. Through a continuous process, a thing can move from one kind of existence toward another. This is like black becoming deeper, or heat becoming stronger.

Second, philosophers say that a body is made of two substances: matter and form. A body has an extended form, but it also has the potential to receive other forms. One simple thing cannot be actual in one respect and potential in another at the same time. So a body must be made of two parts: one that is potential and one that is actual. Philosophers also argue that the human soul survives death. If it could be destroyed, it would have both the potential to be destroyed and the actual state of remaining alive. Anything that can be destroyed can also continue to exist, so the soul would have to be made of a potential part and an actual part. This is impossible, because the soul is simple and not made of outer matter and form. If that is so, how can the soul be matter for an intellectual form?

We answer that composition is required only when something is potential and actual with respect to the same perfection,825 or with respect to different perfections at the same level, whether sensory or intellectual. A body’s physical form is actual in one respect, while its potential to move is another respect. The soul’s existence as a natural form can be actual, while it is potential to become an intellectual form. These two sides do not require two separate subjects.826 The soul’s being the highest form in the natural world does not conflict with its being the first matter of the world of intellectual forms. It is the bridge between them. No natural thing becomes intellect until it has passed through the lower levels of physical matter, plant life, and animal life.

We have already said that abstracting a sensible form to make it intelligible does not mean deleting some features and keeping others. It means moving from material existence to intellectual existence, by first moving through sense and imagination. The same is true of the soul. The sensing soul is the first level of animal life, after it has passed through the levels of elements, lifeless matter, and plants. At first, it senses in act but only imagines in potentiality, as with certain simple animals that have no imagination, such as worms, snails, and shellfish. Once imagination develops, the soul imagines in act and understands only in potentiality. This potential intellect can both understand and be understood only in potentiality. When the soul takes on intellectual forms, it becomes both knower and known in act. Its existence then becomes a new kind of existence, beyond the natural world and part of the intellectual world. The earlier levels belonged to the natural world or to the world between nature and intellect.

XXVII. How the Potential Intellect Becomes Actual Intellect

In The Origin and Return, Avicenna explains how the potential intellect becomes intellect in act, even though in his other books he rejects the idea that the intellect becomes one with what it understands. He says that when a form free of matter and its features becomes one with the intellect, it makes the intellect actual by being present in it. It does not remain separate from the intellect as a body's form is separate from its matter. If the intellect were separate from the form and understood it, then it would need another inner form in order to understand it. The same question would arise about that second form, and the chain would never end.

He then asks whether the intellect in act is the form itself, the potential intellect that receives the form, or both together. The potential intellect cannot become actual simply because the form is present. Either it understands the form or it does not. If it does not, it remains potential. If it does, then it must understand the form either by gaining another form or simply because this form is present in it.827 If it needs another form, the chain never ends. If the form is understood simply because it is present, then either the mere presence of a form is enough, or it must be present to something capable of understanding.828

If mere presence is enough, then matter and the bodily features joined to forms would also be intellects, since forms are present in them. Natural forms exist in real things, mixed with other things rather than separated from them. But what is mixed with something else is not the same as what is pure and unrestricted.829 If, instead, the form must be present to something capable of understanding, then we have only said that it is present to something able to receive it. That restates the claim without explaining what makes it understood. So understanding is neither the form's bare presence in the potential intellect nor a separate image taken from it. The intellect in act is not simply the potential intellect as a receiver of the form.830

Nor can the intellect in act be the form alone while the potential intellect remains a separate subject that receives it. In that case, the intellect in potentiality would be a subject, not an intellect in potentiality. The form would be actual intellect by itself, and could not also be potential intellect. Nor can the actual intellect be the two together, the receiver and the form. Suppose it understands something outside itself. It would then need an image of that thing inside itself, and that image would be another form. It would not be the very form whose nature we are trying to explain.831 But the form under discussion is supposed to be the first one that makes the potential intellect actual.832 The same difficulty returns if we say that the intellect understands itself through parts: a part like matter, a part like form, or both. Each part would have to understand itself through one or both of those parts.833

Each option fails. If the part like matter understands itself, the part like form does no work. If the part like matter understands itself through the form-like part, then the form becomes the receptive, potential part and matter becomes the active form—the reverse of what was required.834 If the matter-like part understands itself through both parts, its form would be more than itself, which is impossible.835 The same reasoning applies to the part like form,836 and to the claim that each part understands every other part.837

The three options are therefore ruled out. An intellectual form relates to the potential intellect differently from the way a natural form relates to physical matter. When an intellectual form is present in the potential intellect, the two become one. The receiver and what it receives are no longer separate in their being. The actual intellect, in the full sense, is the abstract form itself. If a form makes another thing an intellect by being present in it, then, when the form exists by itself, it is even more fully an intellect. Heat makes a body hot, so heat by itself would be even more able to heat; whiteness makes a body bright to sight, so whiteness by itself would be even more visible. The form does not need another intellect to understand it. The potential intellect already knows itself as a power able to understand other things. This shows that every essence free of matter and its features is intelligible and intellect in act by itself.
