I suspect that Avicenna argued this way to make room for the view held by Aristotle’s followers, rather than because it was the account he himself would have given. Otherwise, he would have had to answer several objections to ideas he and other philosophers defend. The first is that we can choose the first option: the potential intellect itself becomes actual when the abstract form is present, just as the sense power becomes actual when a sensible form is present. Avicenna asks whether the form is understood because it is present in the intellect in any way, or because it is present in something capable of understanding.

The right answer is the latter: it is understood because it is present in a being that can understand. We are not trying to define838 or explain the cause of how an abstract form is understood, so this does not make a thing explain itself. The point is that an intelligible form exists in the potential intellect differently from the way a natural form exists in matter. Matter cannot understand, and forms mixed with bodily features cannot be understood as they are. But abstract forms can be understood by the potential intellect because it can receive them. Another way to put it is that the potential intellect understands an abstract form because it is present as something without position to a being that also has no position.839

Second, the potential intellect is the human rational soul. If it becomes the intelligible form in act, it seems that the human being changes into a separate intellect. Avicenna rejects this kind of change between substances, especially when neither substance is material.840 But the soul’s existence can grow stronger, as we have explained in our discussions of potentiality and change.

Third, the number of separate intellects would increase every time a potential intellect became actual.841 There would also be many individuals of one human kind without matter or any connection to matter. Fourth, Avicenna’s claim that an intelligible form does not need another intellect to understand it depends on saying that the potential intellect knows itself as something able to understand. But, in their account, the potential intellect is not a separate being whose own reality is present to itself in this way.842

Anyone who accepts this high and subtle teaching must examine many basic questions about reality and depart from the path followed by most people. That is what happens when someone seeks the truth about God and leaves behind the familiar resting places. God knows best.

XXVIII. First Principles, Their Relation to Later Principles, and the Defense of the First Principle

First principles cannot be learned through definitions or proofs. In our understanding of things, there are basic ideas such as existence, thing, and being present. These cannot be defined, because they have no parts and nothing is clearer than they are. In our judgments, a first principle is that affirmation and denial cannot both be true of the same thing, and that one or the other must be true. This principle cannot be proved. Any proof of it would go in a circle.

A proof establishes one claim by showing that, if it is true, something else must be true, and if it is false, something else must be false. But if a proof could itself be neither true nor false, it would not prove anything. So a proof of the first principle would already depend on the principle being true. If we tried to prove it through another claim, we would end up proving it by itself. The other basic and reasoned judgments all depend on this first principle. It is the starting point of judgment and needs no further proof.

The Necessary Being is pure, unrestricted existence. A possible thing, by contrast, has a limited kind of existence. To say “this is a sphere” means that it exists as a sphere and not as a human, plant, animal, or some other kind of thing. A possible being has a limited existence because it is not all other kinds of existence. In the same way, every judgment other than the first principle is that principle with some added condition. To say “everything is either necessary or possible” means that everything is either necessary or not necessary, or possible or not possible. This is the first principle stated with a particular subject.843

For example, “the whole is greater than its part” means that the whole’s being greater than its part is not false, so it must be true; both truth and falsehood cannot be absent.844 The claim that things equal to one thing are equal to each other also depends on the first principle. If things of the same kind are equal to one thing but not to each other, their nature would have to be the same and different at once. The claim that one thing cannot be in two places at the same time follows in a similar way: if one thing were in two places, it would not differ from two things there. The second thing would then be both present and absent. So these two judgments depend on the claims that truth and falsehood cannot both hold, and that one or the other must hold. The same analysis applies to other basic and reasoned judgments.845

This is why philosophers and other thinkers agree that a person who denies this first principle cannot be persuaded through debate.846 They give three possible explanations. The person may not understand the terms. Or the person may stubbornly refuse to accept the principle. Or arguments leading to opposite conclusions may seem equally strong, leaving the person unable to decide which is right.

In the first case, explain the meanings of the terms. In the second, some philosophers propose beating or burning the person, saying, “Being beaten and not being beaten are one; being burned and not being burned are one.” I say that a case of this kind belongs to a physician, not a philosopher. Such obstinacy is not simply a lack of developed understanding, as one might find in children, some women, or people whose capacities are limited. It may come from an illness that the physicians of the time attributed to excess black bile, disturbing the brain. They would treat it as they treated melancholy.

In the third case, the remedy is to resolve the person's doubts. Begin with geometry and arithmetic, move to the rules of logic,847 then to the principles of natural science, and only gradually to what lies beyond nature. Pure theology should come last. Most people should not attempt these difficult studies at the outset. Very few are equipped to understand them, and success comes from God, the Mighty and Wise.

XXIX. Every Separate Being Must Understand Itself

Once we understand knowledge as existence present to a thing without absence or concealment, it is easy to show that every separate being understands itself. Matter does not perceive itself, because it has no existence apart from form. Natural forms do not perceive themselves either: their existence is bound up with bodies and places, and each part is elsewhere than the others.848 A body cannot be present to itself as a whole. But a being that is not bodily is present to itself, and therefore understands itself. Knowledge is existence without being hidden from the knower.

What hides a thing is, in truth, absence. To be free of concealment is to exist so fully that one's being is not weakened by the lack and limitation found in lesser things. We have also proved that every form actually understood by the soul understands itself, even if there is no other intellect in the world to understand it. Every immaterial form, whether it has been freed from matter or has never been material, is itself intelligible in this way. It therefore understands itself. This establishes what we set out to prove.

The philosophers have offered four arguments for this conclusion.

The first is Avicenna’s argument.849 He first argues that when an intellectual form becomes one with the potential intellect, it makes it intellect in act.850 If such a form can make another thing an actual intellect by being present to it,851 then a form that exists by itself is all the more an actual intellect. Heat makes something hot, so heat by itself would have the power to heat; whiteness makes something visible, so whiteness by itself would be even more visible. As we have seen, the argument he gives for the first claim is weak. If that part fails, this next step fails too.

The second argument is close to the one we gave at the start.852 Whatever is free of matter and its effects is present to itself. Whatever separate form is present to a separate being is understood by it. So every separate being understands itself. A thing either exists through itself or depends on another thing.853 Avicenna says it is meaningless to suggest that it simply exists without being present to itself. We have already explained how a presence between the thing and itself is possible even though the two are not separate.

We know ourselves directly,854 and we do not have two selves, one that knows and one that is known. We are one self. This shows that knowledge does not always require two separate sides. A separate being is a fully abstract form, and a fully abstract form is intelligible in itself. When it is present to itself, it understands itself.

The third argument comes from the author of The Illuminations. He says he learned it from the spiritual presence of Aristotle in a subtle state like a dream. He told Aristotle that the question of knowledge was difficult. Aristotle replied, “Look within yourself and the difficulty will be resolved.” The author said, “How?” Aristotle asked whether he knew himself through himself or through something else. If it were through something else, there would have to be another self or power that knows, and the question would return. So, he knew himself through himself. The author asked if this happened because his self left an effect in itself. Aristotle said: if the effect did not match your self, then it would not be your image, and you would not know yourself. The author agreed that the effect must be an image of himself. Aristotle asked if that image was the self without any added features or the self with other features. The author chose the second. Aristotle replied that every image in the mind is universal, even if it combines many universal ideas, because it can still apply to more than one thing. But your self is unique and cannot be shared. So you do not know yourself through an image.

The author then suggested that he knew the concept “I.” Aristotle replied that the meaning of “I,” as a concept, can apply to many people. “I,” “we,” and “he” have universal meanings when separated from any particular person. The author asked how, then, he knew himself. Aristotle answered: you know yourself neither through another power nor through an image, whether or not it matches you. Your self is the intellect, the knower, and what is known. The author later summed this up: knowing is the presence of a thing’s form to a being free of matter; more fully, it is the thing not being hidden from that being. Since the soul is free of matter, it is not hidden from itself. It knows itself to the degree that it is free of matter. When it cannot bring a real thing such as the sky or earth into its presence, it brings an image of it into the soul. Particular images are held in the soul’s powers, while universal ideas are present to the soul itself. The image present in the mind is what we directly know, not the thing outside the mind. We call that outside thing universal only in a secondary sense. This account seems to agree with Avicenna that the soul’s powers do not themselves know particular things, though we have already explained why we disagree.855

The fourth argument is that every separate being can be understood. This is clear: every thing can become intelligible either by its own nature or after the mind abstracts it from matter. Someone may object that human beings cannot fully understand God. The obstacle, however, is not God, whose reality is supremely clear, but the limits of our own understanding.856 We know only as much as our powers allow.

This also answers an objection from The Investigations. If God’s reality were existence itself, someone might say, and existence is something we can understand, then we could understand God fully. But existence as a general idea is not the real existence of anything, still less God.857858 The philosophers do not mean that God and possible beings share one reality and differ only through added features, so that possible beings would have more reality than God. Every kind of existence and every perfection comes from God. Existence is good, and the greatest good is God Himself. Absence and limitation are forms of evil. When we say that God is not a body, we do not mean that He lacks something good; we mean that He is free of the limits and harms that come with a body.

If a separate being can be understood, it can also understand. When one separate form is present to another, their forms are together in the intellect. This possibility must belong to what they are, not depend on the intellect’s prior act of receiving them. Otherwise, the possibility of their being together would depend on their already being together, which makes no sense. So a form that exists on its own can be present to every other form, and can understand them. And since understanding anything includes awareness of the self that understands, every separate being can understand itself and other things.859860

In the realm of beings free from matter, whatever is genuinely possible is already actual. There is no matter there, and no motion through which something can pass from an undeveloped ability to a completed one. Such beings have no perfection still waiting to be gained. This is how the argument establishes that the Necessary Being knows both Himself and other things. For the Necessary Being, existence is necessary in every respect: whatever can truly belong to Him must belong to Him by necessity.

Philosophers who use the second argument first show that God understands Himself, then show that He knows other things because He is their cause. Those who use the fourth argument first show that He knows other things, then say that His knowledge of them means He knows Himself. These two arguments move in opposite directions. I think the second part of the fourth argument is difficult to defend by the usual rules of logic. First, the fact that an individual can exist does not show that every possible thing of the same kind can exist, unless the kind applies in the same way to all its individuals.861 A mental image may differ from the outside thing in some features, such as being present in the mind, as these philosophers say.862 Perhaps the relation between intellectual forms is like that.863 Also, features that belong to a thing only as it is in the mind—such as being universal or shared—do not apply to the outside thing. We can also say that “being together” is a broad, unclear kind of relation.864 It does not follow that every specific kind of being together is possible. A physical image, for example, cannot be together with a separate intellectual form in the same way.

Second, the rule fails because nothing can be together with God in this way.865 How, then, can this argument prove that God knows things? It can do so only if one accepts that images of things exist in God’s being. Third, the argument would require every separate intellect to contain actual forms of every possible thing. That would give even the First Effect more distinct aspects than can be counted.866 It would also conflict with the philosophers’ view that each separate intellect has no more than two or three aspects. In short, this argument is hard to apply and does not succeed as it stands.867 Even if it did, it would work only if we accepted that intellect means the union of the knower and the known,868 and that God contains all things in the highest and most complete way.

XXX. Every Separate Being Is Intellect in Itself

This does not need a new proof. Every argument we have given for the first claim shows that a thing’s understanding itself cannot be separated from its being understood by itself.869 The fourth argument can also show this.870 If a separate being can understand something else, it must also understand itself. Since it is free of matter and its effects, anything it can know must already be present to it in act. It cannot be changed by an outside influence or move from potentiality to actuality. Nothing new can arise in it. So if it can be understood, it must already be understood. And because it can understand every thing that is open to its understanding, it must understand itself. Every separate being is therefore intellect in itself, always.

A contemporary of Avicenna raised an objection. The human soul understands universal ideas, so it must be a separate substance. If every separate being is intellect in act, the human soul must already be intellect in act, but it is not.871 If you say that the body keeps the soul from acting, the body must also help it understand, which seems to be true. Avicenna replied that not everything free of matter is intellect in act. It must be completely separate: matter must not make it what it is, bring it into being, or give it the features that prepare it to become actual intellect.872 The proof applies only to a being separate from matter in this complete sense. It is not strange for one thing to block one action while helping with another.

I do not think this answer settles the matter. Avicenna and his followers say the human soul is already a separate substance in its own being, though the body helps bring about its particular existence. The body is not part of the soul’s essence. If the earlier proof works for every separate being, it should show that the soul can understand every intelligible without any obstacle from its own nature, even if we imagine the body and all its distractions removed.873 But that cannot be right. Children and people with little education would not suddenly know every truth if we took away their bodies and all their distractions.

The better answer is that the human soul is not intellect in act at the start of its life. It is free of natural matter and bodily forms, but it still depends on images. Most arguments that prove the soul is separate show only that it is separate from the natural world. A soul is fully separate at the intellectual level only when it can understand universal ideas as universals, and can grasp the true unity and simplicity of intellectual reality. Only a few people reach this level.874

Apart from our life of sense, the soul has two further levels: imagination and intellect. When the soul’s ability to imagine becomes complete, it becomes an actual imaginer. It is then separate from the world of sense and from the bodies, places, and directions found there. Its images are not physical things that can be pointed to. When its ability to understand grows through sound proofs and clear definitions, it becomes intellect in act and is separate from both the sensible and imaginal worlds. It can then understand any reality or essence it chooses. What was only potential when the soul was at the imaginal level has now become actual intellectual form.

XXXI. How the Active Intellect Relates to Our Souls

We have seen that the human soul rises from one form and level of perfection to another. It begins with simple bodily existence, then takes on the forms of the elements, minerals, plants, and animals, until it develops all the powers of animal life. It then reaches the first level that is not tied to bodily matter. As it rises further, it reaches the acquired intellect, the first level fully separate from matter. This is close to the Active Intellect. The acquired intellect contains forms that were first joined to matter and later became separate. The Active Intellect, by contrast, was never in matter and must always be separate.

It is surprising that the acquired intellect and the Active Intellect are of the same kind, since one depends on the other.875 The Active Intellect takes the self that is intellect only in potentiality and makes it intellect in act. It also makes forms that were understood only in potentiality—forms held in imagination—understood in act. A thing cannot make itself move from potential to actual. What does not exist cannot become actual unless something already actual brings it into existence. A body cannot heat itself; it needs something hot. It cannot light itself; it needs something that gives light. So the Active Intellect relates to the potential intellect as the sun relates to the eye in darkness. Sight is a power that is ready to see but needs light. The eye alone is not enough to make sight actual, and colors alone are not enough to be seen. The sun gives light to the eye and to the colors. The eye then sees, and the colors become visible.

In the same way, the Active Intellect, which is always actual, gives the potential intellect a kind of existence. That existence is to the intellect what light is to sight. Through it, the potential intellect understands that existence itself and understands the Active Intellect, which gives it this intellectual light. Through it, forms that were understood only in potentiality become understood in act, and the soul becomes intellect in act. Those forms also become actual intellects.

Our account also says that a sense power becomes one with what it senses. The seeing power perceives visible things through the visible forms themselves, and the intellect in act understands intelligible things through those forms when they become actual. Yet what is directly seen is not the color or shape as it exists in outside matter. We have shown that material bodies and their features are never directly present to a perceiver. What is directly present to sight is a form like the color outside. The relation of outside colors to actual sight is like the relation of outside essences to their intellectual forms. The light that the sun gives to colors is like the existence that the separate source gives to natural forms.876 The relation of actual visible forms to actual sight is like the relation of actual intelligibles to actual intellect. Actual intellect is its intelligibles; actual sight is its visible forms.

There should be a separate substance in the world of sense that relates to actual sight and visible forms as the Active Intellect relates to intellect and intelligibles. My point here is that the Active Intellect’s action on the potential intellect resembles the sun’s action on the light that reaches sight and visible forms. That is why it is called the Active Intellect. In the account given by Aristotle’s followers, it is the tenth in rank after the First Cause among separate beings.877 When it gives the rational power something like the light of sight, the soul draws first and later intelligible forms from the sensible images held in imagination. Separate beings differ in how complete they are, as does the First Principle in relation to them.

We have also said that the Active Intellect is of the same kind as the acquired intellect. The forms of things are always ordered in it from the noblest to the least noble.878 They do not exist there as separate forms or as forms lodged in it, yet they are ordered. This is another wonder.879 Their order in the Active Intellect differs from their order in the acquired intellect. For us, the most general ideas are first, because we learn general ideas before specific ones. But general kinds depend on the more specific kinds for their existence. We understand the specific kinds later, even though they are fuller in existence and harder for us to grasp. So the order of forms in a soul that has become intellect may at first be the reverse of their order in the Active Intellect. As the soul develops, however, it reaches the order required by its intellectual nature and by divine teaching: the noblest and brightest forms first, through their union with the knower. All natural forms are undivided in the Active Intellect but divided in matter. Aristotle is reported to have said in On the Soul: “It is no surprise that intellect, though undivided, contains undivided things, and gives matter likenesses of what is in its own being, which matter can receive only in a divided way.”

XXXII. Self-awareness is the self’s own act and lasts as long as the self exists

Some philosophers argue880 that anyone who understands himself must do so in one of two ways: either he is present to himself, or another image of him is present to him. The second option cannot be right. The image would either match him in kind or differ from him. If it matched him and existed within him, the two would have nothing to distinguish them—not in what they are, in the features that follow from their nature, or in any other respect. They could not be two, though the argument assumes that they are. That is a contradiction. If the image differed from him in kind, its presence would make him understand the thing from which the image came, not himself. So self-understanding must come from the self’s own presence to itself. It must continue for as long as the self exists. That is their argument.

I find this one of the weakest arguments. Two individuals of the same kind are distinguished by their particular ways of existing. Individual human beings differ in this way. The same is true of a mental image of a human being and actual people: they differ in how they exist. According to these philosophers, the image exists in the mind as a feature of something else, while a person outside the mind exists in himself. There is nothing impossible about the same nature existing outside the mind as a substance and in the mind as a feature of something else. So an intellect could understand its own nature through a matching image without anything impossible following from it.881

We often form an image of ourselves, and an image of ourselves thinking about ourselves.882 If it were impossible to understand oneself through an image distinct from oneself, we could never do this. But we do. So the argument fails.

The better account begins by recognizing that a thing’s reality is its existence in some particular way. No individual existence can be understood except through that existence being present in itself, as we have explained before. If an intellect understood itself through an additional image, its existence and the image’s existence would be different. The self is a substance, while the image is a feature of something else; these are different ways of existing. The case would be like one person understanding another who shares the same human nature.

There is another argument, given earlier by the author of The Pointers. Any mental image is universal, either actually or potentially, even if it is limited by many further conditions. But the self that understands is a particular person outside the mind. We also know ourselves as individuals who cannot be shared with anyone else. So this kind of self-knowledge cannot come from another image. It must come from the very existence of the self.883

At the end of The Pointers, he explains this point in the first person:

“I set aside everything else and looked at myself. I found that I am: I am existence. Along with this, I found that I am not in a subject, which is one way of describing a substance,884 and that I have relations to a body, which is one way of describing the soul. The relations to the body turned out to be outside me. Not being in a subject is a negative description. If ‘substance’ has another meaning, I do not grasp it, though I grasp myself and am not absent from myself. I have no defining feature. I know myself simply because I am not absent from myself. If I had a defining feature or some special quality beyond existence, I would perceive it when I perceive myself, since nothing is closer to me. When I examine myself closely, I find only existence and awareness. Since I differ from other things through features and awareness, nothing remains but existence.885

“If ‘awareness’ means something definite beyond what has just been said, it is awareness of something. But I am not made up of my awareness of myself, since that awareness is myself, or of my awareness of something else, since that is not essential to me. My readiness to understand is only a passing feature.886 Anyone who understands himself through the idea ‘I’ finds, on examining what that ‘I’ refers to, only the existence of someone who perceives himself. That existence is itself the one who perceives. It is not hidden from itself, because it is free of matter. This is what the ‘I’ truly refers to.887

“If someone asks, ‘Is there some distinguishing feature of you that you do not know?’ I answer: ‘If I understand what “I” means, then whatever remains unknown to me is something other than me.’”

Someone objected: “Then your existence must be necessary, but it is not.”888 I replied: “Necessary existence is pure existence, without any limit or lack. My existence is incomplete, like the light of a ray compared with sunlight. A difference in completeness does not require another feature to distinguish the two. Possibility is a lack in my existence; necessity is the perfection of an existence beyond which there can be none.” That is the end of his words.

This is a strong and carefully worked-out argument. We have already explained why caused beings are not necessary in themselves: they exist through dependence on another. Their necessity is not eternal; it lasts only while the divine reality gives existence to the intermediaries, and through them to the later beings.

Let us return to our subject: a thing’s awareness of itself is its very self, and the self is always aware of itself. One sign of this is that if people observe their own states, they find that their awareness of themselves lasts as long as they do. Whenever we set out to think or to move, we do not intend merely to think or move in general. We intend a particular act of thought or movement that comes from us and takes place in us.

The same is true of movement. Someone fleeing from an enemy, heat, or cold is not fleeing from an enemy or heat in general, but from a particular enemy or a particular heat that has reached him. Knowing that the heat or cold has reached him already includes awareness of himself. Likewise, anyone who chooses to do something or seek a pleasure does not intend merely that the act happen; he intends to do it himself. Nor does he seek pleasure in general, but a particular pleasure for himself. All of this rests on his awareness of himself. So it is clear that a person’s knowledge of himself is his first and earliest knowledge,889 and is always present, never leaving him.

No one can say that I know myself by way of my actions—that I first infer myself from what I do. If I infer myself from action in general, then all I establish is that there is some agent, not that the agent is me. If I infer myself from an action of my own, I must already know myself before I can know that the action is mine. Otherwise, I would have to know myself only after knowing myself, which is circular reasoning. So a person’s self-knowledge does not come by way of his own action.

Nor does using someone else’s action as evidence give us knowledge of ourselves. We know a thing either through itself, through its cause, through its effect, or through something caused by its cause, as in different kinds of proof.890 But something that is neither a cause nor an effect of a thing, nor an effect of its cause, cannot give us knowledge of that thing.891

XXXIII. Anyone who understands something must be free of matter

The proof follows from what we have already established. Understanding means that the form of the thing understood exists in the one who understands it. But an intelligible form cannot be divided into measurable parts in any way, and it cannot have a position in space, either in itself or because of something else. Blackness, for example, is not divided in itself, but it can be divided along with the body in which it exists. A point has a position only because it belongs to a line. But something that cannot be divided or located in any way cannot exist in a material thing that has a position. So an intelligible form cannot exist in a material thing.892 The converse follows: anything that understands an intelligible form must be free of matter. This is what we wanted to prove. The usual view is that understanding occurs when the intelligible form exists in the intellect as something received by it. Our view is that the intellect and the form become one. On our view, the proof is even clearer, since something without a position cannot become one with something that has a position.

You might object: “We have established that predication means being one in existence. Yet we predicate broader kinds and species of bodily individuals. We say that Zayd, ʿAmr, and a horse are animals. The universal idea of ‘animal’ is indivisible and has no position, while each individual is divisible and located in space. It seems, then, that something indivisible must become one with something divisible, and something without a position with something that has one.”

That is not what happens. Meanings as they exist in the mind—as universal ideas—are not present in outside individuals in that same way.893 A broader kind considered as a broader kind, as a nature understood universally and shared by many, is not found in each individual in that form. The same is true of a species, a defining feature, and other ideas. What exists together with outside individuals is their natural kind considered just as it is, without being called either divisible or indivisible. In reality, it is divided, just as it exists in reality even though, considered simply in itself, it is neither called existent nor nonexistent. This does not conflict with what we have said.894 We mean that something actually indivisible cannot be one with something actually divided. A natural kind—the nature considered just as it is—is not like that.

You might also object: “Prime matter is immaterial in itself, yet it receives size, dimensions, and position. If a subject with no position and no parts can receive something measurable and located, why can’t the reverse happen? Why can’t an intellect with a position receive an intelligible form that has no position?”895

The answer is the same as before.896 Prime matter is not really free of size or position. It is bodily, because its existence depends on bodily form, which comes before it. Measurable size is not something added only after matter is already fully real. So matter is free of size and position only in the sense that it is a potential subject, not in reality. The intelligible form, by contrast, is actually indivisible and has no position.

We can also show that an intelligible form is indivisible, though this is clear to the mind from experience. Take the meaning of “rational animal,” or the statement that “one is half of two.” Neither is in a place or a body, and we cannot point to it with the senses and say it is here or there. Still, philosophers have offered a proof.

If an intelligible meaning could be divided, it would have to divide either into parts that differ in nature or into parts that are alike. If the parts differed, the division would have to end in something indivisible; otherwise, the thing would be made of infinitely many basic parts, which is impossible. So, in understanding any intelligible meaning, the mind would have to grasp an indivisible part.

If the parts were alike, the intelligible whole would divide into two parts similar to the whole. In that case, either each part is needed for the whole to be understood, or each part can be understood on its own, just as the whole can. The first possibility fails for three reasons. First, each part would have to be separate from the whole in the way a condition is separate from what depends on it. Putting the two parts together would produce something beyond the parts—perhaps a shape or a number—so the parts would not be parts of one and the same nature.897898

Second, if the whole could be understood only when both parts were present, then the intelligible whole would be divisible. But we assumed that it was indivisible.899 Third, before division, the two parts would not yet exist separately, so the conditions for understanding the whole would not be met. It could not be understood, though we assumed that it was.

The other possibility is that both parts are present, but each is also understandable on its own, like a body whose parts can each be bodies. This also fails. The intelligible form is present in the smallest amount that can be supposed to be the thing itself. Any further parts would add nothing needed to complete it. So it would be impossible to form a purely intellectual image without some unrelated feature attached to it. Yet, on the philosophers’ account, understanding means stripping away such unrelated features. Every divisible thing is made up of parts, and each part is an instance of the same kind as the whole. The kind is present in each part along with features that do not belong to the kind itself. So an intelligible idea shared by many cannot be a quantity or have a quantity.

An intelligible form cannot have a position either. If it did, it would either be divisible or indivisible. If divisible, we have already shown that this is impossible. If indivisible, it would be like a point: located at the end of a measurable thing or itself the end of that thing.900 But an end is not a thing that exists on its own, while understanding is something real. Anything that exists at the end of another thing is, strictly speaking, a feature of that end, not of the whole thing. The same question then arises about the end itself. In reality, an endpoint is not in an extended object just because the object is extended; it belongs to it only insofar as the object stops there. A point does not belong to a line simply as a length, nor does a line belong to a surface simply as an area, nor a surface to a body simply as something with size. Each boundary belongs to the thing only insofar as it ends there. Knowledge is not like this. So if an indivisible intelligible form had a position, the thing in which it existed would not understand it in itself or because of an absence or boundary. Understanding is a perfection of something that exists, not of something that is absent.

If the intellect were located in one part of the person, the person would not understand with his whole self, but only with that part. Then one and the same person would both know and not know the same thing. That is impossible.

XXXIV. The one who perceives imagined forms must also be free of this material world

This claim differs from the view of most philosophers, including Avicenna and those who follow him. But what matters is proof; truth is known through proof, not through the authority of people. The senses cannot settle what belongs to the intellect; the intelligible is not ruled by what the senses perceive, but rules over it.

Here is the proof. Imagine a square surrounding a circle whose diameter is as large as that of the greatest sphere. The imagined square could either be related to something outside the mind as though it were a shape taken from it—but it is not such a shape—or it could be a shape held in brain matter. But the brain matter is already occupied by a much smaller shape. One piece of matter cannot at the same time hold a tiny size and a vastly greater one, or take on two different shapes at once.901902

The brain’s shape and size are natural to it. The imagined shape, however, can be made as large or small as the soul wishes, like other images and forms. It can also grow in the imagination and expand as far as the soul chooses. A natural body cannot grow except by receiving more matter from outside. So this imagined size does not belong to brain matter or to any other outside body.

The relation between the faculty that perceives the image and the image itself is therefore neither the relation between a holder and something lodged in it, nor the relation between one located thing and another. The faculty must have some relation to the image. That relation is either spatial—like being beside or facing something—or not spatial. The first option is impossible: the imagined shape is not above or below the person, to his right or left, in front or behind him. So the relation must be nonspatial. We have already seen that it is not a matter of receiving the image, with the imagined shape as a form in the faculty. Nor can the faculty be a form of the image, since something that perceives only potentially cannot be the form of something that already perceives in act.903 So the relation must be that of cause and effect. But the imagined shape cannot be the cause of the perceiving faculty: measurable quantities are not efficient causes of things distinct from themselves.904

Also, the faculty remains in us while an imagined image can disappear and return. So the imaginative faculty must produce the image, or help produce it, or take part in producing it. If it were material, it could act only through a spatial relation. Anything that acts through a spatial relation can affect only something that is located in relation to it or to its material basis. Fire heats only what is next to it; the sun lights only what faces it. Yet an imagined image has no place in any direction of this world.

An imagined image also appears all at once.905 A bodily faculty cannot already be related to the image it will produce before that image exists; no relation to something nonexistent is possible. Philosophers have shown that a bodily cause must have a relation to its effect before the effect exists, either in time or in its own order of being. It must have a spatial relation to the matter from which the effect will arise, as fire and the sun do. But imagined forms have no matter of their own. So a bodily power cannot produce them in any way.

Since the imaginative faculty’s relation to these forms is neither spatial nor nonexistent, it must be their nonbodily source. It is therefore free of matter and its features.

To sum up: an imagined form has no position. So it cannot exist in something that has a position, either as something received there or as something separated from it in space. The faculty that perceives it must be free of matter. This faculty is not the intellect, because the intellect understands universal ideas, which cannot be divided. Nor is the intellect, when it understands a universal, the same as the power that perceives imagined forms.906 So the power that perceives images in the imagination is a different power from the intellect. This shows that imagination is free of matter.

Plato the Divine relied on another proof to show that the soul is free of matter. We imagine things that do not exist outside us, such as a sea of quicksilver or a mountain of ruby. We distinguish these imagined images from anything we have seen outside ourselves. These images must exist in some way. When we imagine Zayd and see him inwardly, we know there is a difference between that image and the one we saw with our eyes. If the imagined images did not exist in any way, we could not make this distinction.

Their place cannot be a body. Our whole body is small compared with the huge images we can imagine. How could a large image fit into such a small body? Nor can we say that some images are in our bodies and others in the air around us. Air is not part of our bodies, nor is it a tool the soul uses for imagining. If it were, the soul would feel pain when the air broke apart, and we would notice changes in the air as we notice changes in our bodies.

So the place of these images must be something nonbodily: the rational soul. This was Plato’s argument for the soul’s freedom from matter. It is a powerful proof for what we want to establish. But philosophers took it to prove that the soul belongs to the separate world of intellect, and that does not follow from this proof or similar ones.907 I have not found a clear account in the philosophers’ books of what it means for imagination to be free of this material world, while the intellect and what it understands are free of both the imaginal world and this one. This is among the things God has shown and taught me; I thank Him greatly for this gift. Two objections have been raised against this proof.

The first is that imagined images must have dimensions and extension. Otherwise, they would not be imagined images. When we imagine a square, one side must be distinct from another. This means it has a particular shape and position. If that shape existed in the soul, then either the soul would take that shape and become square, or it would not. If the soul became square, it would not be free of matter. But if it did not become square,908 then the square image would not exist in it.

The author of The Investigations says that this is a very strong objection, and that he has not found an answer fit to include in his book. I answer that an image need not be present to the one who knows it by being received into it. It can be present in one of three ways: by being identical with it, as when the soul knows itself; by existing in it as a feature, as when the soul knows its own states and, according to the usual view, when intelligible forms are received by the intellect; or by being caused by it, as when God knows possible things through their detailed forms. The soul’s knowledge of imagined forms belongs to this third kind.909910

This also resolves the usual puzzle about mental images. If the soul imagines roundness, must it become round? Philosophers say there is no difference between saying “this thing is a sphere” and “the form of a sphere is in it.” The answer is that imagined images are present to the soul as things seen in a mirror are present to us.911 They are not imprinted in the mirror or present in the air, and they are not identical with the material object whose image we see.912 We have shown that material forms are not themselves what perceives. The reflected images are suspended forms, not imprinted in the soul but present in another material thing outside it.

The second objection is this: if prime matter, which has no body or bodily features, can receive an image with dimensions, then a small body such as part of the brain should be even more able to receive a great image. A large and a small shape are more alike than a great shape and something with no shape at all. So large images and shapes could be received by a small bodily power, and their presence in a perceiving power would not prove that it is immaterial.

My answer is as I indicated earlier. Prime matter is not actually free of matter or size in reality. In itself, it exists only as a possibility and has no definite character—not even the character of being indivisible, like a point or an intellect, or of being divisible, like magnitudes and bodies. Yet in reality it cannot be without one or the other; it receives either kind of form. But something that already has a definite character cannot receive a form that is inherently without size, such as unity or a point, or a form with a different size. So their objection fails.913

There is another reason why a great image cannot be contained in a small body. If two sizes are laid over each other, they must either be equal or differ in size. If they differ, the larger has a part that extends beyond the smaller. So if a great shape were imprinted in a small body, only the part equal to the body’s size could be received, and the rest would extend beyond it. That makes it impossible for a large size to exist within a body of smaller size. The imagined image also cannot be in a wholly separate, immaterial subject, as some who interpret Plato’s proof claim.914 We have already explained that something with no size cannot be spatially joined to something with size. This is not like the relation between a magnitude and prime matter.

Here is another proof that imagination is free of matter. We judge that blackness and whiteness are opposites. The one who makes this judgment must have both before him. So we have shown that blackness and whiteness must exist in the mind or be present to it.915916 It is obvious that they cannot exist together in a body or other material subject. Therefore, the place where they are present must not be a body or bodily thing. The power that perceives such particular images cannot be the intellect, since these images cannot be universal ideas. So the imaginative power is free of matter.

Someone might object: “Blackness and whiteness are opposed by their very nature. Wherever they occur, they must be opposed. Why must they be in a physical subject?” I answer that perhaps they are opposed only in subjects that can be affected by each of them. When blackness exists in a body, it changes the body and causes certain effects, such as narrowing the pupil. When whiteness exists there, it causes different effects. But the perceiving subject is not changed by them in this way. Each can come and go, and they can occur or disappear together.917

That would be the case if imagination received them. But, as I have explained, the images exist for the soul through the soul’s activity, not through passive reception. The soul’s relation to them is one of producing them, not being affected by them. Even if it did receive them, its capacity to receive them would be inseparable from its capacity to produce them, as with the knowledge of separate beings. In short, opposites conflict only when they exist in a material subject that can be affected by them. So there is no contradiction in their being together in a nonmaterial subject or in a higher substance.918

Another objection says: “When we imagine blackness, whiteness, heat, or cold, it is only their images that exist in us, not blackness, whiteness, heat, or cold themselves. So the soul does not become hot, cold, black, or white.” I answer: Do these images really have the nature of blackness and whiteness? If they do, then the soul would indeed become hot or cold, black or white, straight or round, and so would be a body. If they do not, then perceiving things cannot mean that the nature of what is perceived is received in the one who perceives it.919

Our direct experience tells us that when we imagine or see these things, we see the very same blackness, whiteness, or heat that we sensed outside. The truth, as we have explained, is that the soul produces these images.920 This relation is stronger than the relation of a passive subject to something it receives: producing something is necessary, while receiving it is only possible.

Here is another proof. A body or bodily thing can have opposites at the same time in different parts. One part can be black while another is white; one part hot while another is cold. One part can face something while another does not. But the soul cannot know and not know the same particular thing at the same time. We cannot know Zayd’s writing and be ignorant of it at once. The same is true of desire and anger, love and dislike: one person cannot desire something and be angry with it, or long for it and recoil from it, in the same respect. This shows that the powers of understanding and desire are not bodily. They are not the intellect, either, because they perceive particular images rather than universal ideas. So they are free of this material world, though they do not reach the world of intelligible forms.921

Someone may ask whether the soul itself could be an indivisible point and so bodily. But a point is an endpoint, and an endpoint cannot receive something as a subject. The true subject would have to be the extended thing whose boundary it is; that would be measurable, which we have already ruled out.922

Someone may object that, according to the philosophers, opposites cannot be present in different parts of the heavens. So perhaps the heart or the subtle spirit within it is like the heavens: a body that cannot receive opposites. I answer that the heavens do not receive some opposites because they cannot be affected by one of them. Air, for example, cannot be black or white, because it cannot receive either quality. But if a thing can receive one of two opposites, it can receive the other in another part. Also, the heavens do have other opposites in different parts: one part touches a sphere while another does not; one part is north while another is south, or east while another is west. So the heavens are still bodily.

These are strong and decisive proofs. They will be very useful for understanding the next life. I will return to them in the discussions of the soul and the afterlife. This principle is especially important because it resolves many difficulties. For example, Alexander believed that souls which never reached intellect in act perish. Avicenna struggled to answer this in one of his works, The Ten Proofs.923 If human beings had no other nonbodily power besides intellect, then a potential intellect would perish when the body perishes.

Nothing of the human being would remain, though the revealed laws teach that every human soul survives—happy or unhappy, complete or incomplete, learned or ignorant.

XXXV. The human soul’s understanding is not essential or necessary to it

This passage comes from some who believed that rational souls existed before their bodies.924 Although the view is attributed to established philosophers such as Plato and his followers, it may be understood as a subtle symbol beyond the reach of most people. The human soul has different stages, some before its connection with the body and others after it comes into being.

Serious philosophers who came after Aristotle—his students Themistius, Porphyry, and Alexander of Aphrodisias, and later followers such as al-Farabi, Avicenna, and their peers—say, openly or by implication, that after the human soul has gained knowledge and become free of matter, it reaches an intellectual existence. It becomes an acquired intellect, like the Active Intellect in being a simple intellect.925 They hold that every simple intellect understands itself and what necessarily follows from itself, but not what is separate from it.

The method we have followed shows that the soul becomes the intelligible forms themselves and becomes one with the Active Intellect. Our proof also shows that a simple intellect contains all intelligible forms. Knowing them all is therefore essential to it, and the soul can become one with them.

The famous claim that Plato considered souls eternal does not mean that the many individual souls, all sharing a particular human nature, existed eternally. That would conflict with proof that many individuals of one kind cannot exist in the eternal world of creation, beyond matter, potentiality, change, and time. Plato means that the soul’s source and creator is eternal, and that the soul returns to it after leaving this world.926 Understood this way, the claim that all the things the soul knows are essential to it can be interpreted as follows: understanding all beings follows from understanding the first intellectual cause.

But the argument usually given for this view shows that its supporters have accepted it without a sound basis. They say that if souls were empty of these acts of understanding, that emptiness would either be essential or accidental. If it were essential, the soul could never understand anything. An essential feature cannot disappear. If the emptiness were a passing feature, it could only happen to a soul whose understanding is essential. So the soul’s understanding of things must be essential to it.927

This argument is extremely weak.928 It assumes that the absence of knowledge must either be essential or accidental, as if these were the only two options. It also treats things that are not opposites as though they were. The fact that knowledge is not essential to the soul does not mean that the absence of knowledge is essential to it. We are not saying that the soul requires knowledge never to exist. We are saying only that it does not require knowledge to exist. The soul can gain knowledge if the cause of that knowledge is present. If the cause is absent, the knowledge will not be there. But not everything that is absent must be impossible; otherwise every possible thing would always be absent.929930

If knowledge were essential to the soul, it would never be separated from it. The supporters of this view say that souls understand intelligible forms, but their attachment to the body and complete absorption in managing it keep them from noticing their own inner state.931 This cannot be right. Either the intelligible forms are actually present in the soul or they are not. If they are present, the soul must be aware of them, since the presence of one immaterial thing to another is awareness. If they are not actually present, then knowledge is not essential to the soul.

They might say that these forms are stored in the soul as in a storehouse. But to say this is to say that the soul has the ability to recover them by connecting with that storehouse. That ability is acquired only through earlier acts of understanding.932 If merely having the forms in an intellectual being—such as the Active Intellect—and being able to connect with them were enough to count as understanding, then every soul would already know everything in the Active Intellect in this sense.933 This would bring us back to the symbolic interpretation just described. There is an obvious difference between knowing something in act and having the potential to know it.

XXXVI. Learning is not recollection

The claim that learning is recollection is closer to the truth than the claim just discussed. Some careful thinkers who believed souls existed before bodies saw that knowledge could not be essential to the soul. They therefore said that before joining the body, souls knew all things. This knowledge was not essential, so it disappeared when the soul became absorbed in managing the body. On this view, thinking is a kind of remembering, and learning is recollection.

They support this view by saying that thought is a search. But it is impossible to search for something wholly unknown, and impossible to search for something already known. When someone finds what he was looking for, he recognizes it as the thing he sought. For example, when a runaway servant is found, the master recognizes that this is the same servant who ran away. If knowledge were not already present before the search, it would be impossible to seek and acquire it. If, instead, the knowledge had been there all along and thinking were recollection, then the thinker would recognize the answer as the thing he had been looking for.

The answer is that the proof that the soul comes into being will be given later. Their argument is a familiar puzzle discussed near the beginning of books on logic, where its solution is also explained. Every statement has a subject, a predicate, and a relation between them. When we seek to know a statement, we do not seek to understand its subject, its predicate, or the relation between them. We seek to establish that the relation holds or does not hold—that is, to judge whether the predicate belongs to the subject. Once thought leads us to accept or reject the statement, we know that we have found what we were seeking. We knew the parts of the statement as ideas, but we did not know whether the statement was true. The parts were already understood; the judgment we sought was not yet acquired. The same applies when we seek to understand a concept.934

What we acquire through thought is not the same as what we knew before we began. Each thing we seek has a sign by which we can recognize it once we find it. The seeker knows that it is the answer because it matches that sign. The author of The Summary offers a strong objection about acquiring concepts. By God’s help, I have untangled and answered it.935

XXXVII. Why intelligible forms are not in bodies or bodily powers

If what we know is an intelligible form, no bodily power, or any power in a body, can perceive it.936937 Here is the proof. Any image perceived by a power in a body must either exist in that body or not exist in it. If it does exist there, it is not an intelligible form but a sensible one. We assumed it was intelligible, so that cannot be right.

If it does not exist in the body where the perceiving power is, then the material basis of that power must have a spatial relation to it. We have established that bodily powers can act and be acted on only through such a relation.938 If a bodily power could act or be acted on without matter and its position, it would exist without matter. For existence comes before either acting or being acted on, and both depend on something's existing first.939 Any power that does something by its own being, rather than through its matter, must be self-subsisting. It would be free of matter in its nature and in its awareness.

But we assumed that the perceiving power was bodily. If it perceived the image, the image would have to occupy a position in relation to the body where that power exists. The image itself would therefore have a position. Anything with a position is divisible, either actually or potentially.

If its parts were alike, then the same intelligible thing would be understood not once, but potentially an infinite number of times.940 If the parts differed, some would have to serve as the broader kind and others as the defining features that complete the form. For when a thing's parts are not parts of its measured size, they must be parts of its meaning. Its meaning would then be made up of different meanings. A thing's meaning can be divided only into broader kind and defining features.

But if these parts of meaning line up with parts of size, there can be different ways to divide the size.941 Suppose we first divide it into a broader kind and a particular defining feature. If we divide it another way, either we find the same broader kind and defining feature again, which is impossible, or we find a new broader kind and defining feature. Then the thing would acquire essential parts it did not have before. But the parts that make up a thing must come before it in the order of its nature. A division can reveal those parts; it cannot create them. Since a size can be divided endlessly, this would give one thing endlessly many broader kinds and defining features.942 That is impossible.

There is another problem. Why should the image on one side be the broader kind and the image on another side the defining feature? If the act of imagining a division creates this distinction, imagining would change the thing's form and nature. That is impossible. If the distinction were already there, then we would be understanding two things, not one. The same question would arise for each, and we would end up understanding infinitely many things whenever we understand one.

How, then, could two intelligible meanings make up one intelligible thing? We understand the nature of the broader kind as the same in the nature of the defining feature. They are parts that can both be said of the whole, and predication means that they are one in existence. How could a bodily sign point to one of them in one place and to the other somewhere else, as happens with parts that are separate in position? The form and nature of the defining feature would have to be present in the body wherever the form and nature of the broader kind were. The defining feature of blackness, for example, is that it constricts the eye; this feature is present in the very place where blackness is. This makes it clear that true intelligible forms cannot exist in bodies or bodily matter.

You might object: Aren't blackness, whiteness,943 animals, trees, and other material things intelligible to us? They exist in matter and can be divided by size. Does that not mean that a divided thing, precisely as divided, can be understood?

We reply that being divisible by size belongs to these things because of how they exist outside the mind. Their being divisible, either in themselves or through something else, is part of their material mode of existence.944 Their existence in the intellect is different. In that mode, they cannot be divided by position.

This puzzle is especially hard to solve for those who think understanding means stripping an essence of its extra features.945 Some things have bodily extension and divisibility as part of their definition. An animal or a sphere, for example, remains divisible actually or potentially even after its incidental features are stripped away. If an essence keeps all its essential features in every mode of existence, then it seems that an intelligible animal or sphere must also be divisible. That makes the problem seem even harder.

On our account, a thing's essence is its meaning or concept. Take corporeality: its meaning is “a substance that can have dimensions.” This meaning exists outside the mind, and it also exists in the mind. When the meaning of corporeality exists in the mind, it exists in a different way. That mental existence carries the concept of corporeality as it is, but it is not itself extended or divisible.

Blackness, too, means “a color that constricts the eye.” When it exists in bodily matter, it has the effects that belong to that kind of existence. When its meaning exists in the intellect, it exists in another way. It carries the meaning of color and of constricting the eye, but it does not make the intellect physically colored or cause it to constrict anyone's sight. If that intellectual existence were present to an intellect, the intellect would understand the meaning of blackness without treating its physical effect as present there.946

Things have different kinds of existence, even when their meaning and essence are one. We know the same nature—for example, a human being—through sensation, through imagination, and through intellect. This shows us that one essence can exist materially, purely intellectually, or in an intermediate way.

XXXVIII. The senses do not know that what they perceive exists

That is the work of the intellect. Sensory perception involves the sense organs being affected and images of the things perceived appearing in them. Some say these images exist in the organs themselves, as most people believe. The truth, however, is that they appear in the soul, which uses the senses as a means of showing them. In either case, this happens because the material sense organ is ready to receive them.

Our hand feels heat because it is ready to be affected by heat. The eye senses a visible image because it is ready for sight; the ear hears a sound because it is ready for hearing. The senses do no more than sense: they receive the image of what is sensed, either in the organ or in the soul through the organ's use. The senses, or the soul insofar as it is sensing, do not know that the thing sensed exists outside them.947 We learn this through experience. That is the work of the intellect, or the reasoning soul, not of the senses or imagination.948

Here is proof. A person who is out of his mind may see images in the shared inner sense that have no existence outside him. He may ask, “What are these things I see?” or say, “I see so-and-so,” and be certain that what he sees is really there. For him, these images are present just as other sensory images are. Since his intellect cannot judge that they have no external existence, he assumes that they are outside him.

The same thing happens in dreams. A sleeper sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches things that have no real existence outside him, yet is sure that he is experiencing them. Their images are present in imagination and the shared inner sense just as they are in waking life. What is missing is the intellect's ability to reflect and judge what kind of things they are.

Likewise, when our hands feel heat, whether it comes from outside or from an inner bodily imbalance,949 the senses only register the heat. It is the intellect, through reasoning, that concludes that there must be a hot body, either inside or outside us. When we lift something heavy, we feel its weight and are affected by it. We do not sense that the heaviness comes from an external heavy body; we learn that through experience.

From this, a thoughtful person can see that the soul has another mode of existence beyond the world of material bodies. In that mode, images and qualities can exist without bodily matter to carry them. What we established earlier about sensible qualities helps prove this: the qualities found in our sensory powers are not the very same qualities found in material things. They belong to another kind, the qualities of the soul.

What we hear, see, or touch are sensible qualities that represent things; in reality, they exist in the soul.950951 In the same way, the intellectual forms of material substances—human beings, horses, spheres, stars, water, and fire—are these things as understood, but they exist as intellectual substances, truly united with the intellect in act.952

Such claims are among the remarkable things we learn about the human soul and life after death. We will explain them further, God willing.

XXXIX. The kinds of knowledge

For us, knowledge is a form of existence.953 Existence has three levels: complete, self-sufficient, and incomplete.954 The first is the world of pure intellects,955 forms that are free of dimensions, bodies, and matter. The second is the world of animal souls and imaginal forms.956 The third is the world of forms that exist in and depend on matter; these are the forms we sense.

The material things themselves, which keep changing and coming into being, are so steeped in nonexistence, possibility, and darkness that they are not properly known in themselves.957 We do speak of them as existing, as we do time and motion. But, as we have explained, each exists only for a single instant; the instants themselves exist only potentially. Material things endure for one instant and pass away in all the others. Their existence is therefore called existence only figuratively.958 It is also reasonable to speak of them as not existing. Plato points to this when he asks: “What is it that comes to be but does not truly exist? And what is it that truly exists but does not come to be?”

By the first he means material things, and by the second, things free of matter.

Strictly speaking, then, there are three worlds, each a kind of knowledge, or knowing form. Some Sufis count four, since they include this world of material things as a kind of existence.959 They speak of five Divine Presences: the Presence of the Essence, the Names, the Attributes, the Acts, and the Effects. There is no need to dispute the count, as long as we understand that material things have such weak existence that they are not knowing forms in themselves. They are known only through something else.

We can therefore speak of four kinds of possible things. The first are complete in both existence and knowability: the intellects and the forms actually understood.960 Because their existence is so strong, luminous, and pure, they are free of bodies, images, and number. Though they are many, they exist together in a single, unified existence, with no separation between their realities, for they are all immersed in the Divine. The Qur'an points to this realm in the words, “what you cannot see.” Earlier philosophers called it the Elemental Realm.

The second is the world of the souls of the heavenly spheres, immaterial images, and forms with dimensions.961 These are self-sufficient, yet they also depend on their intellectual principles. Their connection with the fully existing Divine forms makes up for what they lack and draws them into that higher realm.

The third is the world of sensory souls, the lower spiritual realm, and all the images that are actually perceived through the senses and their organs. These, too, belong to the lower spiritual realm. As long as they remain at this level, their existence is incomplete. They rise beyond it and become free of matter as they follow the human soul's ascent into the world of immaterial images.

The fourth is the world of bodily matter and the forms that flow through it, constantly changing, passing away, and coming to be. These exist somewhere between possibility and actuality, endurance and decay: their endurance is their decay, and their coming together is their separation. Since the purpose of creation is knowledge, those who know can, in principle, be divided into three kinds.

The first are complete by nature, like the separate intellects. The second are self-sufficient but need to be perfected; they do not need an outside source to complete them. These include the souls of the heavenly spheres, and, by nature, the souls of the prophets. Once perfected, the prophets may belong to the first group. The third are incomplete by nature and need help from outside themselves, such as revealed books and messengers.

God created all these kinds, fulfilling every possibility that reason can conceive. The Qur'an points to them in the verses “By those who line up in ranks, then drive forward, then recite the Reminder,” and “By those who glide swiftly, then race ahead, then manage affairs.” The order in the second passage may run in the reverse direction, from effects to causes. Those who glide may be the heavenly spheres, as in “Each floats in its orbit.” Those who race ahead may be their souls. Those who manage affairs may be their intellects, which belong to the realm of Command and exist through God's command, “Be.” Or the words “manage affairs” may refer to the very command that comes from God.962

We might also say that there are two worlds: the world of separate intellectual and spiritual beings, and the world of luminous and dark bodies. Since the world of separate beings is the world of knowledge and life, God created within it, corresponding to everything in the world of bodies, an intellectual or imaginal form that is its life and the mirror in which it is seen.963 The Qur'an alludes to these two worlds when it says, “For whoever fears standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.”964

Plato, the noble philosopher, likewise said that there are two worlds: the world of intellect, which contains intellectual forms, and the world of the senses, which contains sensible images. He called the first the world of Being and the second the world of Becoming. It is also reported that he taught in two ways: one through discipline and direct insight into intellectual truths, the other through teaching and learning by reasoning. The first world's “Being” means that it does not appear to the outer senses, just as the “Becoming” of imaginal forms means that they appear to the inner senses. The intellectual world is the source, foundation, cause, and goal of all other existence. We do not see it because it is too fully present, and the distractions of matter veil it from us. The terms may also point to that world's unity and simplicity, in contrast to the many separate individuals in this world.965

The luminous Platonic forms are substances in themselves and in their existence. They are the source of the substances and essences in this world, and the realities of the material things we sense. The proof that supports these forms—and indeed all suspended images—is different from the proof we gave earlier for Platonic forms. It begins from the fact that something sensible exists in the world, such as a human being with its matter and particular features. This is the natural human being. We have also established that a human being exists in imagination with a particular size, shape, and character, even though its matter is not present outside the mind.

The intellect can also understand a human being with all its substance, parts, shapes, and qualities, both essential and incidental. But it understands these in a universal way that can apply to many individuals of the same kind. To understand a thing, the intellect does not have to strip away every feature except its essence.966967 It must strip away its spatial, bodily way of existing, the way that requires it to occupy a direction in the material world.

So the human being exists in nature as a material thing, though in that mode it is neither understood by intellect nor sensed as a mental image; it exists in the shared inner sense and imagination, where it can be sensed; and it exists in the intellect, where it is actually understood. We have shown by decisive proof that the existence of a sensible thing, precisely as sensible, is the very existence of a perceiver, and that the actual existence of an intelligible thing is the existence of an intellectual substance. The knower and the known become one in existence. Since the knower is an immaterial substance, the thing known is also immaterial.

The sensible forms that exist in imagination are likewise the very power of imagination, which must be a substance. What exists as one with a substance must itself be a substance. So the human being has an essential image that exists on its own in the world of images, and an intellectual form that exists on its own in the world of intellects. The same applies to every natural thing, each of which has three modes of existence: intellectual, imaginal, and material.968

There can be only one intellectual form of each kind, because the kind has one defining nature. It can multiply only through matter or through outside, accidental causes. But the other two kinds of existence may have many individuals of one kind: natural forms multiply through the changes of matter, while images multiply through the soul's active power. If one human form is stripped of material existence and imaginal appearance, and reaches the intellectual realm, then another human form of the same kind that reaches that realm does not add a second intellectual existence. It is the same existence and the same effect, as are all the forms of the same kind, whether they arrive earlier or later. Even a thousand images of one kind would be one there.

This proof shows that every natural kind, whether it has countless individuals or only one, has an intellectual form that exists in its own right in the Divine intellectual realm. This is Plato's view of the Divine Forms. I doubt that anyone over all these centuries, apart from Plato and perhaps one of his followers, has fully grasped his purpose through proof. Only a single humble and obscure seeker seems to have reached it.

1. Closing discussion: Terms with similar meanings

The following terms are close in meaning, but they are not all interchangeable.

Perception means reaching or attaining. When the intellect reaches and grasps the nature of something intelligible, that is perception in the sense used here. This matches the word's ordinary meaning.969 Bodily contact, by contrast, is not true meeting; bodies touch only at their surfaces. Some mystics call this world the realm beyond separation.

Awareness is perception without firm certainty. It is the first, still unsteady stage at which knowledge reaches the intellect. This is why we do not speak of God as “being aware” of something.

Conception is when the intellect has fully grasped a meaning.
