  169. Another reply: the claim that one amount destroys another applies to settled amounts, not to amounts that are parts of a gradual motion.

  170. Compared with real existence, all these general kinds and defining features are necessary features of a thing. They count as parts only when the mind considers what the thing is. They can change without destroying the thing if its final defining feature remains, since that feature gathers the earlier forms and their completions. For Mulla Sadra, the true defining feature is real existence, which gives a thing its unity and simplicity.

  171. Matter's persistence is easier to see in expansion and contraction because it remains through the change and is not tied to one particular amount. The body is harder to see as the subject because changing amounts reveal that the measured body also changes. Its general kind remains only as a universal nature or an eternal reality, which is hard for the imagination and the limited intellect to accept. The distinction between original and later parts in plants and animals may also show why matter can be the subject in both kinds of motion.

  172. The final defining feature of a complete human being is actual reason, or the Active Intellect. The old definition of a human as a “mortal rational animal” uses “mortal” in the sense of voluntary death. In a complete human being, this final feature gathers all the changing and passing forms: the defining features of lower kinds become general kinds in relation to it, and their forms become like its matter. It is the form of forms and the feature that gathers what is scattered.

    ↩

  173. The stages on the way to the final human form are changes that bring greater completion, not forms that are simply put on and taken off. There is no loss followed by gain, but gain followed by gain, and finding followed by finding, without end.

    ↩

  174. Another reason a subject remains through substantial motion is that bodily natures are delicate traces of higher realities. Their stable aspect comes from their connection to the separate patterns of their kinds.

    ↩

  175. These intellectual forms do not exist separately for themselves; they are relations to the rational soul. One might ask how an intellectual idea can be an image if, as Mulla Sadra says, knowing a general kind means seeing its separate pattern. An image seen from far away can represent what we later see at close range after returning often to the world of intellect. “Image” is a broad term: it includes things sensed outwardly or inwardly, and things understood by the intellect.

    ↩

  176. This gives another account of what remains through motion. Some features mentioned above belong to the agent, some to the receiver, some to what is received, and some to the category in which change occurs. Each helps preserve the body's unity. If natural form itself is flowing, it may seem unable to provide that unity. The reply is that form has a continuous individual through time, both as the middle stage of motion and as the whole connected process. Matter, then, has what gives it multiplicity and what gives it unity. Its unity does not come only from one separate being; it is supported by these other relations too.

    ↩

  177. The four accidental motions are like a body whose soul is substantial motion, the renewal of nature. Time is like a body whose soul is timeless order. Timeless order is in turn like a body whose soul is eternity. The containers relate to one another as their contents do. What is eternal surrounds what is timeless, and both surround what belongs to time. Timeless order, in all its parts, relates to time as a day relates to its hours, minutes, and seconds—or as the flowing instant relates to time. The point is that changing motions and times are stable in relation to separate beings and to the source of both separate and bodily beings.

    ↩

  178. Nature that comes from the soul is a lower level of the soul and exists through it as its effect. The other nature belongs to the elements and exists within them. The first is naturally ready to obey the soul; the second is made to obey. Fatigue comes from the second, not the first. Physicians and natural philosophers use “nature” for the power that manages the body, preserves its health, and pushes illness away. Plato uses it for the divine power that acts in the body by God's permission—the first kind.

    ↩

  179. This alludes to the Qur'anic account in which God tells heaven and earth to come willingly or unwillingly, and they answer that they come willingly. This applies to nature that comes from the soul, which obeys willingly, and the nature of the elements, which obeys under compulsion. The speech is by God through the soul, which is a divine mystery and a command from the Lord. As Rumi says, every voice comes from the King, even when it comes through a servant's throat. God spoke this way to the heavens and earth of the visible world. His word is complete and the Pen has dried in relation to God's eternal reality, though the world remains in a state of renewal for beings confined by place and time. The earth and its like answer willingly when they see their own beauty as a display of God's names and qualities. Their journey toward God is a source of great joy. If they did not make that journey, they would remain in the pit of matter and the unjust town of ignorance, and suffer a deep loss. At first they resist being moved from their familiar places because they do not understand. Ignorance is the root of evil; knowledge is the root of good.

  180. A clearer distinction would be between two types of helpers: those that belong to the soul and obey it by their nature, such as senses that follow it into the imaginal world and the afterlife; and those that belong to the body and obey it only indirectly. Mulla Sadra identifies the two kinds here with the sources of motion in quality and quantity, and with those in place and position. One might object that both are the same nature that was just discussed. The distinction may be that “nature” earlier means the body's elements, while the powers here come from the soul; or that the earlier term means the lasting root shared by bodily and plant-like powers, while these are its separate levels and branches. This resembles the debate over whether the animal soul is the sum of all its powers or the ruling power of estimation. The better view is that the animal soul is the shared root of those powers, existing in each at its own level.

  181. “Willingly” and “under force” describe how the imagination and thought experience these powers. In themselves, both kinds are natural: both the powers that attract and push, and the powers that move the body. Even walking depends on a nature that is ready to obey the soul, and this nature remains with the soul in the afterlife. Mulla Sadra's contrast is between what is naturally ready to obey and what is made to obey.

  182. These powers serve the intellect only when their actions are directed toward rational ends. Otherwise, the outward and inward powers of perception belong to the animal soul, like the powers that move the body. The note's qualification matters because imagination and estimation do not, by themselves, submit to reason.

  183. This obedient nature belongs to the imaginal body, just as the power spread through the muscles belongs to the physical body. The powers that come from the soul are its domain and the place where its light appears. This answers those who deny bodily resurrection and accept only spiritual survival. They argue that particular bodily perceptions need particular bodily organs, which disappear when the body falls apart. But the soul has its own sight, hearing, and other senses, as well as a body in the afterlife.

  184. My first objection is that this leaves natural powers unable to act, which is as unacceptable as denying them altogether. Some theologians who reject natural causes avoid the problem by saying that powers act only on things outside their own subjects, or that existence flows through nature. Second, why should a spatial relation be required to connect cause and effect? What relation could be closer than the union between a power and its subject? Sadra and many other philosophers say that an agent acts through its very being. In The Journey of the Soul, Sadra compares spatial relation in bodily action with the spiritual nearness through which immaterial beings receive the flow of existence. In Origin and Return, he says that a cause and what it affects do not always need to be separate, as when form acts on matter. So why require position when a power acts on something outside its own matter? For action within its own matter, the author may be applying the rule “consider the outcomes, not the starting points.” Third, even if we accept the argument, it may show only that action is bodily because the matter that receives the power has a position. This is all the proof establishes: if a thing exists through matter, its action depends on matter, and matter exists positionally. This argument also appears in The Divine Witnesses. It fits the Illuminationist view that separate forms for kinds—horizontal intellects—produce all the effects in our world.

  185. This argument works only if there is a gradual change that necessarily belongs to a natural kind and is directly intended by its nature, rather than occurring as a side effect. The commentator denies both claims about natural kinds and says the fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.

    ↩

  186. If motion were not an effect of nature, it would not come after nature; it would exist together with it, in the same primary mode of existence, rather than as a secondary feature that follows from it.

  187. Calling form and matter “co-causes” means that form is not a cause in the usual sense. Existence flows first through form and then through matter. There is no shared causal action between them: a bodily cause acts only through position, and form and matter are united rather than positioned apart from each other. Still, causation does not always require separation. Sadra says in Origin and Return that form causes matter, and philosophers also say that a defining feature causes the general kind, though they are united in what the statement describes.

  188. The examples show that we name the subject by a feature that follows from it. Strictly speaking, a logical defining feature is a feature of the thing: a general idea given in answer to the question “What is it, in its substance?”

  189. There is a subtle point here. Taken as features that belong to the individual, these accidents are signs of individuality, since an individuating feature must apply to the individual. In that respect they are one with their subject, though they are a second level of its existence and an outward appearance of it. We must preserve both levels without losing the unity of the subject. These necessary features are not like unity or individuality, which do not follow existence as later features; they are more like mathematical body and natural body, which, in the experts' view, differ only in how they are considered. This is the way to understand the argument without erasing the nine categories of accidents.

  190. Matter, attachment to matter, the possibility of becoming something else, and motion are what make a thing distinct from the higher reality. But where these marks disappear, so that nothing remains to be attained and even the thing’s possibility is hidden in the light of eternity, it exists through God’s own existence and lasts through His lasting existence. Some of the author’s contemporaries missed this distinction and criticised him in their writings. I have discussed it in my notes on the section concerning divine things in this book; anyone who wishes can consult them.

  191. Worship joined with reflection, free from seeing anything besides the One worshipped, leads to complete servanthood. And servanthood is, in its very essence, lordship. It has no existence of its own, just as the meaning of a connecting word does not stand alone. Or “those who worship” may refer to the powers and natures whose very substance is constantly renewed; their worship is expressed in their being. This message then announces their arrival at their goals.

  192. “Then another form must take its place” and the preceding argument are also refuted by motion in quality and other kinds of motion.

  193. This refers to the argument that instants would have to follow one another.

  194. Matter is also brought into being as an individual.

  195. Here, “form” means the form that underlies a thing's actual motion, like the middle stage of motion, not the general idea of form.

  196. This answers the claim that the kind either remains through change or not.

  197. “Opposite” may mean any opposite, including intermediate opposites, or it may mean only a strict opposite. Avicenna's argument is also refuted by kinds of motion, such as motion in amount, that do not involve opposites.

  198. Avicenna's view is clear: time measures motion, and a measure follows what it measures in either flowing or remaining fixed. The majority view is that a motion considered as one whole from beginning to end is stable and has no parts that pass away; only the path of motion has parts, and they exist only in imagination. If motion itself cannot have parts that pass away, time alone must be inherently unstable. The commentator says their further account of how time's measure remains is another matter. A more precise explanation is that division depends on first treating something as a measure. Without a measure, there is no whole or part, small or large. Philosophers treat division as an essential feature of quantity; division in a physical body is only secondary. On this view, time's parts pass away in themselves, while motion's parts do so only by extension.

  199. Motion means the renewal of a thing; but renewal, considered by itself, is not a separate thing. This resembles the claim that a thing's existence is its being real: that reality cannot itself be another thing, or it would need yet another reality to make it real. Motion, then, is like a grammatical particle that makes sense only in relation to a noun. It is not a separate moving thing or a separate measure. The claim that motion and time are themselves unstable therefore misses the point: they are the renewal of something, its measure, and the thing renewed.

  200. Philosophers and theologians agree that coming into being is not the same as the thing that comes into being, or the process through which it comes to be. Philosophers say coming into being exists in the mind, with only its source in the thing itself. The theologian Abu Hashim says it is a state that is neither existent nor nonexistent: it is not nonexistent because a real thing can be described as coming into being, but it cannot itself be a separate existent, since then it would either be eternal or need to come into being in turn, leading to an endless chain.

    ↩

  201. A possible thing has both a nature and existence: existence drives nonexistence away, and “existent” describes the relation between the thing's nature and its existence.

    ↩

  202. The verse may refer to mountains changing as one form after another comes to be through substantial motion. Or it may point to the human being's gradual ascent toward fuller existence: through motion in place and in substance, life develops through plant and animal stages toward the fully actual human being. This ascent continues through successive cycles because God's outpouring of existence never ends.

  203. This refers to repeated renewal and to the gradual ascent through stages, from human society and plant life toward actual humanity. On the view that the Day of Resurrection includes all the timeless and temporal days, the transformation of the physical earth into an imaginal and afterlife earth takes place in the intermediate world. Reason and scripture agree that this is the first resurrection, though reason calls the earlier stages resurrection too. The heavens undergo similar transformations. These stages do not destroy the identity of what changes, because the process is continuous and its lasting basis is the face of God. Individual identity comes from existence.

    ↩

  204. God wills and brings about this change because the Necessary Being is necessary in every respect. God's will is necessary, not a possibility that might or might not be fulfilled. What is possible for creatures occurs within God's will under necessity.

    ↩

  205. The wording is inverted: the point is that a thing whose causes of preservation are also its causes of destruction must have an existence interwoven with passing away—that is, an existence in motion. Coming into being includes passing away at every stage. Another reading gives no proof of substantial motion: the same powers that preserve a thing can also destroy it. Sight may find something desirable, and desire may consume it. Bodily powers can also bring about illness through excess or restraint. Natural philosophers likewise said that the body's innate heat is both a cause of life and a cause of death.

    ↩

  206. Souls, as rays of the intellects, are what give bodies their stability and light.   207. The “and” here describes a condition: matter would then have no form capable of acting as a cause. It would lack the stable side through which existence can be given. If all coming-to-be were undone and things flowed back toward matter, that would be a return toward potentiality. Just as a soul can become like an active intellect by drawing close to it, a body can be said to return toward matter by approaching that limit.

  208. The “veil” is the imagined division between one stage of change and another, which philosophers call the subject of motion. Mystics speak of these divisions as divine self-disclosures.   209. The Qur'anic verse about the people of Paradise receiving fruits that resemble one another comes from a passage about the forms of the afterlife. As a person's love and insight grow, manifestations of God's acts give way to manifestations of His attributes and then His essence.

  210. “In length and breadth” refers to the world and the afterlife: the afterlife lies within the world, as its inner dimension.

  211. The manuscript may properly include the conjunction “and.” Even without it, the point is clear: since coming into being depends on a being that brings things about, God continually turns toward creation.

  212. The shorter version of this proof relies only on the difference between speed and slowness: speed covers a longer distance in a shorter time, and slowness the reverse.

  213. This is Avicenna's natural-philosophy proof for time, given in The Physics of The Book of Healing. It shows that each individual motion has its own individual time, distinct from the time of other motions, just as each body has its own measure. Each time can serve as a unit by which other motions are measured. The common time measured by the daily motion is a human convention because it is regular and familiar. Mulla Sadra also holds that a natural time, involved in the existence of events, is the measure of the whole bodily nature's substantial motion.

  214. This is one of the proofs for substantial motion.

    ↩

  215. The author points to his view that nature is renewed. Other philosophers say that time measures the changing position of the heavenly sphere; Sadra says that it measures the renewal of celestial nature, since other natures do not change with the same regularity. In this account, nature has quantity as an inseparable feature, just as existence is inseparable from what exists. Or the meaning may be that time is the connected, nonlasting quantity of nature itself—the account previously attributed to other philosophers.

    ↩

  216. The wording is unclear, because if time is a quantity, it cannot be a substance.

    ↩

  217. This is a division of the whole into its parts. The options about whether time measures a material substance or its renewal depend on whether we view time and motion as the same in existence or distinct in concept. Sadra later reconciles the different views of time. Their relation resembles that of mathematical body to natural body: the measured extension is the same, but it is considered in two different ways. If time and nature are one in existence, time is the measure of a substance. If they are distinct in concept and in how they appear to thought, time is the measure of nature's renewal and motion, or of what belongs to a body.

  218. Because its changing states include renewed stages of before and after, it would need another motion and another time, and another agent to bring that about.

  219. The five or six features listed for the body that time measures come from the old idea of an outermost sphere: a round body surrounding the physical universe whose daily motion marks common time. It has since become clear that the celestial bodies imagined in that account do not exist. These features can instead apply to the universal bodily nature, whose substantial motion marks a common, substantial time. The everyday time we use is a convention based on the Earth's daily rotation.

  220. If the body that time measures were removed, its replacement would also have to come before or after it in time, since matter that is formed from it or changed into it would itself be earlier or later.

  221. This means that it must come before other bodies in both time and place. Its priority in place would be lost if it moved, or if something else moved toward it, since changes in amount and quality also depend on motion in place. Its priority in time would be lost if another body or another motion came before it. It would also fail to endure if it could change in amount, expand, contract, heat up, or cool down; each of these changes requires matter that can come to be and pass away. This follows if the author's wording is read as it stands. If “its breaking apart” refers to time, the point is even clearer.

  222. The note means conceptions of goals. A conception of an end can itself move an agent to act, as the idea of sitting moves someone to make a bed. The reference is not to conceptions of positions or motions, or to features that follow from motion as incidental results; the word “proper” excludes those.

  223. This is the immediate goal; the more remote goal is likeness to the higher principles. One objection is that motion is itself an action, so it cannot be the goal of its own action; another is that motion is a seeking, not something sought. The commentator replies that Avicenna may mean the goal of the sphere's existence, nature, and circular tendency. Avicenna says “the goal in motion,” not “the goal of motion.”

    ↩

  224. The individual produced by a particular nature is only an incidental goal in this example. The example concerns particularity: the proper goal of a particular nature is its own completion, including the completion of its matter. Everything aims at itself and at its own perfection.

  225. The conceptions agree or differ because of the positions they represent. Positions encountered during one revolution are different in kind; positions repeated in later revolutions resemble earlier ones in kind, but are not the same individual position. A person turning in place encounters many different positions before returning to the starting point; the repeated positions are like the earlier ones. The contrast also applies to different celestial configurations, such as triangular and six-sided arrangements, conjunctions and oppositions. Here “conceptions” means perceptions of positions, not ideas of goals.

    ↩

  226. The conceptions would have to resemble each other in every respect. Still, “resembling” is loose wording, since two things can resemble each other without being identical.

    ↩

  227. The phrase includes the elemental substances whose positions necessarily follow from them. Knowing a thing also means knowing what necessarily follows from it. These forms arrive gradually and continuously: they have one connected existence, yet many kinds or individuals, as colors appear in succession on fruit during a change of quality.

  228. Mathematical extension, which can be divided in thought, is one of the features that follow from a natural body without being affected by it. Position—the arrangement of parts in relation to one another—is part of the body's existence and identity. A body's existence cannot be without position or arrangement. Change in position is therefore the very change in the body's substantial existence. “Inseparable” here means not later than the body in existence. Even if positions are later features, their renewal shows that the body's nature is renewed too, since a changing effect points to a changing immediate cause.

    ↩

  229. The sphere's different places are counted through its positions or times. In itself, the sphere has one natural place and no motion from place to place.

    ↩

  230. This develops substantial motion from principles accepted by Avicenna and his followers. Since the sphere's natural place and position do not change into something unnatural, its nature must itself be renewed: each degree of position and place corresponds to a degree of nature. In one view, both nature and its effect are one when considered as continuing; when considered as divided into stages, each has connected parts. Another possibility is that the sphere changes position by its own will. Since each position is wanted and then left, the sphere's motion may be voluntary, even if nature is what acts directly. Avicenna elsewhere calls it natural.

    ↩

  231. This proposal aims to connect the many renewed positions to one stable nature. It also avoids the objection that renewed accidents show their source is renewed, and avoids making the natural place and position multiple. The commentator compares it to the common sense: the shared sense receives many different images, but is one power.

  232. The two objections share one basis. One uses the rule that a universal nature has no existence by itself: the individual exists, and the universal exists only through its individual instance.   233. Sadra is identifying the cause of time. The words “as one individual” point out that time itself makes the sphere an individual, or is inseparable from its individuality. So how could the sphere cause time? Calling it an “unrestricted cause” leaves open the possibility that it is an incomplete cause, such as a receptive subject, but the author denies that it is time's agent. A cause cannot itself be qualified by its effect. Since every body is in time, and substantial motion makes a body flow and pass away in its existence, the sphere cannot be an eternal cause of time.

    ↩

  234. “Shape” is added after the more specific features as a general example.

    ↩

  235. One might object that motion occurs only in some accidents. The reply is that all the world's accidents are unstable, but in different ways: the four named categories are directly flowing in existence; time, acting, and being acted upon are flowing in their meaning; and relations are flowing only because they depend on other things.

  236. That is, time is renewed through the celestial body's renewal.

    ↩

  237. The phrase refers back to the claim that the body itself is the source and cause of directions and places, as the same argument shows explicitly.

    ↩

  238. “Precede by nature” is used in the broad sense of priority, including causal priority, rather than only the narrow sense of an incomplete cause.

    ↩

  239. If separate intellects and souls are the surest paths to God, then a cause that acts through position cannot be the source of their existence. Their cause must be immaterial and ultimately be the Necessary Being. The note also points out that time and place are renewed effects, not causes that exist before one another.

    ↩

  240. If the earlier and later cannot coexist by their own nature, they are times. If they cannot coexist only because of an incidental feature, they are things that exist in time.

    ↩

  241. This note connects the phrase “only God” to the earlier proof that a cause cannot depend in its existence on what it causes.

    ↩

  242. A sequence of causes can be allowed if its parts follow one another continuously. But a sequence of separate instants or disconnected times cannot be allowed. The commentator also gives a simpler proof: if circular motion began with an eternal God, its beginning would require a prior condition, and that condition another, without end.

    ↩

  243. Assuming that causes are connected and successive has led to the very things we were assuming did not yet exist: time and motion. The connected reality that changes is bodily nature; its continuous extension is motion, and time measures that extension. The stable middle that runs from beginning to end is motion considered as continuing, and the flowing instant is the setting in which this continuity is present.

    ↩

  244. “Intellectual” here means a real substance that exists in actuality, not merely an essence in the mind. On this reading it could include God.

    ↩

  245. One might ask how the sphere's highest soul can be the cause of time if the argument excludes the soul. The reply is that the soul causes time through its intellectual, unified side; the side attached to the body is its changing nature. The excluded cause is an independent bodily cause.

  246. Creation, considered as creation, is new because it is renewal and change; these are forms of incompleteness and do not come from God as a separate thing. What God brings about is the existence in which this renewal occurs. The Qur'an says that God's command is done, not that God's created world is done.

  247. The question has already been discussed, but here Sadra reviews the argument, tests it, and states his own position more fully.

  248. What belongs to a thing essentially is not explained by a further cause; what belongs to it accidentally needs a cause. The original argument treats renewal as essential to motion.

  249. A separate act of “coming-to-be” cannot be added as another cause. Otherwise, it too would need to come to be, and the chain could not connect changing things to continuous motion.

  250. The commentator allows that the earlier philosophers may have meant that motion's existence is renewed, rather than that renewal is part of its essence; this would answer Sadra's first objection. The second objection applies to both sides, and they answer it by appealing to the stable, middle motion that maintains circular motion as one whole. The remaining disagreement is whether this perpetual circular motion really exists.

    ↩

  251. The commentator strongly defends the earlier philosopher's argument. The philosopher may mean “a renewed position,” rather than “renewal of position.” Sadra's disagreement is about the renewal of the celestial nature itself. Apart from that point, the earlier argument can be defended; some of the disagreement is about wording.

  252. This recalls the familiar point that coming-to-be is not a separate thing: it is the coming-to-be of a thing. Otherwise, that new “coming-to-be” would itself need a further beginning, leading to an endless chain. The same is true of motion. On Sadra's account, motion is the existence of the natural world.

  253. Motion cannot come before an actual event in the order of nature while occurring at the same time as it. Each part of motion is itself passing away, so it cannot remain alongside its effect. Motion is potential, while the event that has come to be is actual. Only something free of potentiality can give actuality. The true source is separate and stronger than the bodily effect; motion is instead the condition that determines when the event occurs. The cause is eternal—God or the Active Intellect—and the later condition is a segment of the sphere's circular motion.

    ↩

  254. The lasting feature of movement cannot mean merely that new positions keep replacing one another. That succession has no separate existence over and above its parts, so it cannot by itself provide the enduring link to an eternal cause. The earlier critic therefore took the claim to require a stable basis within motion and objected that a purely changing process cannot have one.

    But the lasting basis intended here is motion considered as a passage between its beginning and end. In this sense, the movement is one continuous reality, even while its changing positions come and go. This is what the author meant earlier by saying that the continuous and enduring aspect of movement is its passage between the two limits.

    Many philosophers use this distinction to explain how things that begin can depend on an eternal cause. Circular motion, considered as one ongoing passage, is related to the lasting cause; considered through its endlessly changing positions and relationships, it is connected with changing events. What changes is thus linked through what changes, and what endures through what endures.

    ↩

  255. First, the earlier philosopher means that the remote agent—the First Cause or an eternal intellect—is beginningless. The nearby cause and subject of celestial motion are not.

  256. Sadra may be answering that essential renewal needs no separate cause, since what is essential is not caused. But he is also distinguishing the renewal itself from the existence that is renewed: although renewal is not separately caused, the existence in which it occurs is brought about by a cause.

    ↩

  257. The point applies broadly, but time, motion, circles, and powers are especially useful examples. Their intellectual forms are very different from their sensory or imagined forms. A gradual, particular existence is unlike the general, unified reality the intellect grasps; prime matter is pure potentiality, while its intellectual concept is an abstract universal. Water, fire, and separate intellects are more readily understood in both general and particular forms.

  258. This is the same problem raised earlier about how a changing thing can depend on an eternal source, now stated in a simpler form.

  259. An unstated premise is that anything produced without a prepared receiver must be a separate, immaterial form. Prime matter does not count as such a receiver because it has no actual form of its own.

    ↩

  260. If the receiver itself came to be, there would be a break at the beginning of the supposedly continuous renewal of nature. The account would then need to explain what came before that break.

    ↩

  261. The regress is not merely a succession of causes, which some philosophers allow. The receiver in question is the actual bearer of a form, not the earlier bearer of its potentiality. It exists together with the form it receives, so the argument would produce an endless chain of causes existing together.

    ↩

  262. If the receiver is assumed to be eternal, the argument must still distinguish the case where it is sufficient to receive the form from the case where it is not. The question cannot be answered merely by assuming the receiver's eternity.

    ↩

  263. An eternal receiver that is sufficient for the form would make that form fixed, not renewed. If the receiver and giver are present throughout, every stage of the form would be present together. Also, the question assumes no succession of preparations in matter; without such succession, there can be no succession of levels in the form. The original argument divides the cases into four: no receiver, a new receiver, an eternal receiver with no changing readiness, and an eternal receiver with changing readiness.

    ↩

  264. The claim that matter is eternal is rejected by anyone trying to show that the whole world began. It would also imply an eternal matter for each kind, and possibly for each individual form.

    ↩

  265. The challenge can be repeated for each specific form of each kind, and then for each particular form, leading to as many eternal matters as there are forms.

    ↩

  266. Every specific readiness needs something that makes it ready. Matter has a general, distant potentiality; a particular form gives it the specific, immediate potentiality for one kind of change.

    ↩

  267. The upshot of this account is that bodily nature changes in its very being. It remains constant in being changeable, so it can depend on a cause that does not change. These bodily natures are not separate existences: in their flowing reality they are one continuous, substantial nature. To say that this flowing nature is given to matter means that its existence includes a side of lack and nonexistence. Matter is not something separate from it that is already fully actual; that would be a contradiction.

    On this understanding, the distinctions between bodily forms—fire, water, and the others—are like the distinctions between the parts of a motion. We divide and name them in thought; they are not cut apart in existence. Their effects nevertheless differ, as earlier differs from later and stronger from weaker. Each stage of this flowing nature has its particular degree and place through what it is. Just as one part of a journey comes before another because of its own position in the journey, no extra cause is required to give each stage its order.

    That is how bodily natures stand when considered in their continuously changing existence. When we instead consider the kinds that the mind distinguishes, fire differs from air and a human being from a horse, each with its own features and effects. Each particular form requires matter prepared to receive it. A previous form, together with other preparing conditions, gives matter the readiness for the next; the previous form ceases when the next appears. Each new event is thereby connected with its eternal cause through conditions that themselves arise. Those different conditions follow from successive parts of one uninterrupted motion. Together with the corresponding stretch of time and the eternal cause, a particular stage of that motion makes up a complete cause for the new effect.

    ↩

  268. Prime matter is not one numerically distinct receiver that must be either wholly new or wholly eternal. Its unity is generic, as a kind is shared through its forms. We can say it is new in the sense that its substantial existence is renewed with the forms united to it, not in the sense that it was once absent and then appeared as one event. Or we can call it eternal in the sense that this renewal never stops—not in the sense that it remains fixed or has no cause. Its unity is one identity with many levels, not one fixed state. This is especially clear if matter and form are understood as united in existence: pure potentiality has no fixed actuality that would prevent it from receiving any form.

    ↩

  269. All readiness, nonexistence, and deficiency belong to matter, which is one reality because pure potentiality has no distinctions within itself. This keeps deficiencies from being attributed to God. Every actuality, existence, and perfection comes from the source of actuality and good; evil does not come from it.

    ↩

  270. This suggests that we may choose the first answer if we consider specific forms as absorbed in their separate intellectual forms, or focus on the lasting root within them, like the middle motion within a complete path or the flowing instant within time. In this respect, the forms are creative acts, not dependent on earlier matter, readiness, time, or nonexistence. The natural world as a whole is brought from nothing into being; material and temporal things, by contrast, are considered together with their matter and time.

    ↩

  271. Because prime matter is pure potentiality and has no specific readiness of its own, any general form is enough to make it actual.

    ↩

  272. “For it” means the potentiality belonging to a form that is itself clothed in potentiality, such as a form's subject. “On it” means the potentiality belonging to the form that matter can receive. The final option is potentiality for a further perfection. These are alternatives, not mutually exclusive examples.

    ↩

  273. Although matter is what can receive forms, it is equally open to every form. A specific form is therefore needed to give it the particular readiness for one particular form.

    ↩

  274. As noted earlier, existences may differ in their basic reality, and sometimes the feature that distinguishes them is the same feature they share.

    ↩

  275. This comparison concerns kinds as essences and the additional features that distinguish individuals within a kind. Looked at as actual existences, individual things also differ by degrees of existence; Sadra has already used such differences to argue for substantial motion.

    ↩

  276. A connected whole is one individual reality because its continuity gives it one identity. It has no separate parts until the mind inserts a boundary. Any point we choose can divide it, and there is no final smallest division. A line of any length—even one imagined as endless—is one individual while its continuity remains unbroken.

  280. Time belongs to motion as a feature considered in thought, and motion belongs to nature in the same way. They are features of nature that are not later than it in existence.   281. The argument against time is that the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the indivisible present cannot itself be time. The reply is that time exists as a flowing reality, like the continuous middle of motion, which cannot be divided into past and future. A connected path of motion and its measure, time, also exist because their source exists; “existence” includes both a thing and what is real through it.

  282. This may refer to the theologians' “imagined time,” which they say exists only as a mental measure before the world, with God's eternal existence as its source.   283. This view does not give a single, consistent measure of time. One event can be called the time of another—sunrise for someone's arrival, a person's arrival for someone's death—and the reverse could be said too.   305. Suppose a body has existed forever and has always undergone events with no first event, such as a heavenly sphere passing through an endless series of positions. On the argument being examined, the body cannot be earlier than the whole series of events, since there is no first one. Nor can it be earlier than their absence, since that absence is also said to be eternal. Some manuscripts repeat the words 'and is earlier' at this point.

    A contradiction then threatens. The body is not earlier than the events, by the assumption just made. Yet it also seems that it is earlier: it exists together with the supposed eternal absence of the events, and what exists with something earlier should itself be earlier. Or the body is earlier than every particular event; the whole series has no existence beyond those particular events, so it should be earlier than the series too.

    Another problem appears. The body is said not to precede the events, yet it must precede the eternal absence that is earlier than each event. Whatever has truly existed eternally cannot at the same time have been absent; the supposed eternal absence comes to an end when an event begins. This is another way to state the difficulty.

    The reasoning may also be put like this: although the body is not prior to the collection of events considered together, it is prior to each event. Since the collection has no separate existence apart from its members, that difference is hard to maintain. The same point will become clearer in the reply to the eighth objection, where something that always accompanies changing events is said to precede their individual occurrences.

    The wording needs care. 'Of these things' may explain what is meant by 'each one.' The repeated phrase in some copies is probably a copying error. The final claim that such priority is impossible may be intended to support the denial that the body precedes the eternal absence: if the body does not precede the events that come after that absence, how could it precede the absence itself?

  311. That is, the event cannot be described as having no beginning. Yet an endless series of events need have neither a last event nor a first event. This answer is closest to the opponent’s own way of thinking.

    A stronger answer distinguishes the senses in which we speak of eternity. Sometimes we mean the indefinitely distant past. That is still time: a continuous extent whose parts pass away. It would be unworthy of God to say that His existence, attributes or action belong to such a past. Sometimes we mean something like the setting for an existence beyond all completeness, from which the descending order of beings begins. What corresponds to it at the end of the ascending order is called everlastingness. Both belong to the order flowing from God. In a still fuller sense, eternity refers to existence before all particular forms and limitations, without viewing it merely as the beginning of beginnings or the end of ends. True oneness sets aside these relations.

    In the last two senses, eternity is no bounded time. It embraces all such settings of existence, including past and future times, as necessary existence encompasses the essences of things. Scripture and those who speak on God’s behalf use it in these senses when referring to His existence, attributes, and power to act. The same distinctions apply to everlastingness.

  366. This also means that the natural world, whose existence is always unfolding, does not simply cease at some later time. Its nonexistence, like its coming to be, consists of successive stages. The human soul, too, comes to be over time: its powers and habits are formed by the knowledge it gains from the beginning of life to the end, so it is not complete at a single instant. Its creation includes the whole time in which it exists. The same is true of the greater world. This does not mean that God's act is weak or slow. His command is simply “Be,” and it is. The gradual creation of heaven and earth is what is meant by their being made in six days—the span of the world's life, whose length only God knows. God's gift does not stop or weaken; the whole period unfolds within it. The six days also correspond to the call of the six messengers of resolve. The life of each, including the survival of his teachings and his twelve successors, is described as twelve thousand years: one divine day linked to the manifestation of a thousand of God's names, even if it spans thousands of ordinary years. The sixth day is the age of the Qur'an's revelation, from the first appearance of the Seal of the Prophets and his teachings to the last of his community's spiritual leaders and their rightful rule. Its universal reach and fullness do not cease. The Prophet was a prophet when Adam was still between water and clay, and Abraham was among his followers. His spiritual reality embraced all the intellects, like a universal intellect. Even if this period lasts six days or many thousands of years, to God it is like a glance or less. What is to be will be; the pen has run dry.

  382. The word “in” has different meanings in different cases: something can be in a place, in time, in a material, in a subject, or in an essence or existence.   383. The instant is not time, just as unity is not a number; the two are different kinds of things.   384. The note proposes changing the wording from “two motions flank it” to “two periods of rest flank the motion.”

  385. This does not fit easily with the later claim that other categories change only indirectly through the change of substance. The note leaves that tension for the reader to consider.

  386. The reference is to motion from place to place. As explained earlier, this motion comes before changes in quality and quantity because those depend on it. The circular motion of the outermost sphere is the first and oldest motion of all.

  387. Calling changes in other categories “indirect” conflicts with Sadra's view that they exist as modes of their subject, especially if an accident is a level of the subject's own existence. If the subject changes while its features remain fixed, those features would seem able to exist without it, which is impossible. The better view is that these categories truly change along with substance, not merely by association.

  388. “As they exist” means “in their existence.” Earlier in the book, Sadra says that any being, even a body, belongs to metaphysics simply as something that exists; it belongs to natural philosophy as a body, and to mathematics as something measurable. The timeless realm, dahr, contains immaterial beings and changing things considered in their luminous aspect. Stable beings, insofar as they depend on the Eternal, belong to the eternal realm, sarmad. God's eternity is beyond any duration—timeless or temporal—and beyond any extension, whether across space or through a chain of things.

  389. Most copies have this wording. It seems to be a copying error: the discussion of motion is marked as a chapter, so it would be strange for some related points to be marked as a stage.

  390. The clearest argument here is that motion begins from pure potentiality. Some people count the actual state at which motion ends as its starting point, but motion ends in pure actuality, without the potential that it contains. Potential and actuality are opposites in this respect. Still, there is no proof that the starting point and destination of every motion are strict opposites. Where they are opposites, that is only by coincidence.

    ↩

  391. “Larger” and “smaller” here mean the larger and smaller sizes expected within a thing's own kind—not a seed's smallness compared with the size of the outermost sphere.

    ↩

  392. That is, they resemble opposites.

    ↩

  393. The two directions are the natural directions. Most motion occurs between them; in reality, there is no single natural motion from one true endpoint all the way to the other.

  394. The beginning and end of circular motion are not points. They are positions, and the two positions are never the same at the same time.

    ↩

  395. The beginning and end may be found in different, non-overlapping parts of motion. There are also possible beginnings and ends that can coincide because they are relative to what comes before or after. Along with an actual beginning and end, these make three kinds.

  396. This change follows the underlying thing; it is not merely something that happens to it by accident.

  397. “In” here means “within time.” Time is one of the six things on which motion depends. If there were motion in the category of “when,” there would have to be another time in which that motion occurred.

  398. Motion occurring within motion would only slow the first movement. In the same way, if there were motion in the category of “when,” it would slow the passage of time. There is no impossibility in that unless it leads to an endless series. When all the categories change along with a changing substance, they do not change merely in name. Each has a change suited to it and a corresponding time, so that none falls behind the substance it belongs to or runs ahead of it. Think of someone aboard a ship, who moves with the ship while also being able to move about or sit still on board.

    Neither of Avicenna's arguments settles the question. First, motion in the category of “when” would be a different individual motion from the motion through which the body comes to have a time. Nothing has shown that this is impossible. Second, another “when” would only make the substance more deeply involved in the first time, slowing its passage. There is no difficulty unless this leads to an endless regress.

    ↩

  399. Sadra reads Avicenna's words this way because “when”—existing in time—belongs to motion and to what moves. The movement and its time extend continuously together. A change from one month, hour, or minute to the next therefore proceeds gradually: there is no actual break in either time or what exists in it. Sadra takes Avicenna to be referring to the point already established: although a process unfolds gradually, the existence of that process considered as a process does not itself unfold in stages.

    I have another reading. Avicenna says “transition,” not “motion.” He may be speaking of passing from one kind of time to another, as from night to day, or from one particular hour to the next. That transition happens at the instant that separates them. Though time has no actual gap, its different kinds and individual stretches have a boundary; without that boundary, we could not distinguish them.

    ↩

  400. Avicenna means that a thing's time depends on its motion. Time is the setting in which motion occurs, and so it exists whenever the motion exists. To say that motion is “in” time does not mean that time is its subject, as a path is the subject of motion; it means that time provides the setting for motion.

    ↩

  401. This would mean that motion in the categories of acting and being acted upon is the same motion viewed from two sides: as motion of the mover and as motion of the moved thing. The question remains which category motion itself belongs to. Sadra treats it as a way that existence appears in the world of nature.

    ↩

  402. The change could also be from weak heating to stronger heating. If someone objects that change in quality passes through several shades, we reply that a quality is a stable state that can exist at an instant; it need not remain unchanged in the next instant. There need not be a pause between its degrees. Acting and being acted upon, by contrast, are gradual processes and cannot be complete in a single instant. A pause between them is no more surprising than a pause between two opposite motions.

    ↩

  403. This argument can be challenged. If a category exists only together with motion, then it must have instantaneous limits or instances where motion ends. These would be possible even if they are always potential. Just as an extended quantity can be divided again after an earlier division, a number can be divided into units that themselves contain tens. So the instant that is a boundary for one motion can be part of a time for another motion. The instant need not become time for the motion it bounds.

    ↩

  404. The more natural reading reverses this point, unless the text is deliberately reversing it or means the instant on the assumption that motion occurs within it.

    ↩

  405. All features change along with nature, but not all have the same kind of change. For some, change is part of their existence, as with the categories in which motion occurs. For others, such as acting, being acted upon, time, and motion, change belongs to the idea of the category. For still others, such as relation, change belongs indirectly to the thing from which the relation is drawn.

    ↩

  406. This reply would work only if motion had first been defined, and then used as the standard for defining rest. Why not define rest first and motion from it?

    ↩

  407. Time measures motion; the instant is a boundary of time, and before and after are temporal relations. Motion can be defined without using rest: its first completion and its gradual passage from potentiality to actuality are enough. Even if rest were defined first, motion could then be defined from it.

  408. The note simply says that this point is disputed.

    ↩

  409. The change comes from within the body in the relevant place. So it does not follow that the change occurs without a cause.

    ↩

  410. At every instant, the moving thing is described as moving through the whole stretch of time, though its motion is not contained in one instant. What depends on a thing in its own realm cannot be separated from what it depends on in a higher realm. For example, time-bound existence depends on timeless existence, and the existence of the heavens depends on the universal intellect.

  411. If a body's motion stops and later resumes, the new motion is not the same individual motion as before, because a different time has passed. The personal continuity that made it one motion was broken. If continuity is not broken, what occurs later is still part of the same individual motion.

  412. The wording falls short. For a motion to remain one individual motion, five things must remain the same: its subject, time, path, starting point, and destination. Changing either endpoint changes the individual motion even when the others stay the same, just as changing the path does.

    You may object that a change of starting point or destination makes motions different in kind, as the author will say below. But a change of path can do so too. Moreover, an individual motion belongs to a kind, and that kind depends on what makes it the kind it is. A change that produces a different kind must also produce a different individual motion.

    Changing the mover alone need not produce a new motion. Two people may keep the same wheel turning, or two sources of heat may warm the same water, provided its continuous change is not interrupted. This does not mean that two independent causes each produce the very same effect. In short, the loss of any one of those five things ends the motion's individual unity, and a difference in any of them makes it another motion.

    ↩

  413. The motion's defining principles are like the essential features that make a thing a particular kind. These are its starting point, the kind of change, and its destination—not its agent, its subject, or its time. A change in kind in one of these principles gives a different kind of motion; a merely individual difference gives a different individual motion. The path can distinguish a kind as well as an individual, so there is no contradiction in mentioning it in both ways.

    ↩

  414. Speed and slowness do not even make motions different individuals, much less different kinds. The same motion becomes faster as it nears its goal.

  415. This is a concession to the objection. In fact, motion is more unified than a straight line, which is one continuous quantity. If even ten, whose nature is to be many, has a unity and identity of its own, then motion must have them all the more, since its many parts are only potential.

    ↩

  416. This supports the earlier reply. Everything in the world combines what has passed with what is still to come, what is fading with what is renewed, and parts with a single identity. In this way, it remains one whole.

    ↩

  417. A shadow or patch of light on flowing water may look like one thing, though it is renewed at every instant. This is like the continual renewal of the world: one world passes away and another comes to be, through God's names as the One who takes away and the One who brings forth. This is the way of God, and it does not change. The world, viewed in itself, is always being renewed; viewed in relation to God, the Eternal, it is one and unchanging.

    ↩

  418. This completes the answer to the doubt. In Avicenna's view, motion through the middle of the path of a heavenly body is one, simple, and everlasting. This unity is stronger than the unity the doubters reject. Such motion depends on the one, simple, unchanging Creator, while its changing parts depend on changing events. This is how the changing is linked to the eternal.

    ↩

  419. The argument is stronger if based on this: each part of a motion is actual in relation to the part before it and potential in relation to the part after it. The same part cannot be absent between its potential and its actuality. Our senses—sight especially—often mislead us about motion and rest.

  420. This means the resistance that opposes forced motion, unlike the resistance of the medium in natural motion. A body thrown upward through air or water also meets resistance from the medium.

    ↩

  421. You may ask: how can speed and slowness be understood independently of each other when their definitions mention less time and more time, which involve a comparison? I reply, first, that these expressions need not be accepted as definitions. Second, the discussion concerns speed and slowness in themselves; here “less” and “more” can simply mean a small or large amount. We can also speak of one motion as faster than or slower than another, but those are relative descriptions.

    The distinction is like one made earlier about length: length in itself need not be longer or shorter than anything, though comparative length is relative. Number can be many without comparison, while being more numerous than another number is a relative property.

    ↩

  422. If true opposites must differ as greatly as possible, speed and slowness do not seem to be opposites: for any fast or slow motion, we can imagine one faster or slower still. The proposed limits of moving and resisting powers do not resolve this. Opposition depends on what things are by nature, not on which examples happen to exist.

    In truth, what belongs to every motion is its speed, understood as its way of passing and coming to an end. When we compare motions, we describe one as faster or slower than another. The same motion is slower than one motion and faster than a different one. These are relations, not two qualities opposed in themselves. Just as existence can be described as stronger or weaker by comparison, speed admits similar comparisons. Speed belongs to motion itself even though we divide motions into fast and slow; likewise unity belongs to existence even though we distinguish one and many.

    The slower motion has more composition, just as multiplicity comes from a more complex existence. The simpler the motion, the faster it is; greater complexity makes it slower. I know of no leading philosopher who has put this conclusion in these words, but the arguments leave no way around it. Consider it carefully.

    ↩

  423. Time is included in the definitions of speed and slowness. This is why motion can be divided into faster and slower forms by time, as well as by the other things on which it depends.

  424. This is like the relation between existence and what a thing is. Without a particular existence, we could not draw out what the thing is; in that sense, what it is depends on existence. In thought, we can treat what a thing is as the subject and existence as what is said of it, but in the world they are one. The commentator's own answer is that motion beyond time causes time, while motions within time depend on particular times. This fits Sadra's view that nature is always changing, and that time measures this renewal.

  425. For example, heat and cold can each be agents in a process of becoming black.

  426. “Beginning” and “end” here do not mean rest at the start and finish. They mean the connected states through which motion passes. Motion is a flowing state, understood by its relation to what comes before and after; as Sadra says, its nature is to leave and to aim.

  427. A line is simple in a way a body is not. A body can keep its matter while its form changes. Straightness and curvature either define a line or belong to two kinds of line; either way, changing between them means the line itself changes.

  428. This is another way to deny that straight and circular motions oppose each other: straight and circular paths are not opposites, as the previous chapter explained.

  429. That is, the point a straight motion begins from would be the point a circular motion moves toward, so the two motions would run in opposite directions.

  430. The author says “motions along them” rather than “motion along the chord,” so the point applies to every circular path compared with other circular paths.

  431. If the arcs were all one kind, they would share one definition. But their essential features differ, so their kinds differ too.

  432. The commentator distinguishes the celestial body's position at the end of one day's motion from its position at the start of the next.   433. The reply misses its target: it assumes a shared endpoint, though none has been shown. If they joined without rest into one continuous motion, they would be one individual motion despite belonging to different kinds, which is impossible.

  434. The commentator clarifies that the argument uses “becoming black” for the movement that follows reaching the darkest point and turns toward white.   435. The proof uses an inward tendency in the body. It can begin at an instant and can be felt as the body resists what blocks it. This avoids the earlier problem about motion having no first part: separation takes time, though it has a boundary instant.

  436. This is not a special exception added to the proof. Turning back means leaving the destination of the first motion altogether; passing a point along the path is not the same thing.

  437. The source word here means the felt tendency by which a body resists what blocks it. It does not mean desire or love, which the commentator says runs through all things.

  438. The ball's motion in this example comes only from its connection to the turning wheel, not from itself. The argument concerns motion a thing has in itself; carried motion is like rest when considered on its own.

  439. The objector is not agreeing that the stone rests. The point is that rest would not occur because the force blocking it had been removed; the force is still there, and no cause of rest has yet been shown.

  440. Motion shows that the unusual force is present. If air resistance exists only while the stone is moving, it cannot explain how that force disappears: its supposed cause of removal depends on the very motion that reveals the force.

  441. Once the critic has asked what causes the unusual force to disappear, he asks what causes the stone to rest above.

  442. The question is not why the obstacle is missing after the resistance ends. The point is that Avicenna claims an extra power is needed to make the stone rest, though a balance of powers should already explain rest. The claim that this balance must last is weak: bodily powers have limited effects, especially forced powers, which do not act forever or most of the time.

    ↩

  443. “Condition” is intended here, not “preparatory cause.” A condition remains with what depends on it; a preparatory cause can act earlier. The weakening and its cause prepare for rest, while balance is a condition.

    ↩

  444. Nature resists forced movement, just as a living body resists illness and tends toward recovery and its natural activity.

    ↩

  445. The air's impacts prepare the body for rest and weaken the unusual force. A preparatory cause does not need to be present at the moment its result occurs. Nature itself is the direct cause of rest.

    ↩

  446. Someone who denies rest between motions will not accept rest at the final instant of the first motion. They accept it only after the return or turn has been completed. The proof needs rest at the upper point.

    ↩

  447. The commentator explains that an absence can still need a cause. Rest may be a possible absence, or it may follow from a positive state; either way, a cause is involved.

  448. The eight heavenly spheres move by following the outermost sphere. Their motion is neither in themselves nor forced, since nothing forces the heavens.

    ↩

  449. Carried motion is still connected to one of the three main kinds. The heavenly spheres move by following the outermost sphere; a passenger on a ship is carried along while at rest in themselves.

    ↩

  450. The pulse should not be called voluntary, even if breathing can be controlled in some ways. The heart and arteries pulse several times during each expansion and contraction of the breathing organs, and are refreshed by what comes from the chest and lungs.

    ↩

  451. The claim that the pulse is movement from place to place is weak, since it does not change location. Unless it means a tightening motion, the pulse is better understood as a change in size: expansion and contraction, with rest between them. If it were a change of position, it would resemble a person gradually lying down and standing up, passing through countless positions with a pause between movements. The note means that “most doctors” refers to less careful medical writers, who usually classified the pulse as a change of position or size, not movement from place to place.

    ↩

  452. The passage appears to combine different views about the pulse. One holds that the heart and arteries contract and expand through their own nature. Another holds that the movement comes from the living power in the heart, as discussed earlier. A third places that power in the arteries. I have recorded other views in my poem Gems of Insight. Perhaps saying that the heart and arteries produce the movement simply means that they receive it. — س ره

    ↩

  453. “Air” here means smoke.

    ↩

  454. The pulse, breathing, and growth in animals are examples of motion directed by the soul through nature. This is why the author adds a fifth kind of motion, alongside the four already listed. Celestial motion is also placed in this fifth kind.

    ↩

  455. These explanations avoid two misunderstandings: that the heavens' form is a nature like the four elements, and that their motion is natural in exactly the same way as the elements' motion. Both explanations say that celestial motion is chosen, but resembles natural motion because it follows one steady pattern.

    ↩

  456. That is, “nature” is being used in one of its several meanings described earlier.

    ↩

  457. This is the view of Thābit ibn Qurra. He says the earth is not held at the center because the heavens push or pull it. Those are two other explanations. The higher does not pay attention to the lower.

  458. We could also choose the first answer: the earth seeks the center in the sense that it seeks to have its own center coincide with the center of the world. It does not seek to occupy a point at the center. As for the earth's parts, no part exists on its own until something separates it. Until then, the earth is one continuous body. A part separated by force joins the whole again when the force is removed, so it is not an independent thing whose aim we can judge by itself. But the view that heavy bodies seek the center and light bodies seek the outer edge—even with the meaning we have given it—would mean that water and air are always being forced out of their natural places. The better answer, as the author says, is that water's natural region is around the earth, while fire's is inside the outermost sphere. Then neither needs to be constantly forced from its natural place. Someone may object that if this is so, water should not move toward the center when we dig down toward it, and air should not rise toward the outer edge if there is no fire in its way. But both move that way to prevent empty space. Their contact with air in these cases is forced, and they flee from it, as in the hanging-brick example discussed below.
