  459. Someone might say that empty space could be avoided by more air flowing in. I reply that all things naturally resist empty space. Air and oil enter the space left by a burning wick. Blood, flesh, and other matter rise into the space inside a cupping glass. This is a natural aversion to emptiness, not a choice made after thought that can be set aside when something else acts. When a flame rises from the wick, the oil follows so that no empty space forms, even if another flame or air is already there. In the same way, when a cupper draws out the air, blood and flesh rise into the space inside the glass.

    ↩

  460. You may say that a body already has a natural straight tendency. But my point is that it can also receive forced circular motion, and so it may have a natural circular motion too.

    ↩

  461. The kind of jagged form remains, but not the same individual jagged form. If the individual form lasted, the body would have to remain forced forever. Particular jagged forms, such as those of mountains, do not last through earthquakes or the breaking that comes from severe cold. They are changed and come to the “gate of gates,” since the flow of existence never stops. This is one way to understand the verse, “You see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds” (Qur'an 27:88).

    ↩

  462. Nature resists the body's forced state and keeps turning toward its natural goal. The outside condition is temporary and goes away. Natural tendency, by contrast, belongs to the body itself and is strong; impacts from the air do not remove it.

    ↩

  463. If the stone only received an upward tendency, without any change in its specific form, there would be no likeness between the effect and its source. The problem goes away if the body's substance changes continuously, in a weakened or partial way, as Sadra says.

    ↩

  464. Iron and fire each have a broad range of forms. Sadra does not mean that they are made by combining two separate forms. Rather, the iron's form lies between the two. You could call it an iron form, and you could also call it a fire form. This resembles a mixture of hot and cold, dry and moist. The form that produces the mixture remains in a middle state, not in a pure state. This all follows from the theory of substantial motion: the change here is not only in qualities, such as tendencies that come upon a body. The body's very nature also changes.

    ↩

  465. The matter has already been fully shaped and made into a stone by the stony form. The form that makes it light then belongs to a subject that already has its own form. In that way, the lightening form is an accident.

    ↩

  466. This passage can be read in two ways. First, the outside force gives the body an unusual, forced tendency that lasts until the motion ends. Avicenna is reported to hold this view. Calling an accident a “power” is not unusual, as we saw in the discussion of power and action. Second, the cause that lasts until the motion ends may be nature. The outside force gives it this role by changing nature into an unusual state or by creating a form that makes the body light. On this second reading, there are five possible views, not four. When Sadra says that one sound view remains, he means the second reading. He does not discuss the first separately because it leads back to the view he has already explained.

    ↩

  467. Sadra first mentioned number, size, and time. Here he speaks only of number and time because a power's effects are actions and motions, and a motion has no fixed spatial size. Its measure is time.

    ↩

  468. A difference in strength results from a difference in duration. There is no problem in treating the cause and its effect as two kinds of difference. In this passage, “duration” is set against an increase in duration. The author takes the rest of this explanation from al-Tusi's commentary on The Pointers, where he discusses whether bodily powers have limits. He uses it here to show the difference between variation in time, in number, and in strength.

    ↩

  469. This applies to effects that are motions. If an effect is not motion and its source is not bodily, it may be unlimited. For example, divine power is unlimited in strength, as God is unlimited in light. His creative act lies beyond motion and time.

    ↩

  470. This concerns bodily powers that spread through a body and qualities that exist throughout it. They can increase or decrease just as a quantity can. They are unlike powers and qualities that do not depend on bodies. A length, for example, can keep getting smaller without reaching a final smallest length; whiteness can do the same. The same applies to whether two quantities can be measured by a common unit. If one amount is greater than another, we can keep subtracting the smaller from the larger without reaching a final point. Quantity can be divided without end, unlike number, which ends at one.

    ↩

  471. This means weakness, decrease, and increase in strength. As we have already seen, a bodily power cannot be infinitely strong.

    ↩

  472. The proof can be summarized this way. If a body had no natural tendency, it would not move. We know from experience that this conclusion is false. The link in the proof is this: if the body moved without a tendency, its motion would either take time or not. If it took time, the three examples would force the time to match that of a body with a tendency. If it did not take time, it would lack one of the six things that motion must have. So motion without a natural tendency is impossible, and every body must have such a tendency.

    ↩

  473. The claim is a conditional: “If this motion occurred, it would take time.” Saying that the conditional is true does not mean that the motion actually occurs.

    ↩

  474. Someone may say that equal times do not follow from the assumptions. I reply that saying a motion without any tendency would take time is like saying, “If an immaterial being moved, its motion would take time.” This does not mean that a real motion has one amount of time for the movement itself and another for its speed, slowness, or resistance. Motion and speed exist together, just as a general kind and its specific form exist together. If two motions agree in one of the three measures discussed above but differ in another, the third must differ by the same ratio.

    ↩

  475. This is the natural tendency within the body that resists the tendency imposed by the outside force. The body's natural tendency and the outside force are held constant in the examples, while the three motions differ. So the differing motions cannot all come from the same unchanged cause; their tendencies must differ too.

    ↩

  476. On this reading, there is no need to use all three motions in the proof. A shorter argument is enough: if forced motion had no inner resistance, there would be no speed or slowness. Without speed or slowness, there would be no motion. So forced motion would not exist, which is false.

    ↩

  477. The same point applies to motion from the soul. Even if the soul's imagination and choice were at their strongest, they would not necessarily produce the same motion in all three examples. If someone says this also applies to an outside force at its strongest, “outside force” here does not mean an agent acting by choice. It means a force that acts by nature. A natural force always acts in the same way.

    ↩

  478. Al-Tusi is setting out a general point, apart from how it is used in this particular proof. His point is sound. The objector's quick response is unfair. If neither nature nor the outside force varies, but the motions do vary, then there must be some resistance that accounts for the difference. This is the result the objector wanted.

    ↩

  479. Someone may ask what sets the strength of the tendency if nature itself does not vary. The best answer is the one given by the author. A tendency is a quality that can be stronger or weaker. It lies between nature and motion: it connects the changing motion to the stable nature. It varies in itself, and outside causes help produce it.

    ↩

  480. The point is about tendency. Even when there is only one inside or outside resistance, motion can still have different degrees of speed and slowness. So the three motions in the proof cannot be set by the same resistance while their speeds differ. The same issue would arise if someone argued against empty space by using only the inside tendency, and left out resistance from the medium.

    ↩

  481. The argument can be made more briefly: if anything in the world moves by force, then nature exists. Forced motion goes against nature, so it cannot happen where there is no nature. The cause of forced motion is always a bodily power with a position. It acts by pulling or pushing, or by preparing a body to become hot, cold, or something else. A body can receive such an effect only if it already has a particular nature. Matter by itself cannot receive it until it has a definite substance and belongs to a kind. In the stages of an embryo's growth, for example, the elements prepare matter for the form of semen, and the semen prepares it for the form of the embryo. Forms do not oppose each other, and one specific form does not turn into another. Sadra points to this principle here. He could have made a shorter argument from it, though changing the proof in the middle of a reply may be poor form in a debate. If he is pointing to a different proof, however, the change is acceptable.

    ↩

  482. Sadra is answering a possible doubt: someone may be surprised that such a long argument is needed to prove both that bodies have powers and natures and that empty space is impossible. He says there are many ways to prove these claims. Some were given earlier, some here, and one short proof can be drawn from his argument: if there is forced motion in the world, there must be a natural tendency, because forced motion goes against nature. Another proof was given above: if there were no tendency, motion would have to remove itself as soon as it began.

    ↩

  483. In other words, without nature there would be no motion, since a separate, immaterial cause is too exalted to produce motion directly.

    ↩

  484. A specific form, which is called “nature” in simple bodies, makes a body the kind of thing it is. A body is a real kind in the wider order of things, but it is not a complete kind of thing among bodies until it has a specific form. Matter may already have a bodily form, but it still needs a specific form to become a particular kind of body. That form is the source of the body's different effects and the starting point of its motion and tendency. In this sense, it is called nature: the first source of a body's own motion and rest.

    ↩

  485. The phrase “within them” means that these powers are spread throughout bodies and divided with them. They do not merely sit on the surface.

    ↩

  486. This rules out the view that God directly produces these motions without powers or natures acting between Him and bodies. It also addresses the problem of how a changing effect can be connected to an unchanging cause.

    ↩

  487. The proof is clearer if we distinguish forced from natural motion. Suppose an outside force could move a large body without limit. It would move a smaller body more easily, because the smaller body offers less resistance. The larger body’s motion would therefore end before the smaller body’s. If it did not, the greater resistance would make no difference. Now consider natural motion. The power spread through a whole body is greater than the power in one of its parts. If both produced motion without limit, the part would do as much as the whole, which is impossible. If the part’s motion is finite, the ratio between the two powers is also finite, because it is the ratio of the part’s size to the whole’s. The whole body’s motion would therefore be finite too, contrary to the assumption.

    For natural motion, a large body and a small one are equally able to receive the motion from nature, since both are bodies. Their difference comes from the power that moves them: the large body contains more of that power because it is spread throughout the body, while the small body contains only part of it. In forced motion, the difference comes from the body receiving the force, since the larger body offers more resistance. These points prevent someone from saying that the greater force in the large body is cancelled out by its larger size, or that the smaller force in the small body is balanced by its smaller size. The forces differ because their bodies differ in size, and their effects must differ too.

    ↩

  488. If the sizes of two bodies have a finite ratio, then the motions of the bodies also have a finite ratio.

    ↩

  489. In natural motion, the larger body moves farther than the smaller one. In forced motion, the larger body reaches its limit sooner.

    ↩

  490. Since unity and existence do not exist as things placed inside a body, they are not divided with it. This gives us another way to answer the objection.

    ↩

  491. This objection does not apply to the proof as we have set it out. There is no need to divide the power into a part and a whole in the way the objection assumes. The effect of the small part is known, just as the effect of the whole is.

    ↩

  492. This example was discussed earlier, in the question of how a simple thing can come from a combination of things.

    ↩

  493. The objectors use a comparison between two endless series of past events. They imagine removing, for example, ten revolutions from one series and then claim that the remaining series is smaller. The philosophers reply that the events in a time sequence do not all exist together, so they cannot be compared or lined up in this way. The same applies here: the effects of bodily powers may continue one after another without limit, but they are not all actual at once and cannot be compared as a completed number.

    ↩

  494. “In potential” here means that the effect is contained in the power as strength or capacity, not merely imagined as a possibility. “Together” means held in one source, rather than separated into a sequence. This follows from the principle that whatever gives something must have it in some way. The power contains its effects in a higher, folded form; each effect then appears separately when the power acts. Since the capacity itself is real, we can compare the capacity of a part with that of the whole even before either effect has happened.

    ↩

  495. This means that a body cannot keep the same nature and identity forever, even before we consider changes in its qualities. Each power is renewed through a succession of powers. Each one has a limited existence and a limited effect, even though the succession continues without a break. This includes bodies that seem to continue on their own and bodies supported by other principles. We have already seen that everything a thing has comes to it through its existence. If a power cannot have an unlimited effect directly, it cannot have one through another cause either.

    ↩

  496. Rest still occurs in time. Avicenna's point is that we should not mistake this duration for an action produced by the earth's power.

    ↩

  497. The better word here is “contradiction,” not “opposition.” This is a detailed objection to one premise of the proof. A formal counterargument would assume the opposite conclusion and offer a separate proof for it, without attacking the original proof's premises.

    ↩

  498. The comparison concerns two powers of the same kind, where one is part of the other. It does not concern powers of different kinds, between which there is no ratio of greater and smaller. The actual effects of the moon and Saturn's movers do not exist all at once, so they cannot be compared by number. The point is the difference between what each power can do, not between effects that have already occurred.

    ↩

  499. This could also be treated as a general counterargument: if every step in the proof were accepted, the motion of the heavens would have to be finite, against the view that their revolutions continue without end. Each sphere has parts like itself. The power in a part is part of the power in the whole, so if the part's motion were finite, the whole's would be finite too. We cannot make an exception to the general rule without a reason.

    ↩

  500. A separate, immaterial power at its greatest strength could produce motion without time, even though time is one of the things motion requires. This point has been discussed above.

    ↩

  501. For example, wishes may gather in the soul's power of desire, and nature may draw closer by degrees to its final goal.

    ↩

  502. Otherwise, the agent's choice and the receiver's readiness would be fixed for no reason.

    ↩

  503. The answerer is Avicenna in The Pointers. He uses this argument to establish separate causes that move the heavens toward their ends. If the heavenly motion came entirely from bodily souls acting on their own, it would eventually end. Someone may ask: if a bodily power can serve as an intermediary for unlimited actions in the heavens, why can it not do so in earthly bodies? The answer is that the receiver here is either a simple element, which can be destroyed, or a compound body, which eventually breaks down. Also, in the view held by Aristotle’s followers, simple, universal intellectual causes do not act directly through lifeless, plant, and animal bodies; below animals, there are no conscious causes. The Illuminationist school holds that every body has a source of effects along with a separate intellect, but Avicenna does not accept that view.

    ↩

  504. An “intermediary of description” is something that seems to have a quality because it is joined to the thing that really has it. A passenger is said to move because the ship moves, though we can also say that the passenger is not moving in the strict sense. An “intermediary of cause” is something through which an effect truly happens. The thing that depends on it really has the effect. The intermediary may also have that quality, as fire does when it heats water, or it may not, as with the sun, which is neither hot nor cold. The same point applies to the heavens and their movers. Once we see the difference, we can see the weakness in the author's statement.

    ↩

  505. I say there is still room for an answer. Powers do have effects at their own level. Existence itself and the things that exist are not the same. Saying that only God affects existence does not mean that the heat of fire is not an effect of the nature of fire as heat and fire. Heat as something that exists comes from God. In the same way, people say that God is the giver of existence, yet still classify causes as natural, habitual, crafted, chosen, essential, or accidental. If asked what makes a chair, they answer: the carpenter. The material is wood; other things prepare the wood for the chair. But the chair's existence, simply as existence, comes from God. From the viewpoint of God's decree, only He acts. From the viewpoint of the powers He has given things, their powers act by His strength. Both ways of speaking are true. This is why philosophers still need to discuss whether the effects of bodily powers have limits. Sadra's other reply—that these powers are renewed continuously, even in the heavens—is also sound, as he has said several times.

    ↩

  506. If this reply were complete, there would be no need to discuss whether a bodily power can have an unlimited effect in the first place.

    ↩

  507. On this clear account, it is easy to show that each bodily power has a limited effect: each power that follows another exists and acts for a limited time. The succession can continue without end because it is continually renewed. If someone asks how this renewal can continue without end, the answer is that this follows from the unbroken flow of existence, which has been proved. To allow that flow to stop would go against reason and religion.

    ↩

  508. This means existence in general, not one particular kind of existence. We have already said that something is possible if it accepts existence in general—some instance of it can exist—and impossible if no instance of it can exist.

    ↩

  509. Philosophical discussions of general subjects are often built by drawing ideas from everyday speech and setting aside their incidental features through abstraction and generalisation. Examples include existence and nonexistence, mind and world, unity and multiplicity, and, among them, coming-to-be and eternity. In ordinary speech, people may choose a point in past time and compare two people by how close their existence is to that point. The one who has existed longer is called older; the one who has existed for less time is called more recent. A father, Amr, is old in relation to his son, Zayd, who is recent; Noah is old in relation to Moses, who is recent. This way of speaking means that the recent thing is preceded in existence by the older one, but not the other way around. We can take this meaning as a real feature and apply it to existence in general: existence either is preceded by something else—or, put another way, by nonexistence—and is then originated, or it is not, and is then eternal. Thinkers later found that existence can be stable or changing, and that priority and posteriority work differently in each. In changing existence, what comes before does not remain alongside what comes after. In stable existence, a cause can precede its effect while both exist, as can the essential nonexistence that is said to precede an essence. This is why they divided coming-to-be and eternity into temporal and essential kinds.

    ↩

  510. Given the definition of temporal coming-to-be as existing after a period of nonexistence, temporal eternity should be defined as not existing after any period of nonexistence. Eternity is the opposite of coming-to-be, so it is defined by negating it. If we defined it this way, time itself would be temporally eternal, as would things entirely separate from matter. The note adds an important point: coming-to-be and eternity are both based on being before or after something. That relation requires a fixed starting point from which we can judge what is before and what is after. Once such a point is set, we can speak of coming-to-be or eternity in relation to it, as when we compare the Necessary Being and possible things by existence or necessity, or compare existence and nonexistence in relation to an essence. On this account, both an eternal and an originated thing can exist in the essential sense, because we can use existence or necessity as a shared starting point. But only an originated thing can exist in the temporal sense, because only it can be related to a starting point in time. All temporal events and parts of time can be so related. A temporally eternal thing, by contrast, would have to be related to a point in time that nothing else came before. Nothing in existence fits that description. Time itself and things entirely separate from matter have no relation to a starting point in time. This also explains why the author changes the definition of temporal eternity from “a thing is not preceded by time” to “the time of its existence has no beginning,” and then denies this kind of eternity to time itself and to things wholly separate from matter.

    ↩

  511. If temporal eternity were defined as “a thing's existence has no beginning in time,” then time itself and things entirely separate from matter would count as temporally eternal. The author of Al-Muṭāraḥāt may have had this in mind.

    ↩

  512. Both arguments try to show that anything with an essence—in other words, anything possible or caused—has come to be essentially. This means that God, whose existence is not preceded by nonexistence, is eternal in Himself. The arguments differ in how they define essential coming-to-be. The first defines it as existence preceded by nonexistence in itself; the second, as existence preceded by something else in itself. The difference comes from looking at the matter in a broad or a precise way. On close examination, nonexistence has no standing in the world outside thought. The mind draws the nonexistence of each thing from the existence of something else. So, strictly speaking, a thing's existence is preceded by its cause's existence, rather than by nonexistence.

    ↩

  513. One could object that this makes the essence's entitlement to existence itself come after its lack of entitlement to existence, which is not the point. The point is that the essence's existence is preceded by its own nonexistence. The reply is that, in either case, we consider the essence as the subject and existence as what is said of it. What is said of a subject must come after it. So existence is preceded by a state of the essence that conflicts with existence: nonexistence.

    ↩

  514. More precisely, a possible thing, considered in itself, is entitled neither to existence nor to nonexistence. A negative statement does not require that its subject exist, while a positive statement does. The rank in question is therefore empty of existence. Avicenna's phrase “or would have no existence if it stood alone” is a negative statement that adds an alternative to “would be entitled to nonexistence if it stood alone.”

    ↩

  515. This does not mean that the essence is generally prior to existence. In reality, considering something as existing comes before every other consideration of it.

    ↩

  516. The commentator means that Avicenna's phrase “would have no existence if it stood alone” is joined to “would be entitled to nonexistence if it stood alone” as another negative statement.

    ↩

  517. This may be hard to understand because “lacking entitlement” was just described as a negative statement. A bare negative has no subject, since it can be true even when the subject does not exist. So how can nonexistence come first? Recall what we explained near the beginning about how a thing can be described. The mind strips an essence of every kind of existence and considers it on its own. In that respect, the essence has no existence; this makes it possible to call it prior by nonexistence. But in the basic way of describing it, the mind has stripped it of both existence and nonexistence. This lets us say that what comes first is nonexistence, and that coming-to-be is existence preceded by nonexistence.

    ↩

  518. The author says this because he rejects the idea that an essence comes first through its own substantial reality. Those who regard essences as real, however, say that an essence comes before its being illuminated by existence, despite having no claim to exist in itself. They call this priority by establishment or by meaning. The scholars who say that an essence comes before existence include al-Dawānī, the learned Sayyid al-Dāmād, and their followers.

    ↩

  519. This argument shows that essential coming-to-be means existence preceded by something else, just as the first argument showed that it means existence preceded by nonexistence. In both, “preceded in itself” means the shared idea behind causal priority and priority by an essence's own constitution. The first definition is broader, because “something else” includes both nonexistence and a cause.

    ↩

  520. This hints that kinds of coming-to-be differ according to the kinds of priority and posteriority. That is so, as the author indicated at the start of this discussion.

    ↩

  521. The claim that being later is an actual quality added to a thing is absurd, as the author says. Scholars generally treat it as a “second-level concept”: things truly have this feature in the world, but the mind is what applies it to them. In other words, it exists in the world only as a relation; it does not exist there as a thing in its own right. Even those who believe in such “states” nearly all agree on this point. Being later applies to things that come to be as a concept, not as an additional feature in their existence.

    ↩

  522. The main claim contains a fallacy: being preceded is a relation, not a quality.

    ↩

  523. This disproves the claim that coming-to-be comes to be through itself. That claim would mean that coming-to-be is its own essence, just as existence existing through itself would mean that existence is its own essence. If coming-to-be is its own essence, how can it also be a quality? The author gives several reasons why coming-to-be is not a quality. First, the two ideas can be understood separately: what we mean by coming-to-be is not the same as what we mean by a quality. Even someone who claims that coming-to-be is a quality must accept that distinction in thought. Second, coming-to-be applies in a way suited to each category, as existence does; it is the very existence of things that come to be. A quality, by contrast, has one meaning that does not change except through the different things it is related to. The author then adds that, although existence differs with the essences of things, it is not an extra feature added to them in the outside world. The scholar says that it is. His third reason is that the scholar's view requires an extra positive quality to be added to a newly arisen nonexistence.

    ↩

  524. The two features may be removed one at a time—as independent factors, conditions, or parts of a cause. The conclusion that a thing would be necessary and eternal if they were removed applies separately to each feature. The claim that a possible thing that is eternal would not need a cause is held by most theologians. Another reading is that the two features are a condition and a part, in which case both must be removed together. The phrase “its existence” means existence as attributed to an essence. The author clarifies this later when he says that he does not deny the role of an essence's possibility.

    ↩

  525. Put another way, the essence's possibility comes before the relational existence attributed to it: possibility comes before the possible thing exists in the sense of being described as existing. It is better to say that the philosophers mean possibility serves as a step in showing why the thing needs a cause, because it is a step in establishing that need.

    ↩

  526. This applies only to coming-to-be in time. That is clear.

    ↩

  527. The word “real” here simply stresses that this possibility is not just an abstract idea. The incidental cause is the thing's readiness or potential. Coming-to-be is the reason we recognise that readiness; it does not make the readiness exist. This is also how we explained the philosophers' statement that nonexistence is one of the causes.

  528. That is, a substance that does not exist in something else, such as a body or prime matter. This leaves two other options: existing in a subject, as a quality does, or existing in matter, as a form does. After rejecting self-subsisting existence, the author allows that the possibility might be a form in matter. He does not separately reject that option because its weakness is already clear.

    ↩

  529. Something separate from all things would relate equally to them all. There would be no reason for one thing, rather than another, to have it.

    ↩

  530. This confirms the earlier meaning of a preparatory cause.

  531. The first option is the subject that bears an accident; the second is matter, which bears a form; the third is the body in relation to the rational soul.

  532. Nonexistence is one of the three first principles in a statement attributed to Aristotle by the learned Sayyid al-Dāmād. He says that the Creator brings the world into being from no existing things and does not create it from things that came before. God arranged the universal natures as He wished from the first principles of creation. The first principles and beginning of what God created are necessarily three: form, the first and noblest; matter; and nonexistence, which is not in time or place. The note then quotes the rest of that account.

    ↩

  533. This refers to accidental motion in the four familiar categories of change. That is how the earlier thinkers' view is being explained. For the author, however, changing nature is interwoven with nonexistence, so the claim that nonexistence is a direct cause extends to nature itself. He discusses this at length in Sharḥ al-Asmāʾ.

    ↩

  534. In a chain of causes and effects, priority by rank can reverse depending on which direction we follow; priority by causation cannot.

    ↩

  535. The point is about order in the chain. Not every endless sequence is impossible. The argument against an endless sequence applies to things that exist together in an ordered chain.

    ↩

  536. Even someone who rejects both views just mentioned must accept priority by essence, also called priority by substantial constitution. The essences of a broader kind and its defining feature come before the essence of the species in this way. An essence also comes before its essential feature, considered simply as an essence. In both cases, the priority is fixed in the order of thought, without considering existence.

    ↩

  537. Even principles that are joined to God, let alone those separate from Him, are aspects of His own being and degrees of His action. The measure of this further kind of priority is that what comes first and what comes later are treated as one thing, unlike the other kinds.

    ↩

  538. The essence of every agent comes before the essence of what it affects by causation. But the existence of an agent before the existence of what it affects is this more subtle kind of priority. True existence is not made up of different realities, individuals, or parts. It has levels in which what distinguishes one level is the same as what it shares with the others; these are the inner aspects of the One God. You might ask how the author can say there is no action and response in existence when he often writes that existence itself is made, just as the maker is a cause. The reply is that, when we consider existence as the one source preserved through all its levels, there is no separate action and response. Also, although existence itself is what is made, its being made becomes clear only through essences. An essence therefore helps us recognise that existence is made.

    ↩

  539. Both people being compared are measured against the same fixed point in time. Their existence is related to that point, and they differ in how near or far it is. The point is the same for both, and the earlier person is nearer to it. The author explains this further below.

    ↩

  540. The measure of priority in time is not time itself, but being at a time—when something exists—which cannot be divided. Another measure is the thing's relation to a fixed starting point, such as the present moment. The same applies to priority in place: it is not place itself that makes something prior, but its relation to a fixed starting point. Avicenna later says that the earlier thing has something the later lacks, and the later has nothing that the earlier does not. The commentator says Avicenna is the person being criticised, but the author does not name him out of respect. Avicenna says that the different kinds of priority nearly share one meaning by degree: the prior has something, simply as prior, that the later lacks. But he also explains the measure of time priority by a fixed point, as the author does here. The author need not repeat that qualification because the definition already refers to what comes later; definitions are also commonly understood with “in this respect” as an unstated limit.

    ↩

  541. One might ask: the phrase “because of priority” seems to say that priority causes the greater claim, while “this priority” says that priority itself is what is being compared. How do these fit together? The answer is that if priority made one thing more entitled to be prior, then priority would cause the very advantage that makes it prior. The author first rejects priority as the cause of that advantage, then rejects the idea that the prior thing is itself more entitled to priority.

    ↩

  542. This is not the same as the earlier objection that “the meaning of priority is what we want to explain.” The earlier objection was that the definition assumes what it is meant to define. Here the problem is that it explains priority through something even less clear.

    ↩

  543. In reality, all the kinds share a common meaning. But people seem to have discovered them gradually, from the clearest to the least clear, and then used priority for each new, less clear meaning by extending or figuratively transferring the word. Eventually, these uses became accepted as ordinary meanings in particular fields.

    ↩

  544. There are two kinds of priority here, and they do not conflict. The times of arrival are ordered in time; the two cities are ordered by place, without considering time. When the author says that Hamadan does not come before Baghdad by itself or simply by its place, the point is that priority depends on each city's relation to a fixed starting point. This is what makes priority relational, whether the order is chosen or natural. Avicenna often reduces the number of kinds of priority, as he reduces kinds of statement in logic to a single form. His deeper aim may be to show that the true coming-to-be of the whole world is essential coming-to-be: the world's true prior is its cause itself. Its temporal coming after imagined time or nonexistence that shares a rank with it is not real priority for him, because he accepts only essential priority as genuine.

    ↩

  545. Natural priority should not change according to the direction someone chooses. Here it does change when the starting point is changed. The author's point is that there is no real priority or posteriority in this case. Once someone imagines the relation, however, the order is temporal, not a separate kind of rank. The answer is the same as before.

    ↩

  546. This means being seated first at a gathering or being allowed to start an activity. The priority belongs to the seating or starting order, not to excellence itself. For example, the first and second intellects are ranked by excellence. On this account, using priority for excellence is simply another use of the word.

    ↩

  547. The word priority is used with its own meaning in some cases, figuratively in others, and as a separate word-sense in still others.

    ↩

  548. Two features account for the observed order between parts of time. First, the actual state at each point depends on the potential state of the point just before it. Potentiality and actuality, taken in their distinct forms, cannot exist together. As with a motion that grows stronger, the weaker state does not coexist with the stronger state, though the stronger depends on the weaker. Second, the two parts that contain potentiality and actuality belong to one connected, flowing existence. Because time is connected, it can be divided into parts that exist only potentially. Because time flows and never settles, no part exists separately while all the others remain; they do not coexist as separate things. And because the actual state of each part depends on the potentiality of the preceding part, the part containing potentiality comes first. It is closer to the fixed starting point in existence, which is existence in general. So priority and posteriority between parts of time concern existence, not essence. This supports the Illuminationist view that temporal priority and posteriority reduce to priority by nature. We need only divide natural priority into two kinds: one where the prior and later cannot exist together, as with time, and one where they can, as in cases that do not involve flowing existence. One might object that this should apply to motion too, since motion is also one connected flow made of potential parts, each earlier part holding the potential for the later part. The reply is that motion relates to time as a natural body relates to its measurable size. Time is motion measured at a certain speed. Motion itself is open-ended until time gives it a measure, so we cannot say what comes first or later in motion without also considering time. Time itself is the direct subject of this priority; motion is so only indirectly.

    ↩

  549. This seems to mean that time is one continuous whole, with no actual divisions between its parts, so there can be no dependence in existence between them and thus no priority by nature—only an order if we divide it in thought. But the discussion is about priority and posteriority under the assumption that time is divided. The later actual state does depend on the earlier potential state, so there is room for priority by nature.

    ↩

  550. Avicenna seems to require that the prior thing differ from what it is prior in, just as the difference between essences lies in their essences, while what they differ in is existence. The author is right: in existence, what differs and what makes the difference are one and the same. Time is one of these cases.

    ↩

  551. Change belongs to existence, not essence. Priority and posteriority are intrinsic to parts of time in the sense that the mind draws them directly from how those parts exist, not because they are parts of time's essence or necessary features of it. Since this order depends on the relation between potentiality and actuality, it returns to priority by nature. We need only divide natural priority into two kinds: one that requires the prior and later not to exist together, as in parts of time, and one that does not require this, as in parts of a cause and its effect.

    ↩

  552. In this account, “existence” is used broadly for both the essence that can either exist or not exist and existence itself, which cannot be nonexistent. The feature that makes priority by essence is the essence's own reality or established nature.

    ↩

  553. The argument as given is narrower than the claim it is meant to prove, since it does not cover one person being earlier than another—for example, Noah and the Prophet. A better reading of Bahmanyār is that temporal priority exists in thought because the earlier thing no longer exists outside the mind. The mind must bring it back in order to judge that it came first. This explanation applies both to time and to things that exist in time.

    ↩

  554. The parts exist outside the mind in an ordered flow, even though they are not separate parts or divisions there. A positive statement does not need more than the existence of something that makes the statement true.

    ↩

  555. You may feel certain that being together is a positive feature, not merely the absence of priority and posteriority, just as blackness is not merely the absence of whiteness but a quality of its own. But two things are either alike, unlike, opposed as relative pairs, or opposed in some other way. There are four familiar kinds of opposition. Being together cannot be like priority or posteriority, and it cannot be unlike them, since it cannot exist alongside them in the same thing. Nor is it their relative opposite, as the author explains. It is not the opposite of two contrary features that take turns in one subject either: first and second intellects, which are the primary subjects of priority and posteriority, cannot be together in essence. The author has already ruled out simple affirmation and denial. What remains is that being together means that priority and posteriority are absent from something that could have them in one of these senses. So the feeling that being together must be a positive feature comes from imagination, not reason. In itself, being together is a relation whose two sides are equal.

    ↩

  556. What must be named is the one cause that they share—the point where their connection lies. For example, an off-center circle and its surrounding sphere are together by nature in relation to the spheres that come before them. Their descriptions as container and contained are also together in essence, but they are essentially later than the point where they connect. Water and fire in generated things are together by nature, as are their relations of being parts, differing, and opposing one another.

    ↩

  557. For example, prime matter and the form that comes from the Active Intellect. They are also an example of two things that depend on one another.

    ↩

  558. “Like brothers” is a comparison, not a strict example.

    ↩

  559. For example, the powers of sensing and moving by choice in relation to an animal. Natural togetherness does not always come with togetherness in rank. Substance and its capacity to receive dimensions, or growth and sensation in an animal, are examples.

  560. The relation of cause to effect comes later in one sense; even the relation of causality comes after the effect, while the cause—the feature that makes it a cause—comes first. The author then turns to togetherness between two existences. If there is no delay between them, they are not earlier and later in how their existence is formed. He replies that they are together in time or in the timeless order, but not in the way their very being is constituted: one depends on the other, while the other does not.

    ↩

  561. This follows if coming-to-be is defined as a thing's existence being preceded by its nonexistence. If it is instead defined as being preceded by something else, it may be reduced to priority by causation, especially when the term applies to existence itself.

    ↩

  562. This is priority of what something needs over what needs it. Its measure is existence. Existence is not in a rank in the same way as other things; it is simply not considered at that point. This is not priority by the essence's own constitution, because the essence is only an idea and has no established existence before existence. Priority by essence through constitution fits better with the view that essences are real.

    ↩

  563. That is, we are not saying that the essence is nonexistent at that rank, or that it “does not have existence” as a positive claim. We are saying only that existence is not affirmed of it there. This simple denial can be true even of something that is neither existent nor nonexistent. So the rank itself is not a state of nonexistence, and both sides of the contradiction do not disappear.

    ↩

  564. The general rule does not apply to essence, existence, and nonexistence as the author assumes. It applies to things with no relation of cause and effect or of being attributed to one another, such as a person's ability to speak and a donkey's ability to bray. Each can exist without the other. Essence and existence do have a relation of attribution, even though neither causes the other. Essence does not cause existence; it is below the act of being made. Nor does existence cause essence.

    ↩

  565. The wording is incomplete. It should say: “there cannot be a complete, simple cause.” A simple cause, if there is one, still exists, as the author says later.

    ↩

  566. This refers to God, who is necessary in Himself, and His first effect.

    ↩

  567. There is no reason to limit a cause to what an effect needs in order to exist. A cause is anything an effect needs for its existence or its basic make-up. If it includes everything the effect needs, it is a complete cause; otherwise, it is an incomplete cause.

    ↩

  568. The effect and its features belong to the effect's side, not among the things the cause depends on. That is why possibility and related considerations do not make the cause composite; the complete cause of the First Effect remains simple.

    ↩

  569. The answer wrongly limits a general principle of reason. The essence's nature and make-up depend on its broader kind and distinguishing feature. These, too, depend on the existence of the essence. Its existence depends on its make-up, and its make-up depends on these parts. Anything that depends on something which itself depends on another thing also depends on that further thing.

    ↩

  570. That is, the agent or efficient cause—the thing that brings about the effect.

    ↩

  571. On the author's account, a complete, simple cause is not limited to the First Intellect. Every existence has a complete, simple cause; each existing essence has a composite cause, as he says: the agent, the essence that receives existence, and its capacity to receive it. The essence of the recipient is the essence considered in itself. The effect as a whole—the essence as existing—is not counted among the things on which the cause depends. The note adds that this applies to existence in general; when we consider particular levels of existence, it applies specifically to the First Intellect. For example, Zayd's existence has, beyond the higher causes, earthly causes and a later condition: the existence of a particular heavenly motion.

    ↩

  572. In short, this seems to lead to a circle: we understand other things through knowledge, yet try to understand knowledge through something else. The answer is that other things become clear through knowledge as it exists, not through our idea of what knowledge means. There is therefore no contradiction if our idea of knowledge becomes clear through some other idea.

    ↩

  573. A better argument would be: our awareness that we are aware is immediate and inward; general knowledge is part of this awareness; and what is part of something immediate is itself immediate.

    ↩

  574. This gives only a general sense of the thing, not the detailed understanding that sets it apart. To know that a feature belongs to a thing, we need only some idea of each one, not a full understanding of either.

    ↩

  575. The proofs already given establish this point for the knowledge we gain through mental images of things outside us. They can be extended to prove the broader claim that all knowledge of something outside the knower involves an image of it. A closer argument starts from the fact that image-based knowledge can be reduced to direct awareness. It follows that, in image-based knowledge, the knower becomes one with what is known in some way, whether the object is universal or particular, an immaterial intellect or an imaginal being. This will be explained later.

    ↩

  576. After showing that we do not need to ask what knowledge is, the author now asks the simple question of whether it exists. The proofs of mental existence answer this question. The word “especially” points to the fact that impossible things exist only in thought, not in any other realm.

    ↩

  577. That is, the essence is considered without the condition of existing in either way, even though an essence is still being specified.

    ↩

  578. Many things in nature are mixed with unrelated features. Whiteness, for example, appears in subjects, times, places, and other conditions. The mind can grasp pure whiteness by leaving these features aside. Since the mind can point to this whiteness, it must exist in some way; nothing nonexistent can be pointed to. Outside the mind, whiteness exists only mixed with other things, so this pure idea exists in the mind. The author says “many things” because existence itself is a special case.

    ↩

  579. If what touch senses were not the same as the material feature in the sense organ, it would have to be free of matter in some way. If it were in the organ as a material feature, two identical things would be imprinted in one place. The sensed image would therefore exist in the soul as something produced there, like images seen or heard. The author does not avoid this view; he later says that these are qualities of the soul and mental images. But in The Beginning and the Return he seems to say otherwise: he says that the breaking apart of a material connection is known through direct awareness. See that work for details. A further consequence is that all the things we directly sense, both with the outer and inner senses, belong to our inner world. This gives a subtle account of the world's coming-to-be and passing away, beyond the kinds of coming-to-be discussed elsewhere: the world we know comes to be and passes away with the coming-to-be and passing away of embodied human beings. The verse says, in effect, that when a person falls asleep, their tent and its ropes come loose.

  580. The idea of heat in the sense of touch is in the soul, not in the sense organ; the idea of taste is in the soul, not in the tongue. Otherwise, anyone connected to the same sense organ would feel exactly what the first person feels. The mental image could then be pointed to by the senses, and we could not bring back the very same image after it had vanished from the organ. The apparent claim that the sense organ contains no material image of the qualities we sense cannot be accepted.

    ↩

  581. The critic seems to have noticed that those defending mental existence say a thing has its effects only when it exists outside the mind. So the critic first tries to show that the mental image also exists outside the mind—and that is true in one respect. Mental existence is mental in relation to the existence of the thing represented; considered in itself, it is a real existence. An image in a material subject and an image in a soul without matter both exist in their own right. But the critic tries to establish this by removing the uncertainty surrounding what the thing is. The answer is that even if we grant that mental existence is real, things exist in different ways. Each way has effects that cannot be demanded of another.

    ↩

  582. The underlying nature of heat is still present. So the soul would have to be hot, even if it lacked the further effects that heat has in material things, such as ripening, tempering, and turning a substance into vapour. Heat remains heat in every kind of thing that receives it.

    ↩

  583. Avicenna's words do not show what people claim they show. By “meaning” he means either the basis of the definition or a description of something through a feature that follows from it.

    ↩

  584. Here “image” means what makes a thing actual, not a copy that matches it, as in image-based knowledge. Avicenna may mean an image-based definition of the soul, in contrast with direct awareness of it. For example, the soul can be described as an immaterial substance that understands general ideas, begins with the body, or exists before the body.

    ↩

  585. “Flowing from” does not mean a relation that exists alongside the things it relates. It means the source of a relation. Anyone who reads Avicenna as speaking of an added relation has misunderstood him.

    ↩

  586. The difference from the earlier account of knowledge as images is this: on that account, knowledge has the same category as the thing known. If the thing is a substance, knowledge is a substance; if a quantity, knowledge is a quantity; if a quality, knowledge is a quality. Knowledge is not always a quality in the broad sense. Some say calling it a quality is only a loose comparison.

  587. Suhrawardi's division leaves us with two basic cases: a thing is light to itself, or it is light to something else that is itself light. Natural bodies are dark in themselves. Sunlight, moonlight, and lamplight are light to something else; these are the ordinary examples of light. Other bodily qualities are dark forms for something else, according to the Illuminationists.

  588. There is an objection to both Suhrawardi and the author's account. Suhrawardi's definition does not cover God's direct knowledge of bodies, which are dark in themselves, because they are not light for themselves. The author, too, holds that direct knowledge of bodies and their dark features is not a relation between two lights. The answer is that something lit by another is not knowledge of itself or of the thing it receives light from. But it may be knowledge when considered as light shed on something else by an active light. The relation meant by the author is this illuminating relation between a light for itself and a light for something else.

  589. If knowledge meant being free of matter, and this meant being known, then saying that Zayd knows the sun would mean that the sun is free of matter for Zayd but not for Amr. Nor does it follow that the sun's image is free of matter, since this account says knowledge is freedom from matter itself, not a mental image.

    ↩

  590. The author first objects that knowledge cannot be an image if knowing ourselves is simply our self. A second, broader problem concerns anyone who says that an immaterial being's knowledge of itself is identical with its own being. The answer is that the rejected “image” means the essence by which a thing is what it is. In that sense, knowing ourselves can be our very self. But what can be understood as an image is not identical with the real existence that is knowledge itself. On the author's view, the real existence of knowledge is known only through direct awareness.

    ↩

  591. When he later explains his preferred view, the author will say that this further positive state is the luminous existence of the essence.

    ↩

  592. One might ask why this view is attributed only to the author of Al-Mulakhkhaṣ. Many philosophers say that knowledge is a quality and also has a relation to what is known. The difference is that the author seems to make it just a quality, like a mere likeness. The philosophers combine the quality with an image of the essence itself. The author objects to keeping essences in the mind as qualities; he returns to this below.

    ↩

  593. Suhrawardi may mean a relation of illumination. If so, the objection does not apply, because a free existence that takes the form of an image is itself an illumination and a relation.

    ↩

  594. The stronger objection is that, on Suhrawardi's view, bodies are dark in themselves, while knowledge must be light to itself or light to something else. The reply is that bodies, though dark, are lit by the Light of Lights. In this way they become light to something else—not as things that receive light, but as things that give it.

    ↩

  595. A relation exists only in the mind, and only as a dependent kind of existence. It is not an independent object that can match or fail to match another thing, as an idea can.

    ↩

  596. One might ask how this applies to simple ignorance, where there is no mental image. There are three replies. First, the author's own explanation applies. Second, confused ignorance is a kind of knowledge, so it can be said of an image. Third, ordinary reasoning would place the relation in the case where some kind of knowledge is present, even if it is false. Why, then, could that relation not be knowledge?

    ↩

  597. The objection confuses two meanings of “ignorance” and two meanings of “knowledge.” It assumes that ignorance always means simply not knowing.

    ↩

  598. This point supports the author's view. Just as direct knowledge of an immaterial thing is evidence against treating knowledge as a relation, this example also shows that knowledge need not be a relation.

    ↩

  599. Once knowledge has been defined as existence free of matter and position, this objection no longer applies. It is also answered by what the author says about the image account, so it may be better to omit it.

    ↩

  600. The image can be like the thing, so this explanation should be read in light of the clearer one. By “image,” the author means either the essence itself, which he has already rejected, or an essence existing as light. He means the latter.

    ↩

  601. That is, knowledge is possible only through direct awareness. This occurs when a thing knows itself or what comes from it. A human being may know the reality of existence in this first way by becoming absorbed in it.

    ↩

  602. The objection is tied to the author's view because, if knowledge is an immaterial existence and our souls are immaterial existences, then our knowledge of ourselves would be our own existence, as he says.

    ↩

  603. If one thing is joined to another, and that second thing is joined to a third, the first and third are joined too.

    ↩

  604. This leads to two problems: a simple, unified self would have to contain many complex forms, and there would be an endless chain of knowledge about knowledge. Both problems are clearer if essences, rather than existence, are taken as the basic reality, since each concept would then be a separate thing.

    ↩

  605. If our awareness that we know ourselves is not the same as our knowledge of ourselves, and knowledge is different from what is known, then our knowledge of ourselves cannot be the same as our self either.

    ↩

  606. On this answer, our knowledge that we know, and each further level of knowledge, is our self in reality but different in the way the mind considers it. The chain stops when the mind stops considering another level.

    ↩

  607. The answer does stop the endless chain, but it does not answer the worry about one simple, unified self containing many forms and combinations.

    ↩

  608. Al-Tusi seems to mean that direct awareness of ourselves is our own individual existence. It is different from our self only as a concept: the concept “knowledge of self” is not the same as the existence of the self. This brings his answer back to the one the author approves.
