  609. Direct awareness of ourselves exists as our own being. But our learned idea of ourselves—for example, that our soul is an immaterial substance that governs the body, or that it began with the body or existed before it—is not the same as our being. The author's answer is better because al-Tusi's works for direct knowledge.

    ↩

  610. That is, acquired knowledge that knowledge is a quality of the soul, or has some other nature. In short, it is knowledge of what knowledge is.

    ↩

  611. Al-Tusi's account of the sense organ is not the point at issue. Both authors agree that an individual image is present. They disagree on two things. First, others say the image seen exists in the sense organ; the author says it is produced by the rational soul in its lower activity. Second, others say the image seen flows from the First Emanator, while the author says it flows from the soul. He explains this elsewhere.

    ↩

  612. The point is that material bodies hide some of their parts from one another. Their existence therefore includes the possibility of nonexistence: the whole is not fully present to each part, nor each part to the whole. But for a perceiver to know something, the whole thing must be present to it. Material substances and their features cannot be known as they exist in matter. Put another way, a physical image cannot itself be a mental image. This could be shown more clearly by starting from the body's motion within its substance: mental images are certainly present to us, but the parts of a moving material thing are not all present together. So mental images must exist free of matter. This argument also avoids some wording objections.

    ↩

  613. What has no unity cannot be one thing with another, so it cannot exist. One might object that a continuous whole has a single unity. But can its parts and whole really be one and the same? For a claim to be true of both, the parts must not be separated in position. The parts of a continuous whole do not meet that condition, even though they are connected in existence.

    ↩

  614. This is especially true when we think of a body as extending and changing through time. Substantial motion makes it more potential and increases its nonexistence.

    ↩

  615. Material qualities crowd each other out within one subject. Mental images do not: the soul is one, simple, and without size, so it can receive them all. The concepts represented by those images can still conflict in any kind of existence.

    ↩

  616. The soul's ability to receive all forms at once depends on its being free of matter. This also underlies the teaching about bodily resurrection: the soul has no size, so it has no parts of its own, and it can hold the five kinds of sensory images together at one time. It may imagine heat or cold, a taste and a smell, while also seeing and hearing. It can hold opposite images together too, such as black and white, or loud and quiet. In this way the soul shows that nothing keeps God from attending to many things at once.

    ↩

  617. “Position” here means the category of place, not any arrangement within an image. The imagined body of Zayd may have its limbs in order, but the image itself has no position as a material thing. As we have said, an imagined length cannot actually be divided; if we imagine half of a forearm, the mind makes a new half rather than uncovering two existing parts.

    ↩

  618. This refers to the intellectual image. The understood reality is the thing stripped of its material distinctions. It is one and the same whether it is known by one intellect or a thousand.

    ↩

  619. Each person is a complete world and does not need the contents of another person's world. The same is true of the life to come: each believer's paradise is as wide as the heavens and the earth, not only in length but in every direction.

    ↩

  620. That is, this holds when the image is an accident, not a natural form.

    ↩

  621. This difference concerns a divinely supported soul. In its direct knowledge of itself, its image is already complete and it can develop by its own resources, like the souls of the heavenly spheres.

    ↩

  622. This is true of general ideas. Particular images are said of their objects in the ordinary, concrete sense. Directly imagined images are like what is directly sensed, as we explained when discussing mental existence.

    ↩

  623. This view seems more useful than the account in the current book. It says, for example, that an intellect understands a substance as a substance by its definition, not by being that kind of substance in the ordinary sense. But this can make it seem that the intellectual image has no real substance, much like the idea of an impossible partner to God. The author will soon clarify that intellectual realities are higher than substance, not lower. The soul, on this view, has no separate essence of its own, and is not simply an accident either. This question may be resolved either through the unity of knower and known, or through the view that universals are known by seeing their separate exemplars, the immaterial intellects. Suhrawardi, for example, says that these intellects have no essences.

    ↩

  624. At first glance, mental existence seems to be a state in which the thing's outside effects do not occur. So we affirm the idea in its own terms and deny it of the mental image in the ordinary, concrete sense. On closer inspection, however, the mental image is an imaginal or intellectual form: it is more complete than material existence and has effects suited to its own level. It seems to have no effects only when we compare it with the material effects. This is a difference between levels of stronger and weaker existence. The form may be said to be both the same as and different from its material counterpart, depending on whether we mean their shared reality or their different levels.

    ↩

  625. “Kind” here means a level of existence, not a species. The imaginal and intellectual images share the same species in essence as their material examples, but exist at a different level.

    ↩

  626. “Substance” applies when something is actual and does not depend on a subject, even as a possibility. This is like a body, which can have three intersecting lines even when no lines are drawn in it, as in a sphere.

    ↩

  627. “Meanings” here refers to the world of meanings, including the divine realm and the separate intellects. Rumi says: “Generations passed, one after another; those meanings remain, enduring.” Every reality has a meaning and a form, a deeper reality and its outward appearance, a root and its branch. Its root is present in the soul. After God and the completely separate intellects, the soul is simple in its reality, and a simple reality gathers within itself, in a higher way, the existences beneath it. When the soul wants to know something, it turns to the page of its own being, where the form of that thing is already present. By “form” I mean what makes a thing actual.

    As explained earlier, a reality in the soul can both be affirmed and denied of it: we deny its material boundaries and imperfections, which are absent from the soul's single, simple existence; we affirm it because its higher existence is the root and source of the material thing. Thus when the author says that the understood animal includes the understood body, growth and sensation, he means that the soul gathers these meanings in a higher, simpler existence. The soul knows itself directly, rather than through a separate image residing in it. That is why the difficulties about how a mental image could itself be a substance, grow, sense or move do not arise in the same way once the knower and what is known are understood as one. The same applies to bodily extension: the soul contains bodily existence in a higher manner, without sharing its limits. A fine verse puts it this way:

    “O you who are a complete copy of the divine book, and a mirror of the King's beauty: nothing in the world is outside you. Seek within yourself whatever you desire—for you are that.”

    ↩

  628. It is not right to deny these realities of this all-embracing existence, which is a reflected unity. In natural existence, one human being contains the powers of matter, plant life, and animal life. More generally, being does not have to belong to one thing only. Concepts such as existence, unity, identity, and light can be true of many things. An essence and its defining features can also exist in a broader reality. These ideas are all present together in the higher, intellectual existence.

    ↩

  629. By “animal,” Avicenna means the natural kind of animal; he actually uses the example of a human being. The intellectual universal in the author’s earlier discussion has another meaning. Al-Tusi also understands Avicenna’s words as referring to the natural universal, as is clear to anyone who reads the beginning of the fourth section of The Pointers. The intellectual universal is not without the natural universal.

    ↩

  630. The point is that an accident is not just a description that can be added to something; it is a kind of existence that depends on a subject. To exist in a subject is the way qualities such as blackness and heat exist. Existence itself does not truly attach to an essence as another feature. The mind separates them in thought. So an essence's existence is not like a passing feature that can change while the essence remains. A substance could not keep the same essence while its very way of existing changed from depending on a subject to not depending on one. Comparing existence with other incidental features is not a sound comparison. Existence is not truly added to an essence; it is the thing's being real. More exactly, each kind of existence must suit the essence that exists: an accident exists in a subject, and a substance exists on its own.

    ↩

  631. The truth, as we have explained elsewhere, is that knowledge is not a quality, as al-Dawwānī says. It is the existence that the soul spreads over all the essences present in the intellect, imagination, and common sense. It is the soul's light shining on the forms that receive it, just as God's light shines on all things in the worlds of intellect, soul, and matter. God's giving existence is not itself a substance or an accident; likewise, the soul's light is neither substance nor accident in itself. It takes the nature of the things it illuminates. This view is more satisfying than al-Dawwānī's, because for him knowledge belongs to the same category as what is known.

    ↩

  632. The proof appears later, in the discussion of how intellect is intelligible to itself and understands itself.

    ↩

  633. The claim rests on a broader principle: when something exists for another, its existence in itself is the same existence it has for that other. This applies to accidents and their subjects, forms and matter, and—if a cause and its effect have direct awareness of one another—to causes and effects. If we consider a dependent existence apart from what it belongs to, we must also consider the thing that owns it. If that existence can stand on its own, then owner and owned are one thing at the same level, as when a substance exists in itself or an immaterial soul knows itself. Otherwise, the dependent existence belongs at a level within the existence of what it depends on, as a dependent being belongs within the being that supports it. This shows that an accident is a level of its substance’s existence, matter and form are one in existence, and an effect is a level of its cause’s existence (and a cause, in turn, is a higher level of its effect). But this principle does not prove that knower and known have one existence at the same level. The commentator therefore rejects the claim that an understood form can be intelligible in act whether or not any intellect understands it: we cannot set the form apart from its knower, even by placing it at a higher level. He also points out that a relation between knower and known is a real opposition between two sides, which cannot belong to one thing in one and the same respect.

    ↩

  634. In short, an object of thought in itself and in act has no feature or aspect other than being understood; being understood is its very existence. It remains intelligible even if we set everything else aside, because its existence is luminous and aware. Although we form the idea of “being understood” by reference to an intellect, setting the intellect aside also sets aside the object’s existence as understood. If its existence remained, it would still be something and still be intelligible, which would contradict the claim that it had no intellect. One might object that an effect is essentially an effect, and so would have to be its own cause. The reply is that being an effect is essential to the effect in the sense that it needs no further feature in order to be called an effect; it still needs a distinct cause. An intelligible form, by contrast, can be understood without another intellect, as in the case of the Necessary Being.

    ↩

  635. The point is not that, because knower and known are related and matched in level, either one must be found wherever the other is found—including in the other’s own essence. Their being matched means they exist together, not that one has the same existence as the other. The author’s point is that the actual knower corresponding to an actual object of thought cannot be a separate soul that contains it as a vessel contains something. If the soul were the knower while remaining separate from the known form, then it would be only potentially a knower of it. When the form is understood in act, the form itself is what knows it. This is a second proof, distinct from the earlier proof that an actual object of thought has no existence apart from its luminous intellectual existence. If the first proof does not rely on the general rule about related things, how do we know that there is a knower at all? We rely on the principle that the known form’s existence in itself is its existence for the knower—not on the general logical category of relation. The form’s being understood in itself does not prove that it is joined to another thing by such a relation. The author later allows an illuminative relation: the understood form depends on the soul for its existence, and the soul depends on it in turn.

    ↩

  636. To truly possess something is to have it in one’s own being, not merely to stand in a relation to it. A person who only “has” something in a secondary sense still lacks it in their own being; their possession is only a relation. Existence itself belongs truly to existence, not to an essence that becomes real by receiving existence as an extra feature. In the same way, knowledge truly belongs to the intellectual form itself; the form is knowledge because it is what is known.

    ↩

  637. “What is other than the image” means things outside the mind. They may be called objects of thought in themselves because their images are present to the knower. The images, however, are mirrors through which attention sees the things; they are not always what attention is directly fixed on. If every image had to be understood by means of another image, the process would go on forever.

    ↩

  638. Unless these things are levels and aspects of your own existence.

    ↩

  639. The proof given here treats the presence of an understood form to its knower, the presence of an impressed image to matter, and the presence of an accident to its subject as cases of one kind: a dependent feature exists within what it describes. The subject does not stand outside the existence of that feature; it is found within the feature’s range of existence. The same applies to direct awareness between cause and effect. The knower and known may exist at one level, as when the soul knows itself; or one may be a level within the other’s existence, as when an effect knows its cause or a cause knows its effect. On the author’s account, all direct knowledge falls into these cases. But this does not mean that knower and known must exist at exactly the same level. If they did, we could not know accidents, which would then have to exist in themselves, or know a cause and its effect without making them equal in rank. Think carefully about this distinction.

    ↩

  640. Here we have the beginning of a proof that the knower and what is known become one, as Alexander argued. This is particularly clear if, as the author and al-Sayyid al-Sanad maintain, matter and form make one being, rather than two things merely joined. The soul is like matter and what it perceives is like its form. If matter and form have this kind of union even among physical things, how much more is it possible in understanding? A subject and an added quality, by contrast, are united only in a different, more limited sense.

    By union we mean being one in existence, not having the same meaning. The various things understood have different meanings, and their meanings differ from that of the knower; yet their existence can be one. Otherwise the intellect would consist merely of concepts, like the independent essences assumed by the Muʿtazilites. When we speak of clearly distinguished forms of knowledge, they are one with the knower as the knower becomes manifest, not with the hidden depth of the knower's being. But the simple, all-embracing intellect, which contains knowledge without separate parts, can be one with that hidden depth. The higher unity contains many within one, and detail within what is undivided; detailed knowledge displays unity within multiplicity. This distinction between levels is needed if we are not to collapse all forms of existence into one undifferentiated thing.

    There are other proofs. First, what the intellect understands is free of matter, and everything free of matter understands itself. If it is objected that an understood form depends on something else, as an image supposedly depends on the soul, I deny that such forms exist merely by being housed in another: the universal forms of substances are substances, and an essential feature cannot cease to be essential. Even the claim that imagined images reside inside something has been challenged; it is still less suitable for intellectual forms.

    Second, we have explained that understanding universals is a way of witnessing the separate intellects. Earlier philosophers also held that the intellect receives such knowledge from them. Definitions and proofs point in this direction, and the soul stands in a direct relation of awareness to these intellects. They are themselves capable of understanding.

    Third, the real bearer of a description is the reality from which that description comes. Existence itself is what truly exists, and whiteness itself is what is truly white; in the same way, knowledge is the true knower. The philosophers call the soul an intellect in possibility when its understood form is still possible, and an intellect in actuality when that form is actual. Thus it is an intellect, or a knower, through what it understands.

    Fourth, the soul in the higher depth of its being gives rise to the distinct forms it understands. What gives existence and completeness cannot be wholly without them; it must possess them in a higher way. This reasoning applies whether their source is the simple intellect, the inward depth of the soul, or the Active Intellect.

    Fifth, the outward world and the world of the mind correspond, like twins nourished with the same milk. To say that Zayd exists outside the mind is to place him within a level of the outward world. In the same way, what is understood exists at a level of the soul and its powers: the mind is not a container holding mental objects. Together with the opening argument from matter and form, these make six proofs. Insight also supports them. As Rumi says: “Brother, you are thought itself; the rest is bone and sinew.”

    ↩

  641. This argument assumes the common view that an accident has an existence separate from the existence of its subject. On the more accurate view, which the author supports elsewhere, an accident is a level of its subject’s existence. The issue is then like the union of knower and known.

    ↩

  642. Avicenna argues that if a form could receive another form, it would have to change into something else, and the forms would not be incompatible. The commentator objects that this argument is refuted by the all-embracing existence that flows from God: it is one, yet united with many different possible essences, such as the essence of a human being, which has no capacity to receive the essence of a horse and does not turn into one. The key is that this all-embracing existence has no single, fixed boundary; it has degrees, from stronger to weaker. The rational soul is like this too: its unity is a reflected unity. If Avicenna insists that every existence joined to one essence must be wholly separate from every existence joined to another essence, then the essences themselves would have to be simple, separate existences. This leads to serious problems, including the famous doubt attributed to Ibn Kammūna, and would leave no real unity. The commentator therefore reads the differences among such existences as differences in the essences they manifest, not as divisions in existence itself.

    ↩

  643. This happens in the immaterial soul. The soul can prepare itself through acts of thought and receive divine or angelic thoughts as lights from the Active Intellect. When it understands absolute, simple existence, or recognizes itself as life, universal light, knowledge, will, and love, its existence turns toward these perfections. It does not take on their self-standing existence; it joins them through a dependent, intellectual illumination, whether near or far. The soul then grows and becomes one with these perfections in the way described earlier.

    ↩

  644. The commentator distinguishes the soul’s essence from its existence. Perfections are added to the soul’s essence, but not to its existence. In the separate intellects, knowledge, will, and power are their existence, so no further perfection is waiting for them. These perfections are still “added” to their essence in the sense that an essence, considered on its own, is only what it is.

    ↩

  645. The passage refers to one continuous individual of motion, extending from its beginning to its end. A changing quality has three possible kinds of individual: one is a single, continuous, time-stretched individual, from rest to rest; another consists of the portions that the mind can distinguish within that duration; a third is a series of supposed instants, each with a separate individual before and after it. The first is one individual with different degrees of completeness and existence, and can support different concepts as it changes.

    ↩

  646. “Matter” here means what something depends on or is attached to. It does not have to mean bodily prime matter.

    ↩

  647. In the beginning, the soul was the specific form of a bodily being. It was like a sensory or imagined form, but less fully actual, because the soul can undergo growth and change while those forms resist it. This potential for development, despite its weakness, is far better than being fixed in a fully actual state. The commentator notes that Avicenna’s objection is about an intelligible form, while the author’s reply first speaks of a specific bodily form. The reply still addresses the point behind Avicenna’s objection: before it understands anything, the soul is already a form, and Avicenna says a form cannot receive another form.

  648. Strictly speaking, this kind of growth is not “receiving” a new form. It is a weaker existence being absorbed into a stronger one as it grows. If “receiving” is used here, it means that the soul comes to be described by a further perfection. Even if one grants that an actual form cannot receive another actual form, that does not undermine the union of knower and known, because that union does not depend on such reception.

  649. The first kind of potentiality is accompanied by the thing’s actual absence from the outside world, as when one form replaces another. The second belongs to growth toward a higher level: the thing exists, but its expected perfection does not yet exist. If we compare it with what comes later, that absence is in thought; if we compare it with what came earlier, what is absent is its earlier lack or incompleteness. The second kind is not an external absence in the thing itself.

    ↩

  650. The author’s phrase “a form connected to matter” means that the form can grow because it is attached to matter; considered simply as a form, it cannot receive another form or change. Through its relation to bodily matter, the soul can grow from intellect in act toward the Active Intellect and beyond. Imaginal forms that have no matter cannot develop in this way. That is why the afterlife is not a place where the soul continues to grow, even though what it sees and understands may become clearer over time. The world is the field where the soul grows; the afterlife is where it gathers what it has cultivated. As the saying goes, wheat grows from wheat and barley from barley. The clearest answer is that an essence cannot receive another essence; only existence becomes stronger or weaker. The body’s matter supplies the receptive capacity for this growth.

  651. The intelligible forms are manifestations of the soul’s own being, not its hidden essence. Their appearing existence is the soul’s existence as it shines outward; they do not move away from the soul or diminish it.

    ↩

  652. The true intellect in act is the understood form, not the soul as the subject in which that form is found. The soul remains potentially intelligible to itself until that form appears.   653. Avicenna does not mean that the soul’s bare self, with no relation to intelligible forms, is the knower. He means the soul as related to the forms it understands: the relation is within the knower, while what it understands is outside it.

  654. The point is that an intellectual form is an intellect in itself, even if Avicenna says the soul is an intellect because of that form. The form is intellect for itself; it is not intellect merely for the bare soul that receives it.

    ↩

  655. The Active Intellect exists in itself and also exists for us. Our souls become one with the way it exists for us, not with its own existence in itself. Its existence for us has endlessly many levels, though its own being is one. The multiplicity lies in how it appears. So it does not follow that a soul must understand everything the Active Intellect understands, or that every soul joined to it must know everything known by every other soul joined to it.

  656. The claim is not that many separate existences literally turn into one, which would be impossible. Nor is it that their existences remain separate but count as one because they are copies or reflections of a single thing; that would be unity in multiplicity. The point is multiplicity gathered within unity: one simple intellectual existence is the higher mode of all the things understood, and contains them within its unity as its manifestations and aspects.

  657. This is a formal argument: pure existence is pure being, and nothing that is pure has any distinction mixed into it. If we suppose two instances of pure whiteness, they must differ by their subjects, their times, or something else. Then neither is pure whiteness alone; each includes something beyond whiteness. The same argument applies to pure existence. The intellectual meaning of pure existence or whiteness is therefore one and the same wherever it is understood, whether by Zayd or by the Active Intellect; the two do not have separate copies of it. Otherwise, we would have to ask what universal meaning they share, and the same problem would continue without end. The commentator compares this to radiating lines that meet at one center. The direct awareness each soul has of itself is likewise one in meaning once incidental features are set aside.

  658. Intellectual unity is a true, reflected unity, not numerical unity. If the soul becomes one with one aspect of an all-embracing intellect, it does not follow that it becomes one with every other aspect. A single intellect can have many inherent aspects. Likewise, knowing the divine does not mean knowing every feature of the divine being.

On the second reading the passage would not prove union with something other than itself.   663. Each intellect that serves as the lord of a particular kind has its own rank and care.   664. The commentator questions the author’s decision to identify “universal life” only with the natural universal and “universal intellect” only with its intellectual form. The example is not simply that one universal meaning is found in many individuals; it concerns a wider intellectual existence that contains and gives rise to them.

  665. I say: this takes a needlessly long route. It would be better to say that the intellect that comes to be is a manifestation of the separate intellect corresponding to its kind, its lord. Here “coming to be” is contrasted with “being brought forth”: the soul begins with the body, or through the body’s coming to be. It does not mean the “is” that connects the parts of a statement.   666. “Parts” may mean intellectual manifestations of the whole, such as the perfected intellects of divinely guided people, or the meaningful parts of an understood animal: its understood head, hand, and foot.   667. The commentator considers al-Rāzī’s account very weak. How could a bare relation exist within one simple, immaterial being? Al-Rāzī’s strongest reply is that the knower must turn its attention toward itself or toward an image of something else, and that this attention is a relation. The commentator answers that attention is itself awareness, so the explanation cannot show that awareness is only a relation. Every act of knowing something else also includes awareness of oneself. If knowledge remained only when the knower also knew that it knew, then awareness of awareness would be needed in turn, without end.

  668. “Relation” by itself is too broad a category. It needs distinguishing features before it becomes a specific kind of relation. The critic has not proved even that knowledge is a relation in the broad sense; he has only asserted it. He points to some conditions for a relation, such as the existence of both sides, and tries to remove objections concerning self-knowledge or knowledge of what does not exist. That is a serious failure of explanation: it would have been better not to attempt the argument.

  669. Al-Rāzī accepts that the difference between the two descriptions is only a difference in meaning.

Since the opposite is plainly the case, be fair: this is an exalted question, difficult to reach.

  673. This refers to the familiar argument that two identical things cannot exist together in the same place.

  675. That is, a reversal in the wording of the two propositions.

That account seems to be attributed to Avicenna as a way to explain phrases like “my self” and “your self,” not to explain how an immaterial being knows itself. He insists on this view in several of his books, including the section on the soul in this work and The Keys to the Unseen. I find this claim puzzling as stated. Love, hatred, and similar states occur in many individuals, as different animals have different appetites and at different times. Time and the features surrounding a soul also help make such states particular. There are particular meanings of love, desire, and will, yet the intellect does not grasp particular meanings, and neither does sense or imagination. Perhaps the author means a mistaken estimate, since falsehood and evil are not independent realities. He often keeps divine unity in view. The author may say that in animals, these states are perceived by the intellects that govern their kinds, rather than by our intellect. Calling them “meanings,” as opposed to forms perceived by the outer senses, does not make them a different kind of act that requires a separate faculty. The better view is to set aside estimation as a distinct faculty and assign its work to the common sense.

  689. The commentator counts sensation, imagination, and intellect as the real kinds, setting aside estimation just as he sets aside sensation as a separate kind.   690. In this respect, the intellect has an angelic role, like Azrael. By reviving ignorant souls through teaching, it also has a role like Israfil or Gabriel. The human being is a comprehensive whole containing all these roles.

  691. The common explanation mistakenly treats universality as a feature of the object known, and only indirectly of the act of knowledge. The correct account treats knowledge as universal in itself, while the known thing is universal only indirectly. Knowledge is luminous existence: it is wide-ranging, simple, and all-embracing.

  692. The universal humanity applies to many people; the humanity in each one does not.

  693. The universal humanity is not the humanity found in two people together, or in all people as one collective whole. The humanity in one person is not identical with the two-person whole. A better reply would ask whether the universal known exists outside the mind. If it is the universal in individuals, or a collective whole, the same objection defeats it. If it is an essence considered in itself, it is not universal. If it exists in the mind but is distinct from the mind, as al-Qūshjī argues, it is refuted by the earlier discussion of mental existence.

  694. Defining universality as “applying to many” raises problems, so philosophers shifted to defining it as “being shared.” Since that definition also has difficulties, they explain sharing this way: when the universal exists in matter, it is the individuals; when those individuals are understood, they are the universal.

  695. The point is that this all-embracing existence is universal and shared because it contains its individual instances and is equally related to them. Its intellectual individuality does not conflict with this reach.

  696. If the soul’s ordinary subject and its surrounding features remained in place, they would make the intellectual image particular. But understanding is the knower becoming one with what it knows, so the knower changes into it. To truly reach a meaning, the soul must become it and pass away into it. This does not mean that the soul simply disappears: its unity is not numerical or limited, but a true, dependent unity. When it changes in one respect, it remains in its other aspects. This change happens in the potential intellect, not in the soul’s imaginative level, where it already has actual particular images. The potential intellect has many levels, like prime matter. When prime matter becomes fire, for example, it can also become air or a human being; one change does not rule out its receiving other forms.

  697. The author does not say that its relation to individuals is equal, because the universal intellect does not depend on individuals; when it exists, they are not yet there. Individuals, by contrast, depend on it and must be related to it.

  698. Abstraction does not mean that the soul stays in its own intellectual place while images move from matter through sense and imagination to intellect.   699. “Becoming one” here means actual realization, not merely being related to something or thinking about it. It is an existence that becomes the thing, not just knowledge or thought about it.

  700. This is more complete than merely having a sense image of the heavens.

  701. In the same way, if the features of existence—that is, the essences—are set aside, one underlying reality remains.

  702. The commentator says it would be more accurate to say that giving intellectual things bodily images is the work of imagination, not intellect. That description confuses the faculties. The intellect understands true light, while imagination pictures sunlight. The intellect understands all-embracing reality, while imagination pictures spatial extension. Still, “multiplying one” can mean either the mistaken imagining described above or a proper act of intellect: distinguishing different aspects, names, and attributes of God, or distinguishing the levels of existence from simple beings up through plants, animals, and human beings.

  703. The soul’s potential to understand is counted as a kind of understanding because a thing’s potential is its first trace: without it, the thing could not exist or rise from a lower state to a higher one. Avicenna does not specify this potential stage; instead, he divides acquired knowledge into two kinds, as the author explains below.

  704. Even the potential intellect’s knowledge of itself is only potential. It might merely imagine itself, as an ignorant soul does, or imagine itself as something with a position and face.

    ↩

  705. The second kind means detailed intelligible forms held in the intellect. It is the first of Avicenna’s three kinds, but because imagination helps arrange those forms in sequence, he says they are held in an imaginative power. He may instead mean an intellectual power mixed with or related to imagination.

  706. This objection confuses intellect with imagination and rejects a general truth because it is absent in one particular case. Because a person cannot find the forms in imagination, they assume they cannot be in intellect—as though the soul were nothing but imagination. They wrongly assume that because the forms are not present as many, they cannot be present as one. Avicenna and other careful thinkers should not call this state potential knowledge while a person is eating or drinking; they should call it strong knowledge. The soul has faculties of sense, imagination, estimation, detailed intellect, and simple intellect. Four may not be perceiving, while the fifth still knows. This is especially true when the person is almost pure intellect and the partial faculties have been brought into line with it. Notice that such a person need not acquire anything new through effort. Simple intellect is a manifestation of the One who is not distracted by one affair from another. True speech is grasping universals and communicating with immaterial beings. A prophetic report says that among the community are people who receive direct insight. This is one way of reading the revealed Book in a single timeless act. This intellect belongs to the world of pure intellect and timelessness, even if its outward form is in the natural world and it still uses bodily faculties. Its higher activity does not keep it from ordinary activity. A person with firm spiritual grounding sees particulars as mirrors of universals, not the other way around. Anyone who rejects this sees the body, or the soul merely as soul, as the self—and so fails to see that self’s higher capacity. “Knowledge of your soul is no trivial matter; if you know it truly, you know what it is.”

  707. This means knowledge either unfolded in detail, or knowledge held more strongly.

  708. A fact cannot be established for something unless that thing exists. When the speaker says, “This is present in me,” the word “this” points intellectually to something that exists in act. In either reading, the answer to the question is already known in act.

  709. This refers to the way intellectual forms exist for separate beings in simple intellect, not to material forms or images that belong to the soul’s own psychic world.

    ↩

  710. The union must preserve simplicity. If the knower existed through one existence and each intelligible through a separate existence, however closely connected, they would make a composite whole. Simplicity is preserved only if all exist through one existence and multiplicity belongs to the meanings understood.

  711. Someone might say that the Active Intellect is usually taken to be the storehouse of intelligibles, and that in every act of knowing our partial intellect connects with or faces it. How, then, can Avicenna call simple intellect the storehouse, especially before knowledge has become a settled habit? There is no conflict if, as explained earlier, the horse understood by the Active Intellect and the horse understood by a thousand intellects is one. Avicenna’s account works only if intellect and intelligible are one, though he rejects that view. His position is inconsistent.

    ↩

  712. “Intelligibles” here means intelligibles in themselves, in detail; “things” means things known indirectly, that is, external things. The essences are one in both, but existence differs in strength, weakness, completeness, and incompleteness. The differences between levels of existence are not differences between wholly unrelated realities.

  713. The commentator says “what follows from His attributes” means the essences that follow from God’s attributes. Their existence is contained in the existence of those attributes, which is itself contained in God’s existence. Their meanings are not later in existence, as a geometrical body follows from a natural body, or measured time from successive motion. Unity and individuality also follow from certain kinds of real existence. Or the phrase may mean the effects that follow from God’s acts: the existence of the cause is the higher form of existence for its effects. A thing is fully itself, not in a diminished way; and the stronger its existence, the more it contains meanings. Stronger light reveals more essences, and knowledge of the cause entails knowledge of its effect.

  714. I grant that the form, which makes a thing actual, is one. If by “form” we mean a single essence, it cannot represent many different essences. But if it means one existence, united in a true unity and infinitely intense in its light, it can reveal all existences and contain many meanings and essences. As the saying goes, “God’s hand is with the gathering.” The same is true of the human simple intellect: its existence is one and powerful, yet it is one with the many essences that appear distinctly in detailed thought. All these essences exist in it as meanings, while their existence is one. If we look at their one existence, we see how one act of knowledge can know many, even countless, things. If we look at the many essences contained in simple intellect, we see how many acts of knowledge can be present together. But remember that the knower in both cases is pure intellect, not the soul’s detailed understanding and certainly not imagination. “You are too great to appear in a small mirror.” If someone imagines that neither kind of knowledge is actually present in simple intellect, they are mistaking themselves for imagination or ordinary understanding. As the verse says, “As long as you imagine yourself confined to a before and an after, you are bound to the body and deprived of the soul.” In God, detail exists within an all-at-once knowledge, and unity within detailed knowledge: the many known things are one in the act of knowing. Knowledge and its object are one, though—as with existence and essence—they differ in how we conceive them. This avoids the two objections raised by the critic.

    ↩

  715. The commentator asks how someone who does not know the real nature of the answers can be sure that all the answers are present or that they will address the questions. Any answer does not fit any question. By contrast, we can know that something moves the body without knowing what it is, because we know one aspect of it while other aspects remain unknown. Whether the soul is a nature, a bodily mixture, or immaterial, it can move the body.

    ↩

  716. In this respect, simple intellect manifests the divine names of the One whom no thing hides from another and whom no affair distracts from another. Even the common sense gathers five kinds of sensation in one moment: sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste. While seeing, we may also hear, feel the air’s temperature, smell, and taste. The common sense is then aware of five worlds at once. When it senses something while awake and imagination combines or separates images that it presents at the same time, there are at least two acts of perception; with the perception of particular meanings, the soul has three. So what should we expect of intellect, especially simple intellect? The endless number of intelligibles is also clear. One general claim, such as “Everything that comes to be will pass away,” branches into countless claims about animals, plants, minerals, incomplete compounds, particular animals, and countless land and sea creatures. The same applies to relations, opposites, and other general truths. These unrecorded examples point to countless other propositions and concepts, all intelligible as one simple reality to the true intellectual human being, in one timeless act.

    ↩

  717. The wording is loose. “Several acts of knowledge in one moment” means that they are grasped together, without a sequence. Immaterial knowledge is not itself measured by time or by a moment.

    ↩

  718. This explanation does not fully answer the objection. The author elsewhere treats imagination as immaterial like intellect, so why can it not hold all its images together without sequence? Two things may explain the limit. First, the imaginative powers have material organs in the body—eyes, ears, and parts of the brain—that perform material operations and prepare the soul for particular perceptions. The resistance comes from these bodily powers, not from the immaterial psychic power itself. Second, even if imagination is free of matter, it still has some features of matter, such as quantity and certain qualities. This makes its images occur in an order, and ordered parts cannot all be present together. If we imagine dawn, then sunrise, noon, sunset, and darkness, each stage naturally gives way to the next, even though the whole image is free of matter.

    ↩

  719. We have also shown that sense can gather several perceptions at once. The chapter would therefore have been better titled “Whether the soul can have many kinds of knowledge at once,” since the examples include several sensations, imagination, estimation, detailed understanding, and simple understanding together.

    ↩

  720. You may ask whether understanding is an action or a passive reception, since the soul acts on the body but receives from the immaterial world above it. There are two answers. First, this develops the idea of simple intellect, which the philosophers also distinguish from detailed knowledge. Second, the author treats the grasp of particular things, such as imagined forms, as the soul’s active creation. The soul is active in producing the many, changing images of detailed knowledge.

    ↩

  721. This includes the soul’s life, power, and knowledge of itself: immediate knowledge in which the soul is present to itself, without further divisions. Knowledge can also be divided into acquired and direct knowledge. Direct knowledge includes an immaterial being’s knowledge of itself, a thing’s direct awareness of its effect, and the awareness of a person who has become one with what they know. Knowledge can be general or exact, and general or detailed. The author’s example of human knowledge needs to be read in reverse, as the context makes clear.

    ↩

  722. The prophet’s true self and inner heart connect with the Active Intellect and, through it, with all the separate intellects in the ascending order. The prophet receives direct spiritual teaching and learns the simple realities of things. A saint may connect with the finer, lower-level aspect of the Active Intellect—the one most suited to the people of their time—and receive its images and spoken words. For the friends of God, sages, and those who know God, a complete union of their true selves with the true self of the intellect is rare. Each person is enabled for what they were made to do.

    ↩

  723. The issue is not an endless chain of teachers across different people and times. It is whether one person’s thought about a single subject depends on earlier thought from a teacher without end. If every step in one person’s reasoning had to be taught, the chain would never reach the self-evident ideas from which reasoning begins. For example, the idea of a human being may be learned from the ideas of animal and rational; those from substance, able to have dimensions, living, sensing, and understanding; and those from ideas such as existence and possibility. At the root, the thinker knows existence, possibility, increase, perception, and knowledge for themselves. This is what philosophers mean when they say that the chain of concepts cannot continue forever.

    ↩

  724. Knowing that the Active Intellect is immaterial in both its being and its action, has no unrealized potential, completes souls, and is the storehouse and source of their intelligible forms is not the heart of direct knowledge. The heart of it is becoming and being transformed by that reality. General knowledge is still a means to this direct encounter when its meanings become firm in the soul. “Knowledge is the seed of direct vision.” May God help us join knowledge with action and protect us from error, through Muhammad and his family, the friends of God who reach the universal intellects and rise beyond them.

    ↩

  725. The argument for both claims can be summarized this way. For the first: if a cause is a cause through its full causal reality, then knowing it means knowing its necessary effect. The known cause and effect must be present together in knowledge. If the cause acts through its existence, then direct knowledge of that existence is together with the existence of its effect, since the effect’s existence depends on it. Merely knowing the cause’s essence does not reveal the effect, because causality belongs to existence, not essence. For the second claim: if the effect follows from an essence, knowing it gives knowledge of some cause, since the effect may follow from a broader essence. If it follows from existence, direct knowledge of its existence gives knowledge of an aspect of its cause, but not complete knowledge of the cause. The effect’s essence alone does not establish any cause.

    ↩

  726. This premise is the heart of the argument: the cause and effect are known together. It does not say that knowledge of the cause is a prior cause of knowledge of the effect, as al-Rāzī objects. Saying that the cause’s existence includes the relational existence of its effect does not remove the fact that they are known together. The best reading is that the author means a direct, illuminating relation between them, if this fits the philosophers’ words.

    ↩

  727. Knowledge of real existence cannot be merely a mental copy; it must be direct. Direct knowledge has three cases: an immaterial being’s knowledge of itself, its knowledge of its effect, and a thing’s knowledge of what it has become one with. The author’s claim seems to apply this rule specifically to direct knowledge of existence, as is correct in his view. Other philosophers do not limit it this way. For example, they say that knowledge of a barrier causes knowledge of a hollow, or knowledge of an opposing angle causes knowledge of a crescent shape. Those are not cases of direct knowledge. For them, God’s knowledge of Himself is direct, but His knowledge of effects is acquired through images in His being. The author does not always restrict his rule to direct knowledge; here, his wording “in its real identity” points to that restriction.

    ↩

  728. This objection also fails when a thing has no essence separate from existence.

    ↩

  729. The philosophers say both that knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect and that the reverse does not follow. But if cause and effect are known together simply because they are correlatives, the same should hold in both directions. Also, their question concerns knowing a particular cause and effect, not the broad concepts of cause and effect.

    ↩

  730. The objection also reverses: knowing every aspect of an effect would include knowing that it follows from a particular cause.

    ↩

  731. This word should be read as “all the aspects,” not “if,” since it continues the reasoning and does not begin a new condition.

    ↩

  732. Someone might reply that the argument is about what we need in order to prove something, not what makes it exist. But knowing the part is also part of knowing the whole.

    ↩

  733. There is no need to answer the condition separately; this sentence explains what the philosophers mean by saying that knowing the cause means knowing the effect.

  734. The author’s reply does not fully solve the second part of the objection: that related things are known together in thought and in the outside world, while he claims knowledge of the cause comes before knowledge of the effect. His reply also seems to accept that the category of relation is added to God’s being. A better answer is that the effect is a feature of the cause’s existence and depends on it, so the cause’s existence cannot be present in full without containing its effect. Direct knowledge of the cause therefore gives direct knowledge of the effect. The category of relation applies to the concepts of cause and effect, not to their existence.

  735. This is like an attribute’s existence. It is one simple existence outside the mind. When related to its broad kind, such as color, it exists as a feature and depends on that kind. When related to its distinguishing feature, such as the way it separates light from the eye, it is also a cause, since the distinguishing feature gives the broad kind its specific form.

    ↩

  736. Even those who say that relations do not exist in their own separate right need not say they do not exist at all. A relation exists through the thing that gives rise to it. The argument against a separate existence for relations only rules out that first sense.

    ↩

  737. An essential property, such as evenness, differs from the essence in both its meaning and its existence in the mind. Four is a quantity; evenness is a feature of quantity. The author likely means only that the effect necessarily follows from the cause, not that it has the same kind of existence. His discussion may also apply only to causes and effects in divine philosophy.

    ↩

  738. “Full understanding” means that the mind’s account matches reality. In direct knowledge, it becomes one with that reality. The question may be intended to challenge this full union. Otherwise, there is no point in the argument: a complete cause cannot fail to produce its effect. Philosophers who discuss God’s knowledge of other things all agree that the effect is present in knowledge of the cause, though they differ on whether this is direct knowledge of existence, a mental form, luminous images, or timeless essences. A cause and effect can differ, yet the effect is present when the cause is present, just as evenness is present when four is understood. The point is not to reject full knowledge.

    ↩

  739. This point applies only to direct knowledge. The previous argument used it in that sense.

    ↩

  740. An effect cannot be particular before the cause makes it particular. Its individual identity comes from the cause. Some philosophers say that certain kinds, such as immaterial beings, cause their own individual identity. The commentator rejects this: no essence can produce individuation, because individuality belongs to existence. A particular existence gives the essence its individual identity. A particular defining feature likewise makes the broad kind into a particular species. Al-Rāzī misses this point when he assumes that a broad kind such as body already exists on its own and then asks what makes it one particular type.

    ↩

  741. This is a claim made in the logical book The Demonstration: certainty about something that has a cause can come only through certainty about its cause. Certainty is knowledge that something is so and cannot be otherwise. If we know that an effect exists, then we must already know that its cause exists; otherwise the effect could exist without its cause. Philosophers use this rule to set aside one kind of proof from effects: reasoning from an effect back to its own cause. They accept two kinds of proof: one that starts from a cause and establishes its effect, and one that reasons from general signs of an effect to signs of another effect. Later notes explain the limits of this claim.

    ↩

  742. Some philosophers say that all caused things can be known only through their causes. The problem is that this seems to rule out immediate knowledge, such as seeing. The commentator says the rule should not be weakened. The existence of every effect depends on its cause, and every possible thing depends on God. The mind first knows a cause’s existence and then the existence of its effect. As ʿAlī is reported to have said, “I never saw a thing without seeing God before it.”

    ↩

  743. “Matches” here means is one with. The intellectual form is the real existence itself in direct knowledge; in acquired knowledge, it is the form known directly. It may also mean that what the mind considers matches reality. In reality, each thing depends on God, so the intellect sees it that way. Being one with what is known also brings a kind of union with the known thing indirectly, since the essence appears in the mind and existence follows the same kind of existence.

    ↩

  744. This was explained earlier in the discussion of how things are brought into existence. A cause and effect share the same kind of existence: a cause of existence must itself be existence, and a cause of essence must be essence. Existence is primary in reality. If it were only an idea drawn from things, it could not belong to the highest reality. Knowing an effect that exists would then reveal its cause. If existence were only an idea, its reality would be the essence from which it is drawn.

    ↩

  745. This rule also applies to essence. We know an essence through the parts that make it what it is, such as its broad kind and distinguishing feature. These are causes that make up the essence, not causes that bring it into existence.

    ↩

  746. Particular existence is what removes nonexistence. It is the answer to both “what is it?” and “does it exist?”

    ↩

  747. Existence as existence does not change. Change belongs to the world as a set of objects, not to existence itself. God’s knowledge does not change.

    ↩

  748. Otherwise, there would be a third, independent cause that gives us knowledge of the effect apart from the cause that gives the effect its existence.

    ↩

  749. A relation is like a form, while its two sides are like the matter that receives it; both sides are needed before the relation can be known. This is still knowledge through the cause. A building displays the builder, and a book displays its author. As something received by matter, the building is an effect; as an expression of its maker, it reveals its cause first and itself second.

  750. For example, people may be certain that everyone dies, yet their certainty can fade if someone argues that a natural compound might last forever. Those who know the causes of decay—each compound’s parts tend toward their natural places, its powers are limited, and forced states do not last—cannot lose their certainty that natural compounds will break down. Anyone who says this is only knowledge from experience, not from causes, is mistaken. Experiments help the knower see the cause’s particular features.

    ↩

  751. The first claim—that knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect—is subtle; the second claim—that knowledge of an effect cannot reveal its particular cause—is even more subtle.

    ↩

  752. This is a list where one or more cases must apply, but they need not all apply. The three kinds of knowledge all occur in relation to the Necessary Being: knowing the concept, knowing the full reality, and knowing that it exists. The same three distinctions apply to existence.

    ↩

  753. God’s essence has no definition, but the meanings of His attributes can be defined and supported by proof.

    ↩

  754. This refers to the level of pure unity, to existence extended through all things, and to every essence and every limited existence. It also includes the ranks through which beings descend and rise.

    ↩

  755. The commentator says the author, who manifested God’s names of knowledge, wisdom, and power, knew that words could not express the answer. The question requires three principles. First, the existence of a cause makes up the existence of its effect: the effect’s appearance is contained in the cause’s appearance. Second, true bringing-into-existence is the real, all-pervading existence that flows from God; as explained earlier, this flow has one source. This existence, when related to God, is His act of bringing things into being; when related to created things, it is their existence. Third, God’s creative power has levels. The highest is His direct causation of the intellects; the intellects act through His power, and this power reaches down through the levels of nature. All are expressions of His power.

    With these points in view, a person’s reliable knowledge of themselves comes after reliable knowledge of their source, but only through the source’s illuminating presence and creative act. The cause’s existence makes up the effect’s existence. Knowledge works in the same way: knowledge of the source is its own existence, while knowledge of the self is the effect’s existence. Since the relation between source and effect is one of bringing into being, our knowledge of the source is its existence as it causes us. This knowledge comes before knowledge of ourselves, because the source brings us into being.

    The commentator adds a second answer: if knowing oneself is identical with one’s own existence, then God’s existence cannot remain beside it as a separate object of knowledge. Knowing God’s existence is His existence, just as knowing ourselves is our existence.

    He offers a third answer for a more ordinary reader. The claim “knowing ourselves is identical with our being” does not by itself prove that our knowledge is strong or certain; even an animal has immediate awareness of itself, and people who have forgotten God may still know themselves. Direct knowledge has levels: the soul as sensing, imagining, estimating, or thinking, and the simple intellect of a complete person. Knowledge of oneself through simple intellect is stronger than the ordinary forms of direct awareness. The author’s reply continues from the claim that God has no cause or definition to explain how a complete person can know God through the highest form of direct presence.

    ↩

  756. The main reason philosophers defend this account is to preserve the priority of knowledge: a freely chosen act must be preceded by knowledge and will. In the Illuminationist view, knowledge does not come before the act; it is the act itself. These philosophers seem to posit an intermediate realm between God’s simple, necessary existence and contingent beings: divine knowledge, containing the forms of all things, from the highest pearl to the smallest speck. These forms are grounded in God, not derived from things, so His knowledge is not passive. The Sufis describe a similar intermediate realm as the level of unity, the world of names and attributes and their fixed realities.

    ↩

  757. The author has already shown that God is necessary in every respect, including in His acts. His attributes must therefore also be necessary: He necessarily knows, has power, wills, and so on.

    ↩

  758. This raises two further problems: God would be moving toward greater perfection, and He would be affected by something outside Himself. Every accidental feature depends on a cause.

    ↩

  759. Natural kinds exist, and the universal nature exists in them, much as the continuous motion that traces a path exists through its successive parts. Creation first brings kinds into existence; they are originated directly and do not need an intermediary to connect them with the eternal.

    ↩

  760. “Eclipse” here means a lunar eclipse, as shown by the reference to the moon moving from it toward an opposite position.

    ↩

  761. Avicenna’s main concern is to show that God’s knowledge does not change with the changing existence of things, which would also make His knowledge follow rather than precede His acts. Nor does He know them through images taken from the things themselves, which would make His knowledge passive. He knows them through forms that flow from the principles and causes before the things arise. These forms are specified so that each one points to a single individual. Their role is like a mirror through which that individual is revealed. The individual is known as an individual, even though its form is intellectual. A thing may have many distinguishable features and still be one individual. The author has also said that a bodily form is known through an imagined or luminous intellectual form. These causal forms are far more complete than the things they cause and contain their perfections. Their presence in God therefore reveals the full particulars. Philosophers agree that God knows particulars, though they explain this in different ways. Avicenna’s point is not that particulars disappear from divine knowledge: intellectual knowledge does not rule out particularity. Since no concern distracts God from another, He knows each particular together with all others. The Aristotle’s followers aim to show that God’s knowledge is stable, prior, and active; they hold that this requires forms proceeding from the cause. The doctrine that the simple reality is all things in a higher way can explain this more fully, but the point remains that Avicenna did not deny any form of divine knowledge.

    ↩

  762. The passage seems to admit that the image in knowledge changes when a material particular changes, which would conflict with the claim that even sensory and imagined knowledge is immaterial. The commentator’s answer is that the images themselves do not change. What changes is their appearance to the soul, which depends on bodily acts such as seeing and hearing. When those acts stop, the image is no longer present to awareness, but the image itself remains; otherwise, we could not recall an earlier sensory image as the very one we once perceived. Knowing change, motion, or divisible quantity does not make knowledge itself change, move, or divide. A mental image must match the external thing in essence, not in its mode of existence.

    ↩

  763. The argument assumes that the direct object of knowledge is the same at both times, since the opponent treats the two acts of knowledge as one. Any difference would belong only to the indirect object—the day and night outside the mind. When night arrives, the knowledge must remain one if the claim is true. This restates the problem the argument is meant to expose.

    ↩

  764. This distinction may refer to individual motions of the outermost sphere, which mark time, and to other motions that occur in time. Strictly speaking, even the outermost sphere moves in time. The terms “in” and “with” can be used in different ways: time may be in motion as an accident is in its subject, while motion is in time as something measured is in its measure. The measured thing and its measure are linked. Something may also exist alongside time without motion, as philosophers say of bodily substances. Something “in time” is measured by the flow of the sphere’s motion. What has no motion is not in time by its nature, unless it exists only instantaneously.

    ↩

  765. The first kind is bodies; the second is bodily things or states.

    ↩

  766. “Position” here means the arrangement and relation of parts, as a category. The earlier sense is what allows something to be pointed out by the senses.

    ↩

  767. One might object that this philosopher considers space to be an immaterial dimension. If space is a surface, its material character is clear; if it is a dimension, it is material because it is the place occupied by matter. Or the point may simply be that anything tied to time and space is material.

    ↩

  768. The Illuminationists and this philosopher deny prime matter, but even those who accept it do not regard it as sheer nonexistence. The same is even clearer of bodily extension. When the author calls matter a source of absence, he means that it is not fully present to itself: each part is hidden from every other part, and the whole is not present to each part. But this is not absence in the strict sense, where a negative statement has no existing subject. Matter has an intermediate mode of existence, between nonexistence and a complete, unified existence. A bodily kind or natural form has a fuller existence than matter. Since these are all modes of existence, they are also kinds of knowledge by virtue of existence; they can be present to a knower. Existence, at every level, is light, whether dim or bright. Even a shadow is a kind of light mixed with darkness. At every level, an existent being is present to its source more fully than its existence is present to itself. That forms exist in matter does not prevent their presence to the all-encompassing source. Our knowledge, by contrast, depends on images because our relation of knowledge is not joined to the relation of bringing things into being.

  769. The commentator asks who claims that a sensible thing itself becomes intelligible: it remains sensible, though it is known without a bodily tool. A philosopher such as Suhrawardī, who says God is seeing and hearing and that His knowledge is presence rather than a form, should not hesitate to say that these particulars are directly perceived by God.

    ↩

  770. The philosopher does not mean a categorical relation, but an illuminating relation. The great philosophers say that contingent, changing things are possible and changing in themselves, yet necessary and perfectly stable in relation to God. As existences and manifestations of God, they are necessary and stable. Ancient thinkers also held that times and places are like a single instant or point when seen from higher principles, especially from the First Principle. They illustrate this with a colored thread stretched before a person while an ant walks along it. Dāmād says that successive events in time coexist in the container of eternity, like troops passing one after another through a mountain pass as seen by a person watching from above. To grasp this, compare seeing one white thing with imagining it, then with understanding “every white thing” and making a universal judgment about all of them. The intellect encompasses them all, each according to its capacity. The author says that disappearing from or being absent to some beings does not mean being absent to others. Things with positions are so only in relation to one another, not in relation to separate intellects. Although the author does not explicitly mention existence or its primacy here, elsewhere he rejects the view that knowledge is merely a relation and speaks of the “book of existence.” This shows that he treats existence as real.

  771. No one means that a material thing ceases to be material when considered by higher principles. Rather, relative to a separate intellect, matter is as if stripped of matter; likewise, place and time are as if stripped of place and time, because they are no longer hidden from the knower. The author elsewhere reports Dāmād’s warning not to mistake this kind of language for a denial of the material world.

  772. The example is not literally possible, since the outermost sphere does not truly surround everything. A better example would be a sight that extends through the greatest sphere and all within it, just as existence and necessity extend through everything. From that standpoint, nothing is near or far.

  773. This is general knowledge that includes detailed disclosure: each cause contains all the existences below it in a higher way. Individuality and distinction belong to existence, while the essences of these existences follow from it without being later in existence. More tentatively, the Aristotle’s followers may mean by forms in causes the existences of their effects enfolded within them.

  774. Anyone who says that all knowledge of other things is not limited to mental forms must accept that a cause knows its effect directly. How, then, can perception be limited to forms? Knowledge through a form is only needed when the knower is not the cause of what is known. Those who say all knowledge of other things is acquired knowledge through forms are the ones who must limit perception to forms.

  775. That applies to acquired knowledge. Direct knowledge depends on the cause’s mastery and its illuminating relation to the effect, as explained in the commentary on The Pointers. The forms that arise from a knower are known directly and do not need further forms to reveal them. Pure existence contains all that belongs to its kind and lacks what is alien to it; nonexistence is what is alien to existence. For the Illuminationists, a thing’s being light to itself and to others is the same kind of principle.

  776. “That exists” describes “form”; “to be” may be a complete verb or a linking verb, depending on the reading.

  777. That is, whatever way it is taken to exist, absent or present. The point is that material existence alone would be enough for a relation of knowledge; no mental form would be needed.

  778. If God’s relation of knowledge were not also a relation of bringing existence into being, He could not know Himself as the source of every existence. Knowing Himself would require knowing every existence before it occurs, so the relation of knowledge would be present before its object existed, while the creative relation would not yet be present. That is impossible. The divine realm of knowledge therefore includes both what already exists and what can exist.

  779. The knowing and acting powers are inseparable for two reasons. First, one cannot be lost while the other remains, unlike perception and movement in animals: sight may fail while movement remains, or the reverse. Second, the two human powers do not have separate bodily locations, unlike animal perception, mostly in the head, and movement, in the muscles.

  780. Some judgments need no learning, such as that justice is good and injustice bad. Others depend on custom or reasoning, such as whether killing animals is wrong. To decide to tell a particular truth, a person may reason: this is true; every truth is just; therefore this is just; every just thing is good; and every good thing should be done; so this truth should be told. The practical intellect does not directly carry out good acts. If action means ability, that is opposed to knowledge; if it means movement, it is an animal power, not an intellect. The practical intellect is a more distant source of action and a direct source of knowledge about how to act. It guides the powers of desire and movement. The Second Teacher, al-Fārābī, says that theoretical intellect lets a person know what they cannot do, while practical intellect lets them know what they can do by choice.

  781. The three senses differ in how far they are from one another. The first concerns a power to perceive, as with the potential theoretical intellect; the second concerns actual perception, as with intellect in act; and the third concerns action.

  782. This is a rhetorical argument: if even the lower level is called intellect, surely this higher one deserves the name.

    ↩

  783. “First principles” here means the basic starting points, as opposed to conclusions, not all self-evident truths.

    ↩

  784. Another reading, perhaps better, is that “intellect in habit” contrasts with a mere capacity or absence. The potential intellect is only a capacity; the second intellect already possesses first principles and their actuality. Avicenna discusses it in The Origin and Return.

  785. This means recognizing the Active Intellect through direct encounter, not merely learning about it. Direct knowledge is the highest kind, and seeing the forms within it cannot be separated from encountering it.

  786. “Intellect” may mean the soul itself, one of its levels, or one of its powers; in every case it is either a power or an act of knowing. Or it may be understood as one of the soul’s powers, just as the rational soul has theoretical and practical powers, and the animal soul has powers of perception and movement. The theoretical power itself has the four levels just listed.

  787. The potential intellect may be understood as a readiness close to completion—the intellect in habit—or as a readiness that still needs teaching and preparation, such as intuitive or sacred insight. The wording can also be read as “prepared,” in the passive sense.

  788. “All things” may mean everything in every realm, including the divine realm and the world of names and attributes, most of which has no matter. Or it may mean all things in the natural world.

  789. If we consider the existence of the forms, they are one form, because all exist through the one existence of the soul. If we consider their different essences, they are many forms.

  790. The word “intelligible” is derived from “intellect,” hinting that the knower and what is known are one. It is like calling two things “lover” and “beloved” from the same root, or calling something “ensouled” from the word “soul.”

  791. The comparison with lines or figures pressed into wax suggests that intelligibles extend through the whole subject, not just across its surface. In a note, the author says that the analogy may concern only shapes and arrangements on the body’s surface, since natural forms extend through the body’s depth. The point may be that the distinction between form and matter becomes less clear in intellectual things, and perhaps even in bodily things.

  793. The clearer reading would omit the word “not,” though it appears in the manuscripts.   794. The three descriptions refer to the same single meaning: the form understood may be called actual knower, actual intellect, or actual intelligible; the one who understands may likewise be called by any of these names. The same applies to the intellect itself.

  795. The features may be separable from the form in different instances or at different levels. Some, such as place and position, can vary by subject: the outermost sphere has no place in the usual sense, but it does have an order and position.   796. “Where” has levels: being somewhere in general, being in a particular country, being in a house within that country, and being in a particular room of that house. These all count as “where” in the ordinary sense, but the general concept of “where” is distinct from any one specific place.
